items.content: Back to Articles How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications Team Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 15 +9 Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows. Why Existing Solutions Fell Short Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations. They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. How We Solved It VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first. First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly. Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.30119 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: Self-normalized Bernstein Inequalities for Regenerative Processes and Applications to Learning Without Independence Authors: Imon Banerjee , Pierre Alquier View a PDF of the paper titled Self-normalized Bernstein Inequalities for Regenerative Processes and Applications to Learning Without Independence, by Imon Banerjee and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We prove a self-normalized Bernstein inequality for bounded functions of a regenerative process with independent, identically distributed marked cycles of finite mean length. The bound uses observed cycle lengths and retains explicit terms for truncation and the cycle ending after the observation horizon. Selecting a tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives a version of Bernstein inequality where all terms are empirical but one, related to the tails of the regeneration times. We then study this term in many regimes: it turns out that it is of second-order in many cases of interest. This is important for applications in machine learning: we prove generalization error bounds for classification with non-i.i.d., regenerative data. These bounds can be used to define learning objectives: by minimizing the first-order term only in the bound, we define agnostic classifiers that still satisfy oracle inequalities. We also show that the bound on the average deviation provided by our results is minimax-optimal in the sample size and in the expected regeneration time. Finally, we combine the Bernstein inequality with a regenerative strong approximation to obtain a Gaussian approximation using an observable block variance estimator. items.content: Self-normalized Bernstein Inequalities for Regenerative Processes and Applications to Learning Without Independence Imon Banerjee Note: The authors acknowledge they used AI when preparing this manuscript. AI was not used in the mathematical research. However, AI was used to double-check the results, and to help with polishing the writing of the paper. Affiliation: University of Chicago, Booth School of Business Pierre Alquier ∗ Note: This work was funded by CY Initiative, a programme supported the French government grant: “Investissements d’avenir” #France2030. Affiliation: ESSEC Business School, Asia-Pacific campus, Singapore Abstract We prove a self-normalized Bernstein inequality for bounded functions of a regenerative process with independent, identically distributed marked cycles of finite mean length. The bound uses observed cycle lengths and retains explicit terms for truncation and the cycle ending after the observation horizon. Selecting a tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives a version of Bernstein inequality where all terms are empirical but one, related to the tails of the regeneration times. We then study this term in many regimes: it turns out that it is of second-order in many cases of interest. This is important for applications in machine learning: we prove generalization error bounds for classification with non-i.i.d., regenerative data. These bounds can be used to define learning objectives: by minimizing the first-order term only in the bound, we define agnostic classifiers that still satisfy oracle inequalities. We also show that the bound on the average deviation provided by our results is minimax-optimal in the sample size and in the expected regeneration time. Finally, we combine the Bernstein inequality with a regenerative strong approximation to obtain a Gaussian approximation using an observable block variance estimator. Keywords: Regenerative processes; empirical Bernstein inequalities; PAC-Bayes bounds; Gaussian approximation. 1 Introduction Bernstein inequalities are fundamental tools in statistics and machine learning. By controlling deviations of empirical averages from their expectations through a variance term, they support confidence intervals, model selection and guarantees on the performance of learning algorithms [ 14 , 6 ] . To use such guarantees in practice, the quantities appearing in the bound must be available from the observations or specified in advance. A bound involving unknown features of the underlying distribution cannot be evaluated directly and may also be difficult to use as a learning criterion. This motivates empirical , or agnostic , bounds, which can be evaluated without knowing the data-generating distribution. For independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) bounded observations, empirical Bernstein inequalities replace the population variance with an observable estimate and an explicit correction [ 31 ] . These ideas also extend to PAC–Bayes guarantees for learning [ 45 ] . For time series, temporal dependence creates an additional obstacle. Classical extensions of Bernstein inequalities typically involve mixing coefficients or, for Markov chains, a spectral or pseudo-spectral gap [ 42 , 39 ] . These quantities describe the strength of dependence but are generally unknown, so the resulting bounds cannot be evaluated directly from a single observed trajectory. Although they provide useful rates, their dependence on unknown parameters limits their direct application to statistical inference and the design of learning criteria. Estimating these parameters is one possible response. Here, we develop bounds that use observed regeneration times to account for temporal dependence. In this case, the only non-empirical term is in many regimes a second-order term. In machine learning, we show that ignoring these terms lead to agnostic classification rules who satisfy strong oracle inequalities. We study bounded losses along a regenerative process. Regeneration divides a trajectory into cycles, allowing dependence within each cycle while providing independence between cycles. We assume that the marked cycles are i.i.d., have finite mean length and are independent of the initial delay. This framework includes regenerative Markov chains [ 11 ] as well as processes whose observations are not Markovian. Two features require care: (i) a bounded loss can have an unbounded cycle reward, and (ii) the number of completed cycles is random. We truncate the centred cycle rewards according to cycle length and construct an exponential supermartingale, which we stop at the first cycle ending after time n n . Removing that cycle yields the self-normalized Bernstein inequality in Theorem 3.1 . Selecting its tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives the empirical Bernstein bound in Corollary 3.1 . Its quadratic term is a sum of observed squared cycle lengths below the truncation level, common to all bounded losses. The bound also retains the observed contribution of longer cycles, a correction for the cycle crossing the observation horizon, and an explicit population tail expectation arising from truncation. Thus, the dependence on the cycle structure is expressed through observable quantities and a separate tail remainder, without estimating mixing coefficients or a spectral gap. The main application we have in mind is generalization error bounds in machine learning. Here, we use our version of Bernstein inequality to prove PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for classifiers learned on non-i.i.d., regenerative data. The associated Gibbs posterior satisfies oracle inequalities both in probability and in expectation. We then study the optimality of the scale of our bounds. Under a normalized moment condition of order greater than two on the cycle lengths, and starting at a regeneration time, we obtain a fixed-confidence estimation error of order m / n \sqrt{m/n} , where m m is the mean cycle length. For integer m m , a matching lower bound establishes the minimax optimality of this dependence in Theorem 6.1 . The effective number of independent observations is therefore of order n / m n/m in this comparison. Integrating the Bernstein inequality also gives expected deviation bounds, which we specialize under exponential and polynomial regeneration tails. Finally, we connect the concentration bounds to asymptotic inference. Under the moment and initialization assumptions used for the minimax analysis, for a fixed loss and regenerative law with positive asymptotic variance, we use the Bernstein inequality to control empirical centering in an observable block variance estimator. Combining this control with the regenerative strong approximation of Bashtova and Shashkin [10] yields a self-normalized Gaussian approximation and studentized asymptotic normality. The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Subsection 1.1 reviews the related literature, and Section 2 introduces the model and notation. Section 3 establishes the Bernstein and expected deviation bounds. While the first-order terms in these bounds are empirical, one of the second order terms is more problematic. In Section 4 , we control this term in various regimes. Section 5 presents the PAC-Bayes and oracle inequalities. In particular, we show that ignoring the problematic terms to define a learning objective does not affect the properties of machine learning algorithms. Section 6 shows that confidence intervals derived from our version of Bernstein inequality are minimax optimal. Section 7 studies the self-normalized Gaussian approximation. Sections 8 contains the proofs of all the results in the paper. 1.1 Background and Related Literature Concentration inequalities for regenerative processes use independence between cycles while allowing dependence within each cycle. We refer to the monograph by Bertail and Clémençon [11] for detailed literature survey of regenerative Markov chains. For a positive recurrent Markov chain with an accessible atom, Bertail and Clémençon [12] derive tail inequalities under finite second moments of the cycle lengths and centered rewards, with positive reward variance. Their bounds use truncated population moments and retain probabilities of long cycles and large rewards. Finally, [ 16 ] derive Rosenthal-type moment bounds and Bernstein-type inequalities for additive functionals of geometrically ergodic Markov chains, with leading terms governed by the asymptotic variance and explicit dependence on the mixing time in the remainder terms. Empirical-process results use regeneration to control a class of functions. For Markov chains with a stationary law, small-set minorization and exponential moment conditions on the initial and subsequent regeneration waiting times, Adamczak [2] proves concentration for bounded centered additive functionals. Under one-step minorization, they also control suprema over countable, uniformly bounded, centered classes, retaining their expected supremum and a population bound on the variances of cycle rewards. For positive Harris recurrent, aperiodic chains with one-step minorization, Bertail and Portier [13] develop block Rademacher complexity bounds for uniformly bounded VC classes. Their bounds combine a uniform second-moment bound for block rewards with either a cycle moment of order greater than one or an exponential cycle moment. When combined with [ 2 ] , this leads to novel Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz (DKW) type inequalities for exponentially regenerating Markov chains [ 7 , 8 ] . Concentration bounds can also retain random quantities from the trajectory. Under geometric drift, one-step minorization on Lyapunov sublevel sets, and well-defined conditional second moments, Wintenberger [46] proves an exponential inequality for path functionals satisfying a weighted bounded-difference condition. Its quadratic normalizer combines observed values of the Lyapunov function with transition-dependent conditional moments and coefficients. More directly, Jerison [24] gives a data-dependent Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality, uniform over thresholds of one real-valued observable. They assume i.i.d. regeneration cycles, initialization at regeneration, identifiable boundaries, and a known exponential bound on the tail of the cycle length. The leading term uses observed cycle lengths, while a correction retains the tail constants. The sample contains a deterministic number of cycles, so its observation horizon is random. The theory of generalization for machine learning algorithms was essentially developed for independent observations, see Mohri et al. [37] , Bach [6] for an introduction. However, there were notable attempts to extend some results to the setting of time series and stochastic processes, under various mixing and weak-dependence assumptions [ 50 , 20 , 34 , 44 , 38 , 36 , 44 , 43 , 28 , 29 , 33 , 30 , 1 ] . Unfortunately, while the theory in the i.i.d. case allows to define to distribution free, agnostic criteria for training and model selection, all the results in the dependent case require some prior knowledge on the strength of the temporal dependence. A class of generalization bounds known as PAC-Bayes bounds, introduced by [ 32 ] in the i.i.d. setting, which can be used both as criteria to optimize when training algorithms, and to derive powerful oracle inequalities [ 15 , 5 , 23 ] . PAC-Bayes bounds were also extended to beyond independent observations: Ralaivola et al. [40] , Fard et al. [19] , Alquier and Wintenberger [3] , Banerjee et al. [9] , Eringis et al. [18] . These results suffer the same limitation. This led to a trend in the recent literature, which aims at estimating the unknown mixing coefficients involved in these bounds [ 27 , 21 , 47 , 49 ] . For Markov chains, [ 48 , 26 ] studied the estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap (in the case of finite, and compact continuous state-space, respectively). Together with Paulin’s inequality [ 39 ] , this leads to agnostic deviation inequalities [ 25 , 26 ] . Our results go beyond these works in many ways. First, out bound holds for general regenerative process, including non-Markovian ones. Then, even in the Markov case with a discrete state-space, our results are not limited to a finite state-space as in [ 48 , 25 ] : they can accommodate countable infinite state-spaces. Finally, our inequalities do not require the estimation of any mixing coefficient or spectral gap, which makes them easier to use in practice. It might seems that a drawback of our approach is that only the first order terms in our inequalities are empirical. In other words, we can derive asymptotic empirical confidence intervals from our bounds, but the non-asymptotic coverage is lost. We point out that this is also the case in [ 26 ] . AI was not used in the mathematical research. However, AI was used to double-check the results, and to help with polishing the writing of the paper. Affiliation: University of Chicago, Booth School of Business Pierre Alquier ∗ Note: This work was funded by CY Initiative, a programme supported the French government grant: “Investissements d’avenir” #France2030. Affiliation: ESSEC Business School, Asia-Pacific campus, Singapore Abstract We prove a self-normalized Bernstein inequality for bounded functions of a regenerative process with independent, identically distributed marked cycles of finite mean length. The bound uses observed cycle lengths and retains explicit terms for truncation and the cycle ending after the observation horizon. Selecting a tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives a version of Bernstein inequality where all terms are empirical but one, related to the tails of the regeneration times. We then study this term in many regimes: it turns out that it is of second-order in many cases of interest. This is important for applications in machine learning: we prove generalization error bounds for classification with non-i.i.d., regenerative data. These bounds can be used to define learning objectives: by minimizing the first-order term only in the bound, we define agnostic classifiers that still satisfy oracle inequalities. We also show that the bound on the average deviation provided by our results is minimax-optimal in the sample size and in the expected regeneration time. Finally, we combine the Bernstein inequality with a regenerative strong approximation to obtain a Gaussian approximation using an observable block variance estimator. Keywords: Regenerative processes; empirical Bernstein inequalities; PAC-Bayes bounds; Gaussian approximation. 1 Introduction Bernstein inequalities are fundamental tools in statistics and machine learning. By controlling deviations of empirical averages from their expectations through a variance term, they support confidence intervals, model selection and guarantees on the performance of learning algorithms [ 14 , 6 ] . To use such guarantees in practice, the quantities appearing in the bound must be available from the observations or specified in advance. A bound involving unknown features of the underlying distribution cannot be evaluated directly and may also be difficult to use as a learning criterion. This motivates empirical , or agnostic , bounds, which can be evaluated without knowing the data-generating distribution. For independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) bounded observations, empirical Bernstein inequalities replace the population variance with an observable estimate and an explicit correction [ 31 ] . These ideas also extend to PAC–Bayes guarantees for learning [ 45 ] . For time series, temporal dependence creates an additional obstacle. Classical extensions of Bernstein inequalities typically involve mixing coefficients or, for Markov chains, a spectral or pseudo-spectral gap [ 42 , 39 ] . These quantities describe the strength of dependence but are generally unknown, so the resulting bounds cannot be evaluated directly from a single observed trajectory. Although they provide useful rates, their dependence on unknown parameters limits their direct application to statistical inference and the design of learning criteria. Estimating these parameters is one possible response. Here, we develop bounds that use observed regeneration times to account for temporal dependence. In this case, the only non-empirical term is in many regimes a second-order term. In machine learning, we show that ignoring these terms lead to agnostic classification rules who satisfy strong oracle inequalities. We study bounded losses along a regenerative process. Regeneration divides a trajectory into cycles, allowing dependence within each cycle while providing independence between cycles. We assume that the marked cycles are i.i.d., have finite mean length and are independent of the initial delay. This framework includes regenerative Markov chains [ 11 ] as well as processes whose observations are not Markovian. Two features require care: (i) a bounded loss can have an unbounded cycle reward, and (ii) the number of completed cycles is random. We truncate the centred cycle rewards according to cycle length and construct an exponential supermartingale, which we stop at the first cycle ending after time n n . Removing that cycle yields the self-normalized Bernstein inequality in Theorem 3.1 . Selecting its tuning parameter from a finite deterministic collection gives the empirical Bernstein bound in Corollary 3.1 . Its quadratic term is a sum of observed squared cycle lengths below the truncation level, common to all bounded losses. The bound also retains the observed contribution of longer cycles, a correction for the cycle crossing the observation horizon, and an explicit population tail expectation arising from truncation. Thus, the dependence on the cycle structure is expressed through observable quantities and a separate tail remainder, without estimating mixing coefficients or a spectral gap. The main application we have in mind is generalization error bounds in machine learning. Here, we use our version of Bernstein inequality to prove PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for classifiers learned on non-i.i.d., regenerative data. The associated Gibbs posterior satisfies oracle inequalities both in probability and in expectation. We then study the optimality of the scale of our bounds. Under a normalized moment condition of order greater than two on the cycle lengths, and starting at a regeneration time, we obtain a fixed-confidence estimation error of order m / n \sqrt{m/n} , where m m is the mean cycle length. For integer m m , a matching lower bound establishes the minimax optimality of this dependence in Theorem 6.1 . The effective number of independent observations is therefore of order n / m n/m in this comparison. Integrating the Bernstein inequality also gives expected deviation bounds, which we specialize under exponential and polynomial regeneration tails. Finally, we connect the concentration bounds to asymptotic inference. Under the moment and initialization assumptions used for the minimax analysis, for a fixed loss and regenerative law with positive asymptotic variance, we use the Bernstein inequality to control empirical centering in an observable block variance estimator. Combining this control with the regenerative strong approximation of Bashtova and Shashkin [10] yields a self-normalized Gaussian approximation and studentized asymptotic normality. The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Subsection 1.1 reviews the related literature, and Section 2 introduces the model and notation. Section 3 establishes the Bernstein and expected deviation bounds. While the first-order terms in these bounds are empirical, one of the second order terms is more problematic. In Section 4 , we control this term in various regimes. Section 5 presents the PAC-Bayes and oracle inequalities. In particular, we show that ignoring the problematic terms to define a learning objective does not affect the properties of machine learning algorithms. Section 6 shows that confidence intervals derived from our version of Bernstein inequality are minimax optimal. Section 7 studies the self-normalized Gaussian approximation. Sections 8 contains the proofs of all the results in the paper. 1.1 Background and Related Literature Concentration inequalities for regenerative processes use independence between cycles while allowing dependence within each cycle. We refer to the monograph by Bertail and Clémençon [11] for detailed literature survey of regenerative Markov chains. For a positive recurrent Markov chain with an accessible atom, Bertail and Clémençon [12] derive tail inequalities under finite second moments of the cycle lengths and centered rewards, with positive reward variance. Their bounds use truncated population moments and retain probabilities of long cycles and large rewards. Finally, [ 16 ] derive Rosenthal-type moment bounds and Bernstein-type inequalities for additive functionals of geometrically ergodic Markov chains, with leading terms governed by the asymptotic variance and explicit dependence on the mixing time in the remainder terms. Empirical-process results use regeneration to control a class of functions. For Markov chains with a stationary law, small-set minorization and exponential moment conditions on the initial and subsequent regeneration waiting times, Adamczak [2] proves concentration for bounded centered additive functionals. Under one-step minorization, they also control suprema over countable, uniformly bounded, centered classes, retaining their expected supremum and a population bound on the variances of cycle rewards. For positive Harris recurrent, aperiodic chains with one-step minorization, Bertail and Portier [13] develop block Rademacher complexity bounds for uniformly bounded VC classes. Their bounds combine a uniform second-moment bound for block rewards with either a cycle moment of order greater than one or an exponential cycle moment. When combined with [ 2 ] , this leads to novel Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz (DKW) type inequalities for exponentially regenerating Markov chains [ 7 , 8 ] . Concentration bounds can also retain random quantities from the trajectory. Under geometric drift, one-step minorization on Lyapunov sublevel sets, and well-defined conditional second moments, Wintenberger [46] proves an exponential inequality for path functionals satisfying a weighted bounded-difference condition. Its quadratic normalizer combines observed values of the Lyapunov function with transition-dependent conditional moments and coefficients. They assume i.i.d. regeneration cycles, initialization at regeneration, identifiable boundaries, and a known exponential bound on the tail of the cycle length. The leading term uses observed cycle lengths, while a correction retains the tail constants. The sample contains a deterministic number of cycles, so its observation horizon is random. The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks Francesco Mori Affiliation: Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Harvard University Melanie Weber Affiliation: Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Harvard University Affiliation: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University October 21, 2026 Abstract The success of convolutional neural networks is often attributed to locality and weight sharing. However, how these two properties separately shape learning, and how their effects depend on the spatial correlations of natural images, remain poorly understood. We address these questions in a teacher–student model with a convolutional teacher acting on P P input positions with correlation c c between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension D D . For uncorrelated positions ( c = 0 c=0 ), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly P P times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from 𝒪 D ​ ( D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D) samples, whereas 𝒪 D ​ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log D) samples are needed with a larger kernel. For c > 0 c>0 , spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with c c , whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of c c and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically. 1 Introduction The ability of neural networks to learn from a limited number of examples depends on their inductive biases, i.e., on the assumptions about the task that are built into the architecture and the training algorithm. A natural source of inductive bias is symmetry. When a task is invariant under a group of transformations of the input, a model that respects this invariance does not need to learn the same features separately for every transformed version of the input. Weight sharing is the standard way to build such symmetries into a network ( Shawe-Taylor, 1989 ; Cohen and Welling, 2016 ; Ravanbakhsh et al., 2017 ; Kondor and Trivedi, 2018 ) , and it is expected to reduce the number of samples needed to learn and to speed up training. The main success story of this approach is the convolutional neural network (CNN), widely used in image classification and other computer vision tasks ( LeCun et al., 1998 ; Krizhevsky et al., 2012 ) . CNNs exploit two structural properties of natural images, each encoded by a distinct architectural choice: Weight sharing across positions encodes the approximate invariance of image statistics under translations, while small filters encode the locality of the relevant features. Additionally, natural images are strongly correlated across space ( Ruderman and Bialek, 1994 ) , and the labels used for training are often noisy, resulting in a complex interplay between architectural constraints and the noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). From a theoretical perspective, building symmetries into a model is known to reduce the number of samples needed to learn, typically by a factor of the order of the size of the symmetry group ( Bietti et al., 2021 ; Mei et al., 2021 ; Tahmasebi and Jegelka, 2023 ; Elesedy and Zaidi, 2021 ; Lahoti et al., 2024 ; Waber et al., 2026 ) . However, disentangling the effects of locality and weight sharing remains a largely open challenge, especially in the feature-learning regime. Moreover, most analyses assume independent inputs, thereby neglecting the spatial correlations of natural images. It is therefore unclear to what extent the advantage of weight sharing survives in the presence of correlations and noise. In this work, we address these questions in a teacher–student model whose learning dynamics can be described exactly. The teacher is a two-layer convolutional network with kernel size k t k_{t} , acting on inputs made of P P positions that each carry D D features, with correlation c c between positions. We train convolutional and locally connected students with kernel size k s ≥ k t k_{s}\geq k_{t} by online SGD. The two students have the same receptive fields and differ only in weight sharing, while varying k s k_{s} probes the role of locality. In the limit of large feature dimension D D , the dynamics is described exactly by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for a few summary statistics, which extend the classical analysis of online learning in two-layer networks ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995 ; Goldt et al., 2019 ) . Contributions. Our main contribution is an exact description of how weight sharing and locality shape the online SGD dynamics of convolutional networks, which separates their effects. More precisely: • In the limit of large feature dimension D D and with Gaussian inputs, we derive analytically a closed set of ODEs for the summary statistics of convolutional and locally connected students, for arbitrary kernel sizes and input covariance (Result 3.1 ). • For uncorrelated positions, we show analytically that the locally connected network follows exactly the same training trajectory as the convolutional network, but needs exactly P P times more SGD steps (Result 3.2 ). This is an exact dynamical counterpart of the reduction in sample complexity by a factor of the order of the group size found in previous works. • By integrating the ODEs numerically, we find that locality affects the sample complexity of the problem. Indeed, a convolutional student with the right degree of locality, k s = k t k_{s}=k_{t} , learns the teacher from 𝒪 D ​ ( D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D) samples, while 𝒪 D ​ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log D) samples are required for k s > k t k_{s}>k_{t} (Result 3.3 ). The additional logarithmic factor originates from a saddle point that is symmetric under reflection of the kernel, which the dynamics escapes through the fluctuations of the random initialization. • We show that spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. With a perturbative expansion at small learning rate, we find that the asymptotic error of the convolutional network grows with the correlation strength c c , while that of the locally connected network is independent of c c and lower than that of the convolutional network for any c > 0 c>0 when evaluated at the same learning rate (Result 4.2 ). However, when the learning rate of each network is tuned to the training horizon, we find numerically that the locally connected network has the lower error at early times but the convolutional network wins at late times (Section 4.3 ), with a transition time that we predict analytically from an early-time expansion of the ODEs (Result 4.1 ). The code used in the paper is available at https://github.com/francescomori/CNN_theory . Outline. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model. Section 3 presents the ODEs and the effects of weight sharing and locality for uncorrelated positions. Section 4 studies the effect of spatial correlations, and Section 5 discusses limitations and future directions. Related works are discussed in Section 1.1 , and derivations and additional results are given in the appendices. 1.1 Related works Equivariant architectures. Weight sharing can be viewed as a mechanism for hard-coding symmetries into a learning architecture. Early work constructed neural networks with tied parameters to guarantee invariance under prescribed group actions ( Shawe-Taylor, 1989 ) . This perspective later gave rise to group-equivariant convolutional networks ( Cohen and Welling, 2016 ) , general parameter-sharing constructions for equivariant layers ( Ravanbakhsh et al., 2017 ) , and characterizations of convolution as the natural linear operation associated with equivariance under group actions ( Kondor and Trivedi, 2018 ) . Statistical benefits of symmetry. Another body of literature has quantified the statistical benefits of such symmetry constraints. Sannai et al. (2021) derived generalization bounds for invariant and equivariant networks using quotient feature spaces, while Bietti et al. (2021) showed that learning with invariant kernels reduces the number of samples by a factor asymptotically equal to the size of the symmetry group. Related sample-complexity gains were established for invariant random-feature and kernel models ( Mei et al., 2021 ) , kernel regression ( Tahmasebi and Jegelka, 2023 ) , and for equivariant linear models ( Elesedy and Zaidi, 2021 ) . At the same time, symmetry alone does not remove computational barriers: Kiani et al. (2024) established super-polynomial or exponential statistical-query lower bounds for learning several classes of equivariant models, including convolutional networks. Locality versus weight sharing. Several works studied the separate contributions of locality and weight sharing. In a teacher–student setting for kernel regression with convolutional kernels, Favero et al. (2021) found that locality determines the exponent of the learning curve, whereas translational invariance does not, and Cagnetta et al. (2023) extended this analysis to deep convolutional kernels. Wang and Wu (2023) compared convolutional, locally connected, and fully connected networks, and related the different sample complexities of the three architectures to the symmetries of the learning procedure. Lahoti et al. (2024) compared the same three architectures on inputs made of patches, with the signal planted in one of them, and found that the locally connected network needs more samples than the convolutional one by a factor of order the number of patches. Similarly, Li et al. (2021) showed that, on some tasks, fully connected networks trained by gradient descent need quadratically more samples than convolutional ones. Regarding optimization, d’Ascoli et al. (2019) found experimentally that the convolutional constraint mainly helps during the early stages of training, and Ingrosso and Goldt (2022) showed that localized filters can emerge in fully connected networks because of the non-Gaussian statistics of the inputs. Learning convolutional teachers. For Gaussian inputs with independent, non-overlapping patches, it was shown that gradient descent recovers a convolutional teacher in polynomial time ( Brutzkus and Globerson, 2017 ) , even when the loss has spurious local minima ( Du et al., 2018 ) . Goel et al. (2018) extended these results to overlapping patches and more general input distributions, using a gradient-like algorithm. The very recent work by Waber et al. (2026) studied online SGD in a convolutional teacher–student model with independent Gaussian inputs and a filter that extends over all patches, showing that weight sharing and data augmentation reduce the sample complexity by a factor equal to the number of patches, which is taken to be polynomial in the input dimension. In this work, we consider the roles of both weight sharing and locality, by considering a teacher of arbitrary kernel size and comparing convolutional and locally connected students whose kernel size can exceed that of the teacher. We also investigate how correlations across patches can reduce the advantage of weight sharing, both in the speed of convergence and in the asymptotic generalization error in the presence of label noise. Exact learning dynamics in high dimensions. Classical works ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995 ; Engel and Van den Broeck, 2001 ) described the dynamics of online learning in two-layer networks exactly in the high-dimensional limit, through ordinary differential equations for a few order parameters. These equations were used to explain the plateaus of the generalization error caused by the permutation symmetry of the hidden units ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ) , to predict the asymptotic error due to label noise ( Saad and Solla, 1997 ) , and to derive optimal learning-rate schedules ( Saad and Rattray, 1997 ) . More recent works made this approach rigorous ( Goldt et al., 2019 ; Ben Arous et al., 2022 ) and extended it to different learning regimes ( Veiga et al., 2022 ) , structured inputs ( Goldt et al., 2020 ) , and the design of optimal training protocols ( Mignacco and Mori, 2026 ) . Here, we extend this framework to convolutional and locally connected networks, which gives an exact description of their online SGD dynamics. This allows us to quantify how locality sets the number of samples needed to recover the teacher, when convolutional weight sharing accelerates learning relative to an otherwise matched locally connected architecture, and when correlations and noise can instead make the additional flexibility of the unshared model advantageous. 2 Setup and notation In this work, we study an exactly solvable teacher–student model in which the teacher is a convolutional network and the student is either convolutional or locally connected. Teacher–student models are a class of supervised learning settings in which the labels are generated by a fixed teacher network, which represents the ground truth to be recovered, while a student network is trained to reproduce the teacher’s output ( Gardner and Derrida, 1989 ; Engel and Van den Broeck, 2001 ) . When the input distribution is sufficiently simple, for instance Gaussian, the learning dynamics of these models can often be characterized exactly in the high-dimensional limit ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995 ; Goldt et al., 2019 ) . Our convolutional teacher also belongs to the broader class of multi-index models ( Ben Arous et al., 2021 ; Abbe et al., 2023 ; Arnaboldi et al., 2024 ; Bietti et al., 2023 ; Waber et al., 2026 ) . 2.1 Data structure We consider a supervised learning setting with inputs x x and labels y y . The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks Francesco Mori Affiliation: Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Harvard University Melanie Weber Affiliation: Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Harvard University Affiliation: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University October 21, 2026 Abstract The success of convolutional neural networks is often attributed to locality and weight sharing. However, how these two properties separately shape learning, and how their effects depend on the spatial correlations of natural images, remain poorly understood. We address these questions in a teacher–student model with a convolutional teacher acting on P P input positions with correlation c c between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension D D . For uncorrelated positions ( c = 0 c=0 ), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly P P times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from 𝒪 D ​ ( D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D) samples, whereas 𝒪 D ​ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log D) samples are needed with a larger kernel. For c > 0 c>0 , spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with c c , whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of c c and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically. 1 Introduction The ability of neural networks to learn from a limited number of examples depends on their inductive biases, i.e., on the assumptions about the task that are built into the architecture and the training algorithm. A natural source of inductive bias is symmetry. When a task is invariant under a group of transformations of the input, a model that respects this invariance does not need to learn the same features separately for every transformed version of the input. Weight sharing is the standard way to build such symmetries into a network ( Shawe-Taylor, 1989 ; Cohen and Welling, 2016 ; Ravanbakhsh et al., 2017 ; Kondor and Trivedi, 2018 ) , and it is expected to reduce the number of samples needed to learn and to speed up training. The main success story of this approach is the convolutional neural network (CNN), widely used in image classification and other computer vision tasks ( LeCun et al., 1998 ; Krizhevsky et al., 2012 ) . CNNs exploit two structural properties of natural images, each encoded by a distinct architectural choice: Weight sharing across positions encodes the approximate invariance of image statistics under translations, while small filters encode the locality of the relevant features. Additionally, natural images are strongly correlated across space ( Ruderman and Bialek, 1994 ) , and the labels used for training are often noisy, resulting in a complex interplay between architectural constraints and the noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). From a theoretical perspective, building symmetries into a model is known to reduce the number of samples needed to learn, typically by a factor of the order of the size of the symmetry group ( Bietti et al., 2021 ; Mei et al., 2021 ; Tahmasebi and Jegelka, 2023 ; Elesedy and Zaidi, 2021 ; Lahoti et al., 2024 ; Waber et al., 2026 ) . However, disentangling the effects of locality and weight sharing remains a largely open challenge, especially in the feature-learning regime. Moreover, most analyses assume independent inputs, thereby neglecting the spatial correlations of natural images. It is therefore unclear to what extent the advantage of weight sharing survives in the presence of correlations and noise. In this work, we address these questions in a teacher–student model whose learning dynamics can be described exactly. The teacher is a two-layer convolutional network with kernel size k t k_{t} , acting on inputs made of P P positions that each carry D D features, with correlation c c between positions. We train convolutional and locally connected students with kernel size k s ≥ k t k_{s}\geq k_{t} by online SGD. The two students have the same receptive fields and differ only in weight sharing, while varying k s k_{s} probes the role of locality. In the limit of large feature dimension D D , the dynamics is described exactly by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for a few summary statistics, which extend the classical analysis of online learning in two-layer networks ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995 ; Goldt et al., 2019 ) . Contributions. Our main contribution is an exact description of how weight sharing and locality shape the online SGD dynamics of convolutional networks, which separates their effects. More precisely: • In the limit of large feature dimension D D and with Gaussian inputs, we derive analytically a closed set of ODEs for the summary statistics of convolutional and locally connected students, for arbitrary kernel sizes and input covariance (Result 3.1 ). • For uncorrelated positions, we show analytically that the locally connected network follows exactly the same training trajectory as the convolutional network, but needs exactly P P times more SGD steps (Result 3.2 ). This is an exact dynamical counterpart of the reduction in sample complexity by a factor of the order of the group size found in previous works. • By integrating the ODEs numerically, we find that locality affects the sample complexity of the problem. Indeed, a convolutional student with the right degree of locality, k s = k t k_{s}=k_{t} , learns the teacher from 𝒪 D ​ ( D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D) samples, while 𝒪 D ​ ( D ​ log ⁡ D ) \mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log D) samples are required for k s > k t k_{s}>k_{t} (Result 3.3 ). The additional logarithmic factor originates from a saddle point that is symmetric under reflection of the kernel, which the dynamics escapes through the fluctuations of the random initialization. • We show that spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. With a perturbative expansion at small learning rate, we find that the asymptotic error of the convolutional network grows with the correlation strength c c , while that of the locally connected network is independent of c c and lower than that of the convolutional network for any c > 0 c>0 when evaluated at the same learning rate (Result 4.2 ). However, when the learning rate of each network is tuned to the training horizon, we find numerically that the locally connected network has the lower error at early times but the convolutional network wins at late times (Section 4.3 ), with a transition time that we predict analytically from an early-time expansion of the ODEs (Result 4.1 ). The code used in the paper is available at https://github.com/francescomori/CNN_theory . Outline. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model. Section 3 presents the ODEs and the effects of weight sharing and locality for uncorrelated positions. Section 4 studies the effect of spatial correlations, and Section 5 discusses limitations and future directions. Related works are discussed in Section 1.1 , and derivations and additional results are given in the appendices. 1.1 Related works Equivariant architectures. Weight sharing can be viewed as a mechanism for hard-coding symmetries into a learning architecture. Early work constructed neural networks with tied parameters to guarantee invariance under prescribed group actions ( Shawe-Taylor, 1989 ) . This perspective later gave rise to group-equivariant convolutional networks ( Cohen and Welling, 2016 ) , general parameter-sharing constructions for equivariant layers ( Ravanbakhsh et al., 2017 ) , and characterizations of convolution as the natural linear operation associated with equivariance under group actions ( Kondor and Trivedi, 2018 ) . Statistical benefits of symmetry. Another body of literature has quantified the statistical benefits of such symmetry constraints. Sannai et al. (2021) derived generalization bounds for invariant and equivariant networks using quotient feature spaces, while Bietti et al. (2021) showed that learning with invariant kernels reduces the number of samples by a factor asymptotically equal to the size of the symmetry group. Related sample-complexity gains were established for invariant random-feature and kernel models ( Mei et al., 2021 ) , kernel regression ( Tahmasebi and Jegelka, 2023 ) , and for equivariant linear models ( Elesedy and Zaidi, 2021 ) . At the same time, symmetry alone does not remove computational barriers: Kiani et al. (2024) established super-polynomial or exponential statistical-query lower bounds for learning several classes of equivariant models, including convolutional networks. Locality versus weight sharing. Several works studied the separate contributions of locality and weight sharing. In a teacher–student setting for kernel regression with convolutional kernels, Favero et al. (2021) found that locality determines the exponent of the learning curve, whereas translational invariance does not, and Cagnetta et al. (2023) extended this analysis to deep convolutional kernels. Wang and Wu (2023) compared convolutional, locally connected, and fully connected networks, and related the different sample complexities of the three architectures to the symmetries of the learning procedure. Lahoti et al. (2024) compared the same three architectures on inputs made of patches, with the signal planted in one of them, and found that the locally connected network needs more samples than the convolutional one by a factor of order the number of patches. Similarly, Li et al. (2021) showed that, on some tasks, fully connected networks trained by gradient descent need quadratically more samples than convolutional ones. Regarding optimization, d’Ascoli et al. (2019) found experimentally that the convolutional constraint mainly helps during the early stages of training, and Ingrosso and Goldt (2022) showed that localized filters can emerge in fully connected networks because of the non-Gaussian statistics of the inputs. Learning convolutional teachers. For Gaussian inputs with independent, non-overlapping patches, it was shown that gradient descent recovers a convolutional teacher in polynomial time ( Brutzkus and Globerson, 2017 ) , even when the loss has spurious local minima ( Du et al., 2018 ) . Goel et al. (2018) extended these results to overlapping patches and more general input distributions, using a gradient-like algorithm. The very recent work by Waber et al. (2026) studied online SGD in a convolutional teacher–student model with independent Gaussian inputs and a filter that extends over all patches, showing that weight sharing and data augmentation reduce the sample complexity by a factor equal to the number of patches, which is taken to be polynomial in the input dimension. In this work, we consider the roles of both weight sharing and locality, by considering a teacher of arbitrary kernel size and comparing convolutional and locally connected students whose kernel size can exceed that of the teacher. We also investigate how correlations across patches can reduce the advantage of weight sharing, both in the speed of convergence and in the asymptotic generalization error in the presence of label noise. Exact learning dynamics in high dimensions. Classical works ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995 ; Engel and Van den Broeck, 2001 ) described the dynamics of online learning in two-layer networks exactly in the high-dimensional limit, through ordinary differential equations for a few order parameters. These equations were used to explain the plateaus of the generalization error caused by the permutation symmetry of the hidden units ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ) , to predict the asymptotic error due to label noise ( Saad and Solla, 1997 ) , and to derive optimal learning-rate schedules ( Saad and Rattray, 1997 ) . More recent works made this approach rigorous ( Goldt et al., 2019 ; Ben Arous et al., 2022 ) and extended it to different learning regimes ( Veiga et al., 2022 ) , structured inputs ( Goldt et al., 2020 ) , and the design of optimal training protocols ( Mignacco and Mori, 2026 ) . Here, we extend this framework to convolutional and locally connected networks, which gives an exact description of their online SGD dynamics. This allows us to quantify how locality sets the number of samples needed to recover the teacher, when convolutional weight sharing accelerates learning relative to an otherwise matched locally connected architecture, and when correlations and noise can instead make the additional flexibility of the unshared model advantageous. 2 Setup and notation In this work, we study an exactly solvable teacher–student model in which the teacher is a convolutional network and the student is either convolutional or locally connected. Teacher–student models are a class of supervised learning settings in which the labels are generated by a fixed teacher network, which represents the ground truth to be recovered, while a student network is trained to reproduce the teacher’s output ( Gardner and Derrida, 1989 ; Engel and Van den Broeck, 2001 ) . When the input distribution is sufficiently simple, for instance Gaussian, the learning dynamics of these models can often be characterized exactly in the high-dimensional limit ( Saad and Solla, 1995 ; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995 ; Goldt et al., 2019 ) . Our convolutional teacher also belongs to the broader class of multi-index models ( Ben Arous et al., 2021 ; Abbe et al., 2023 ; Arnaboldi et al., 2024 ; Bietti et al., 2023 ; Waber et al., 2026 ) . 2.1 Data structure We consider a supervised learning setting with inputs x x and labels y y . items.content: Featured projects PyTorch users on AMD MI350-series GPUs can now use FlyDSL through existing operator APIs for dense and grouped GEMM, fused multi-head attention (FMHA/Attention), MXFP8/MXFP4 scaled GEMM, RMSNorm, and TopK, without requiring applications to call custom kernels. The optional backend supports GEMMs through torch.compile , while eligible RMSNorm and TopK calls dispatch automatically in eager mode when it is available and enabled. Unsupported inputs retain existing PyTorch implementations. FlyDSL attention kernels ship as an additional backend in AOTriton, the library behind PyTorch’s ROCm F.scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA), starting with the 0.14b series. Across the reported kernel-level operator suites, FlyDSL provides a 1.10x geometric-mean speedup for the 15-shape BF16 dense-GEMM suite over the faster of ATen and Triton at each shape, 1.58x and 1.68x geometric-mean speedups for MXFP8 and MXFP4, respectively, over ATen across 17 shapes per format, 1.20x geometric mean over Triton across all 24 grouped-GEMM cases, and 1.17x–3.66x over ATen across the 22 RMSNorm cases. For the 10 small-K TopK cases, the geometric mean is 4.82x over ATen with deterministic algorithms disabled. These gains are most relevant when the supported operations account for a significant share of model runtime. For attention, AOTriton 0.14.2b’s published gfx950 throughput ranges from 0.92x to 2.34x of 0.13b for forward and 0.93x to 2.47x for backward, across head dimensions and causal modes. In end-to-end vLLM A/B tests, whole-request speedup reaches 1.13x for BF16, 2.04x for MXFP8, and 3.01x for MXFP4, with the result depending on model and concurrency. Why FlyDSL as a PyTorch Backend GPU DSLs choose different abstraction levels. The block-tensor programming model in Triton lets authors describe program-level tiles while the compiler manages much of the thread, wave, and instruction mapping. FlyDSL makes those mappings explicit through layout algebra: kernel authors can partition tiles across blocks, waves, threads, and values; select tiled-copy and MFMA atoms; define LDS swizzles and staging; and place synchronization or compiler-scheduling boundaries. The two approaches are complementary. FlyDSL is useful for architecture-specific templates where data movement and instruction ownership are part of the algorithm. These controls appear directly in the kernels: HTI and staged LDS in Dense/MXFP GEMM, matched operand-scale lifetimes and scaled MFMA in MXFP, and persistent expert scheduling in Grouped GEMM. FlyDSL expresses them in Python and lowers them through MLIR while preserving explicit hardware mapping. Attention shows why this control matters. The FlyDSL attention kernels use a dual-wave software pipeline, which overlaps the softmax VALU work of one KV tile with the MFMA work of another. At the largest head dimensions, they also split the head dimension: in time through LDS, and across waves for the output accumulator. In FlyDSL, both schedules are written in the kernel itself, so they can be developed and tuned per architecture without changes to the compiler. PyTorch turns those specialized templates into an additive, measurable backend. Unsupported workloads retain existing implementations: Eager execution: eligible RMSNorm and TopK calls dispatch to FlyDSL when the optional runtime is installed and enabled; other calls retain ATen. torch.compile : TorchInductor filters eligible Dense, Grouped, and MXFP GEMM candidates, benchmarks FlyDSL beside ATen and Triton where supported, caches the winner for each workload, and runs the fastest measured kernel. Multi-head attention: PyTorch’s built-in operator F.scaled_dot_product_attention calls AOTriton, which now picks among FlyDSL, Triton, and AITER ASM kernels for each workload using its offline operator-tuning database. Figure 1. FlyDSL kernels reached through PyTorch APIs. Eager RMSNorm and TopK dispatch by input support; AOTriton selects a tuned SDPA implementation; and TorchInductor benchmarks eligible GEMM candidates. Supported Features Current support targets AMD MI350-series GPUs with the gfx950 architecture. The following features are available in PyTorch: Operation Mode PyTorch API Input dtype Layout / shape Output / options Dense GEMM Compile torch.mm FP16, BF16 Static 2D; NN/NT/TN/TT Same dtype MXFP scaled GEMM Compile F.scaled_mm MXFP8, MXFP4 Static 2D; A row-major, B column-major FP16/BF16; block scales Grouped GEMM Compile F.grouped_mm FP16, BF16 Ragged 2D A; grouped 3D B Uneven/empty groups RMSNorm Eager F.rms_norm FP16, BF16, FP32 Contiguous; 1-D norm shape Forward TopK Eager torch.topk FP32 Contiguous; last dimension Largest, sorted; functional/ out= Attention (via AOTriton) Eager, compile F.scaled_dot_product_attention FP16, BF16 D innermost; head dim 32–512 Forward and backward Dense GEMM’s four-layout support accepts row-major and column-major inputs, including eligible transpose views. In the layout names, the first letter describes A and the second describes B; N and T denote non-transposed and transposed input layouts. Grouped GEMM supports different row counts per group, allowing experts to process uneven token assignments. Its current input-layout requirements are separate from dense GEMM’s four-layout coverage. RMSNorm backward continues through PyTorch’s existing implementation. MXFP scaled GEMM accepts FP8 E4M3 or packed FP4 E2M1 operands, with one E8M0 scale per 32 values along the reduction dimension ( BlockWise1x32 ). Applications supply the quantized operands and contiguous, unswizzled scale tensors. Both formats use FP32 accumulation and return FP16 or BF16; the current path requires K to be a multiple of 128. It supports an optional one-dimensional bias whose length is N and whose dtype matches the output; fast accumulation is not supported. Under torch.compile , Inductor’s layout constraint runs before backend selection and requires unit stride along K for A and B—row-major A and column-major B—while preserving compatible leading strides. For incompatible inputs, Inductor inserts a layout copy. The FlyDSL MXFP kernel and the measurements below use these constrained layouts. This constraint is specific to scaled GEMM: Dense torch.mm detects eligible NN/NT/TN/TT strides and passes their layout flags to FlyDSL without applying the MXFP canonicalization. The FlyDSL attention kernels match the flash and memory-efficient attention capabilities of F.scaled_dot_product_attention , with one current limit: FP32 is not supported. The block-tensor programming model in Triton lets authors describe program-level tiles while the compiler manages much of the thread, wave, and instruction mapping.
