In a uniform shape G × M × K × N , G is the number of experts, M is the token count per expert, and K and N are the reduction and output dimensions: Uniform groups (14 cases): all experts use the same M , while G , M , K , and N vary across common grouped-GEMM shapes. Projection dimensions (five cases): G = 8 and M = 512 are fixed while K and N cover MoE up/down projections and a small- N case. Ragged expert loads (five cases): G = 8 and K = N = 4096 are fixed, while each label lists the eight per-expert M values, including empty and highly imbalanced experts. Across all 24 cases, FlyDSL reaches 1.20x geometric-mean speedup over Triton and 1.95x over ATen. Uniform groups reach 1.21x and 2.12x, respectively, with FlyDSL the fastest backend in 11 of 14 cases. The projection-dimension cases reach 1.23x and 1.73x; the ragged cases reach 1.15x and 1.73x, and FlyDSL wins all five. Figure 7. All 24 BF16 grouped-GEMM cases on gfx950, split into three panels. Each bar compares FlyDSL with the faster ATen/Triton result for that case; each panel ends with its geometric mean. The per-case view makes the shape sensitivity explicit: the projection sweep contains a small- N case where Triton is faster and a wide- N case tied with ATen, while all five ragged expert-load cases favor FlyDSL. RMSNorm: Gains Across Hidden Dimensions RMSNorm normalizes and scales activations, a repeated step in many transformer models. FlyDSL accelerates the forward operation while retaining the normal PyTorch API and backward behavior. The kernel assigns one thread block (CTA) to each row and chooses 256, 512, or 1024 threads from the normalized dimension, corresponding to 4, 8, or 16 Wave64s. It loads the vectorizable body with 128-bit copies, handles any remaining elements with a scalar tail, and keeps the loaded input in registers. FP32 sum-of-squares first reduces within each Wave64 using shuffle operations, then combines one partial per wave through a small LDS buffer. The resident values are reused to apply rsqrt and the weight and to return the rstd needed by backward. Figure 8. RMSNorm scheduling. One thread block loads a row into registers, produces 4/8/16 Wave64 partial sums depending on N, combines them through LDS, then reuses the resident values to write the normalized output and backward rstd . For the measured aligned hidden dimensions, speedups over ATen are approximately 1.2x–1.5x. Dimensions one element above an aligned size—for example, 4097 rather than 4096 —show larger gains, reaching 3.66x. Figure 9. All 22 reported RMSNorm cases on MI355X. Labels identify dtype and M × N, where M is the row count and N the normalized dimension. Both panels use the same speedup scale. The split between aligned and off-by-one dimensions shows why the input shape matters when interpreting the peak result. The 3.66x speedup applies to a particular FP16 case; gains on aligned dimensions are more modest. TopK: Faster Selection for Small and Large K TopK selects the highest-scoring elements from each row. The amount of output requested changes the workload: selecting a handful of elements is different from selecting hundreds. FlyDSL provides specialized paths for these regimes. For small fixed K, a gfx950 CTA contains two Wave64s and processes two rows—one wave per row. Each lane reads 128-bit chunks, bitonic-sorts one group at a time, and folds each group into a register-resident local top-K. Butterfly shuffles then merge those candidates across the wave, and lane 0 writes the final K pairs. For larger K, four 8-bit radix passes find the K-th threshold, gather only the surviving candidates, and bitonic-sort a buffer rounded from K to the next power of two instead of sorting the full row. Here, “determinism on” means torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) . The radix path then uses prefix-sum slots to preserve finite-value tie order; with determinism off it uses atomic slot allocation, so equal-value indices can vary. The register kernel itself is reproducible in both modes, although its tie ordering can differ from ATen. NaNs are canonicalized to one ordinal, so exact NaN payload and index selection can differ from ATen even in deterministic mode. Figure 10. TopK scheduling. The register path processes two rows per CTA with one Wave64 per row, then butterfly-merges local top-K candidates. The radix path uses one CTA per row and four byte passes to identify a threshold before sorting only the surviving candidates. For small K = {2, 4, 8, 16} , FlyDSL achieves a 4.82x geometric-mean speedup over ATen with deterministic algorithms disabled, and 4.02x with them enabled. For the larger sampled K bands, the geometric-mean speedup ranges from 1.40x to 1.97x. Figure 11. FP32 TopK on MI355X, compared with ATen under the same determinism setting. The bars aggregate all 33 reported cases by kernel family and K band. The small-K register path shows the largest average gain. The radix-select paths extend the benefit to larger K ranges, although some individual cases are near parity. For applications that inspect indices, equal-value ties can be ordered differently across backends; reproducibility does not guarantee identical tied indices. Attention: FMHA Kernels Through AOTriton Unlike the operators above, SDPA does not reach FlyDSL through a PyTorch-side backend. AOTriton compiles FlyDSL kernels into its own library, then dispatches them beside its Triton and AITER ASM kernels. Forward is one kernel; backward uses separate dQ and dK/dV kernels. For head dimensions up to 256, the forward kernel uses a dual-wave software pipeline. Two KV tiles are in flight per workgroup, and the softmax of one tile runs on the VALU while the other tile’s QK and PV products run on the MFMA units. At head dimension 512, two resident K/V tiles would need about 272 KB of LDS against the 160 KB limit, so a separate wide-head body processes one tile at a time. It splits the head dimension twice: in time, by staging K and V in pipelined D slices through the same LDS buffers, and across waves, with each wave accumulating one slice of the output so the accumulator fits in registers. Backward reuses the forward building blocks rather than deriving new lane maps. dK/dV is the forward loop transposed: K and V stay in registers while Q and dO stream through LDS, and the transposed operands use the forward’s LDS transpose read ( ds_read_b64_tr_b16 ). In dQ, each of the three GEMMs matches one the forward already emits. The K tile is staged once and read in both orientations, which keeps head dimension 512 within LDS. Figure 12. Dual-wave forward pipeline for head dimensions up to 256. Within a wave, each matrix-core step overlaps the softmax of a neighbouring KV tile; across the workgroup, two wave groups run one phase apart, so one group loads K and V while the other computes. Figure 13. Wide-head forward body at head dimension 512. K and V are staged through two LDS buffers in halves of 256 columns, and two waves compute the same scores while each accumulates half of the output. The AOTriton 0.14.2b release publishes throughput for AOTriton 0.13b and 0.14.2b by head dimension, direction, and causal mode. For the gfx950 aggregates shown below, forward speedup ranges from 0.92x to 2.34x and backward speedup from 0.93x to 2.47x. Figure 14. AOTriton 0.14.2b versus 0.13b on gfx950 , using the published throughput aggregates for each head dimension. This release-to-release comparison also includes updated Triton, AITER, and tuning databases, so it is not an isolated FlyDSL-versus-Triton measurement. End-to-End vLLM Inference We used vllm bench serve on one MI355X ( TP=1 ) with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. Each request has a 256-token input and fixed 512-token output; concurrency ranges from 8 to 256. The baseline and treatment use the same serving configuration and per-model KV cache, with only the Inductor GEMM candidate list changed. The figure reports whole-request speedup. BF16. Adding FlyDSL to the ATen/Triton baseline produces the clearest gains for Llama-3.1-8B at low-to-medium concurrency, peaking at 1.13x; Qwen3-32B peaks at 1.06x, while Llama-3.3-70B remains mostly within the 1.79% measured noise floor. The BF16 results report medians from at least two ABBA-interleaved repetitions. Figure 15. BF16 whole-request speedup on one MI355X. The baseline enables ATen and Triton; the treatment adds FlyDSL. Values above 1x favor FlyDSL. MXFP8 A8W8. With ATen (hipBLASLt) as the baseline, FlyDSL improves all 18 model-concurrency combinations: 1.40x–2.03x for Qwen3-32B, 1.04x–1.92x for Llama-3.1-8B, and 1.38x–2.04x for Llama-3.3-70B. Figure 16. MXFP8 A8W8 whole-request speedup on one MI355X. The baseline is ATen; the treatment adds FlyDSL. Values above 1x favor FlyDSL. MXFP4 A4W4. With lm_head left unquantized, all 18 combinations also improve: 1.53x–3.01x for Qwen3-32B, 1.25x–1.85x for Llama-3.1-8B, and 1.50x–2.82x for Llama-3.3-70B. MXFP8 and MXFP4 each have one measured run per cell, so small differences should not be treated as variance-qualified results. Figure 17. MXFP4 A4W4 whole-request speedup on one MI355X. The baseline is ATen; the treatment adds FlyDSL. Values above 1x favor FlyDSL. Try It in PyTorch Use a recent ROCm PyTorch nightly for MI350-series GPUs. This article assumes that it already contains all the FlyDSL integrations described above, including MXFP scaled GEMM. Then install an optional runtime from the supported 0.3.x series: python -m pip install --upgrade "flydsl>=0.3.0,<0.4" The examples below require a gfx950 GPU; ROCm builds use PyTorch’s "cuda" device string. Dense and Grouped GEMM Enable FlyDSL as a candidate and let torch.compile select the implementation: import torch i

items.content: What will our economic future look like? We don’t know yet how AI will reshape the economy. Will it lead to unprecedented growth? Widespread unemployment? Neither, or something else? How can we tell? Anthropic’s Economics team built a model of how AI might affect jobs, growth, and unemployment in the US in coming years. Read about possible economic futures and make your own predictions about AI capabilities to see the economy they imply. Read technical report Jump to explorer Read blog W e study how AI is reshaping the economy because we’re committed to ensuring that this transition is beneficial for society, including workers. By providing better visibility into our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure that everyone benefits from it. While our Economic Index measures how AI is being used across the economy right now, this scenario explorer is about looking ahead. Based on our technical report, Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI (Korinek et al., 2026), this explorer gives you a chance to find out what the economy might look like as AI continues to get more capable. In scenarios ranging from business as usual to an economy where AI increases growth to about twice the normal rate, unemployment stays within the historical range and wages remain flat or rise depending on the industry. But in scenarios where growth is faster than anything in economic history, there are adverse impacts on wages and job prospects for knowledge workers. In those scenarios, society is far wealthier, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are broadly shared. As you scroll down, you’ll see an overview of how AI affects the economy. Then, you can plug in your expectations for how capable AI will be, and how extensively it will be used across the economy in the future. The model will show you what the economy in 2030 might look like if your predictions come true—and how your predictions compare to others. A nurse ’s tasks Tasks unchanged by AI Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI The economy is made out of tasks This model represents all the jobs people do in the economy as bundles of tasks. AI can help people do a given task better or faster. It can automate the task. It might not affect the task at all. And it can lead to new tasks. Think of a day in the life of a nurse You can think of any job as a bundle of tasks that someone does. She does rounds to check on a sick patient. She draws blood. She triages incoming patients, charts patients’ vitals, and orders supplies for the ward. That’s just the start of the list. Each of the tasks listed are based on the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy, listing the tasks for each occupation. Jobs change over time Tasks leave the bundle ( hardly anyone hand-writes paper charts anymore ) and new tasks arrive ( 30 years ago, no one monitored patients remotely ). The bundle of tasks isn’t static, and the job changes as tasks change. Only humans can do some tasks For instance, AI can’t bathe a patient. Some tasks will get augmented AI helps a human do them better, or faster. AI helps the nurse draft discharge instructions, monitor patients remotely, and plan the shift’s care schedule. Some tasks may get fully automated For instance, AI may chart a patient’s vitals, or order the ward’s supplies. And new tasks will appear Historically, new technologies have also created new tasks for workers. For a nurse, that might be checking how well an AI triages patients, or reviewing an AI-proposed care plan. The result: the nurse ’s job changes As the nurse incorporates AI into her job, the nurse is able to oversee and accomplish more. She can spend more time talking with patients and helping them understand diagnoses. Productivity increases. Every task happens millions of times every day, across the country Nurses are doing their work on every ward and on every shift. As more nurses use AI, AI supports a higher percentage of these millions of instances of each task. From tasks to the economy Today, if you add up every single instance of tasks performed in the US, by people and by the machines and software they work with, you get the US economy: over $30 trillion of value created over the past year. So how will AI shape the economy of the future? The answer depends on how AI affects all the tasks that make up the economy, the new tasks it creates, and how fast AI takes on this work. Will AI lead to more task augmentation or automation? How much more productive will it make us? How quickly will it be adopted by workers and companies? The answers to these questions have direct effects on GDP, the labor market, and the share of the pie taken home by workers. There are many possible futures, but we’re highlighting three scenarios The future will depend on how AI’s capabilities advance, and how industries and workers adopt those capabilities. The three scenarios we share capture distinct kinds of impact. In the modest scenario , it’s hard to see the effect of AI in macroeconomic data: its economic impact is something like the internet’s. In the substantial scenario , AI makes a bigger impact than the internet, or the railroad. And in the extreme scenario , AI drives a completely transformed, unprecedented economy, likely driven by recursively self-improving AI systems and a faster rate of AI adoption. Small economic gains In the modest scenario , AI has roughly the same kind of impact as the internet did. It drives real economic gains, but they’re within the historical norm for new technologies, and they arrive gradually. A revolution in knowledge work In the substantial scenario , AI is capable of doing half of all knowledge work by 2030, the majority of it autonomously, but it’s not adopted for all of that work: most knowledge work tasks are still done without AI. The economy grows at twice its normal rate. Wages for knowledge workers don’t rise, but other workers see gains. A profound economic transformation In the extreme scenario , AI is more productive than humans at the vast majority of knowledge-work tasks. It does nearly all of them autonomously, and it creates essentially no new knowledge tasks for people. This scenario would likely require recursively self-improving AI, adopted quickly for knowledge work. As AI diffuses, annual GDP growth rates reach 15 % a year, leading the economy to double in size every 4.5 years. As a society, we’re far richer than we’ve ever been, but many fewer workers have jobs in knowledge work, and unemployment has risen beyond typical recessionary levels. How might powerful AI change the economy? How do you think AI development will go over the next few years? And what would that path mean for the economy? We invite you to consider these questions, and explore potential answers with our scenario explorer. Make your predictions Skip to the scenarios People’s expectations about future AI capabilities vary. In August, we surveyed more than 10,000 Americans about their views on present and future AI capabilities, adoption, and the ease of finding new work if they have to change occupations. The typical respondent’s answers imply outcomes close to the “substantial change” scenario: GDP is 10% higher by 2030 than it would be without AI, and the overall unemployment rate has risen to around 5%. Around 10% of respondents have views in line with the extreme scenario. How people answered the five questions (share of respondents at each answers) Capabilities What tasks can AI do? 0% 100% Adoption How much do people use AI? 0% 100% Autonomy How much does AI do by itself? Almost none Some of them About half Most of them Almost all of them Productivity How much more productive does AI make people? Same 1.5× 2× 4× 10×+ Adjustment How long does it take people to find a new job? 1–2 months ~3 months ~6 months ~9 months A year 2 years 3+ years or never General public n = 10,980 Site visitors n = 32,559 You predicted one possible future for the economy. Here’s what that future could look like. Finding 1: GDP growth AI grows the economy in every scenario, but some more than others AI drives GDP growth in all scenarios, although the scale varies enormously depending on the scenario. US GDP in 2030, by scenario (measured in trillions of dollars)* Modest scenario +1.6% $34.1T GDP Substantial scenario +8.3% $36.3T GDP Extreme scenario +32.4% $44.4T GDP Task types Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI Productivity *GDP is calculated at 2025 price levels But growth isn’t the only economic dynamic we care about. What would these potential futures mean for how much of this growth workers receive in their paychecks, or how many people have to find new jobs? This model isn’t a complete map of reality, but it shows us some interesting findings. The country’s GDP will grow, but a larger share of that prosperity might go to the resources and technology used to create more wealth (capital) compared to workers, even if society as a whole is much wealthier. And in most scenarios, job reallocation and unemployment both stay within ranges history has seen before, with one exception. In the extreme scenario, if we see recursive self-improvement and rapid adoption, unemployment could spike to historic levels. Finding 2: Job reallocation In more transformative scenarios, more workers have to change occupations. That may mean higher unemployment. There is always some churn in the job market—people losing jobs and finding new ones. In normal times, this process can be painful, but works relatively well from a macroeconomic perspective. Most job seekers find new jobs fairly quickly. In our substantial and extreme scenarios, knowledge workers may see a lot of automation and displacement. At the individual level, it means coders and call service center agents may have to switch to jobs like electrician and nurse, which are less exposed to AI. But changing occupations entirely is hard, and it takes many people a long time to land a new job. The more of this switching a scenario requires, the more people will be between jobs. Where workers are in 2030 (percent of all workers) Modest Substantial Extreme 2026 2030 62.2% Knowledge workers 37.8% All other workers 2.5% Displaced 1.8% Crossed over 59.7% Still there 39.6% All other workers 0.7% Still need to move Knowledge workers All other workers Displaced As we progress from 2026 to 2030, the number of jobs available in occupations AI affects (knowledge work) decreases, while the jobs available in occupations AI doesn’t affect increase. Switching to a new occupation is difficult for a few reasons: workers may not want to change occupations. They may need to learn new skills. And even when they do, it’s not easy to get a new job. In the extreme scenario, as large swathes of knowledge work are automated more quickly, affected workers may be unemployed for a prolonged period. Unemployment in knowledge work rises; in other occupations, it falls modest scenario substantial scenario extreme scenario Knowledge workers All other workers Total Finding 3: Wages Across the three scenarios, average wages rise, but this increase is concentrated in occupations outside of knowledge work. That’s because it takes time for workers to switch to occupations where demand is rising. If there’s less demand for human knowledge work, that puts downward pressure on wages. Meanwhile, as AI increases productivity within knowledge work, the demand for manual work that benefits from that productivity will increase. For example, more quickly producing designs and permitting for physical infrastructure could increase the number of construction projects, resulting in rising demand for construction workers, which pushes those wages higher. In the substantial scenario, wages for knowledge workers are essentially flat. In the extreme scenario, they fall by more than 10% by 2030. Pay by occupation group, percent above the same economy without AI modest scenario substantial scenario extreme scenario Knowledge workers All other workers Average Finding 4: Labor vs. capital share The pie will grow, but a larger share might go to capital Today, of each dollar the economy produces, about 60 ¢ goes to workers and 40 ¢ go to capital. If the economy grows, but AI automates more tasks, more of each dollar might go to capital. This can happen even when wages for all workers rise substantially. If capital becomes more useful for more things, it will be in higher demand, which raises its price. In that world, more of the gains from a growing economy flow to owners of capital. We find that the labor share falls noticeably in the substantial and extreme scenarios, and the capital share rises. items.raw_text: What will our economic future look like? We don’t know yet how AI will reshape the economy. Will it lead to unprecedented growth? Widespread unemployment? Neither, or something else? How can we tell? Anthropic’s Economics team built a model of how AI might affect jobs, growth, and unemployment in the US in coming years. Read about possible economic futures and make your own predictions about AI capabilities to see the economy they imply. Read technical report Jump to explorer Read blog W e study how AI is reshaping the economy because we’re committed to ensuring that this transition is beneficial for society, including workers. By providing better visibility into our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure that everyone benefits from it. While our Economic Index measures how AI is being used across the economy right now, this scenario explorer is about looking ahead. Based on our technical report, Economic Scenarios for Transformative AI (Korinek et al., 2026), this explorer gives you a chance to find out what the economy might look like as AI continues to get more capable. In scenarios ranging from business as usual to an economy where AI increases growth to about twice the normal rate, unemployment stays within the historical range and wages remain flat or rise depending on the industry. But in scenarios where growth is faster than anything in economic history, there are adverse impacts on wages and job prospects for knowledge workers. In those scenarios, society is far wealthier, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are broadly shared. As you scroll down, you’ll see an overview of how AI affects the economy. Then, you can plug in your expectations for how capable AI will be, and how extensively it will be used across the economy in the future. The model will show you what the economy in 2030 might look like if your predictions come true—and how your predictions compare to others. A nurse ’s tasks Tasks unchanged by AI Tasks augmented Tasks automated New tasks created by AI The economy is made out of tasks This model represents all the jobs people do in the economy as bundles of tasks. AI can help people do a given task better or faster. It can automate the task. It might not affect the task at all. And it can lead to new tasks. Think of a day in the life of a nurse You can think of any job as a bundle of tasks that someone does. She does rounds to check on a sick patient. She draws blood. She triages incoming patients, charts patients’ vitals, and orders supplies for the ward. That’s just the start of the list. Each of the tasks listed are based on the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy, listing the tasks for each occupation. Jobs change over time Tasks leave the bundle ( hardly anyone hand-writes paper charts anymore ) and new tasks arrive ( 30 years ago, no one monitored patients remotely ). The bundle of tasks isn’t static, and the job changes as tasks change. Only humans can do some tasks For instance, AI can’t bathe a patient. Some tasks will get augmented AI helps a human do them better, or faster. AI helps the nurse draft discharge instructions, monitor patients remotely, and plan the shift’s care schedule. Some tasks may get fully automated For instance, AI may chart a patient’s vitals, or order the ward’s supplies. And new tasks will appear Historically, new technologies have also created new tasks for workers. For a nurse, that might be checking how well an AI triages patients, or reviewing an AI-proposed care plan. The result: the nurse ’s job changes As the nurse incorporates AI into her job, the nurse is able to oversee and accomplish more. She can spend more time talking with patients and helping them understand diagnoses. Productivity increases. Every task happens millions of times every day, across the country Nurses are doing their work on every ward and on every shift. As more nurses use AI, AI supports a higher percentage of these millions of instances of each task. From tasks to the economy Today, if you add up every single instance of tasks performed in the US, by people and by the machines and software they work with, you get the US economy: over $30 trillion of value created over the past year. So how will AI shape the economy of the future? The answer depends on how AI affects all the tasks that make up the economy, the new tasks it creates, and how fast AI takes on this work. Will AI lead to more task augmentation or automation? How much more productive will it make us? How quickly will it be adopted by workers and companies? The answers to these questions have direct effects on GDP, the labor market, and the share of the pie taken home by workers. There are many possible futures, but we’re highlighting three scenarios The future will depend on how AI’s capabilities advance, and how industries and workers adopt those capabilities. The three scenarios we share capture distinct kinds of impact. In the modest scenario , it’s hard to see the effect of AI in macroeconomic data: its economic impact is something like the internet’s. In the substantial scenario , AI makes a bigger impact than the internet, or the railroad. And in the extreme scenario , AI drives a completely transformed, unprecedented economy, likely driven by recursively self-improving AI systems and a faster rate of AI adoption. Small economic gains In the modest scenario , AI has roughly the same kind of impact as the internet did. It drives real economic gains, but they’re within the historical norm for new technologies, and they arrive gradually. A revolution in knowledge work In the substantial scenario , AI is capable of doing half of all knowledge work by 2030, the majority of it autonomously, but it’s not adopted for all of that work: most knowledge work tasks are still done without AI. The economy grows at twice its normal rate. Wages for knowledge workers don’t rise, but other workers see gains. A profound economic transformation In the extreme scenario , AI is more productive than humans at the vast majority of knowledge-work tasks. It does nearly all of them autonomously, and it creates essentially no new knowledge tasks for people. This scenario would likely require recursively self-improving AI, adopted quickly for knowledge work. As AI diffuses, annual GDP growth rates reach 15 % a year, leading the economy to double in size every 4.5 years. As a society, we’re far richer than we’ve ever been, but many fewer workers have jobs in knowledge work, and unemployment has risen beyond typical recessionary levels. How might powerful AI change the economy? How do you think AI development will go over the next few years? And what would that path mean for the economy? We invite you to consider these questions, and explore potential answers with our scenario explorer. Make your predictions Skip to the scenarios People’s expectations about future AI capabilities vary. In August, we surveyed more than 10,000 Americans about their views on present and future AI capabilities, adoption, and the ease of finding new work if they have to change occupations. The typical respondent’s answers imply outcomes close to the “substantial change” scenario: GDP is 10% higher by 2030 than it would be without AI, and the overall unemployment rate has risen to around 5%. Around 10% of respondents have views in line with the extreme scenario. Almost none Some of them About half Most of them Almost all of them Productivity How much more productive does AI make people? Same 1.5× 2× 4× 10×+ Adjustment How long does it take people to find a new job? 1–2 months ~3 months ~6 months ~9 months A year 2 years 3+ years or never General public n = 10,980 Site visitors n = 32,559 You predicted one possible future for the economy. Switching to a new occupation is difficult for a few reasons: workers may not want to change occupations. They may need to learn new skills. And even when they do, it’s not easy to get a new job. items.content: NVIDIA and Supply Chain Partners Expand Capacity to Accelerate AI Infrastructure Buildout New Capacity Agreements and Manufacturing Facilities to Support Volume Growth and Strengthen Supply Chain Resiliency October 21, 2026 News Summary: Substrate agreements with IBIDEN, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Unimicron Technology Corporation will, in aggregate, drive a 2.5x increase in capacity over the next three years. Amkor plans to increase its advanced packaging capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028. KYEC will build new facilities in the U.S., supported by a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance from NVIDIA. SPIL is targeting to increase its optical-engine capacity for co-packaged optics by 15x by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. GTC Berlin— NVIDIA today announced plans with a group of supply chain partners to expand global manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and full-stack AI factory platform. Working with Amkor Technology, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology Corporation, NVIDIA is enabling new and existing suppliers to expand critical manufacturing capabilities across substrates, advanced packaging, testing and optical engines, strengthening the resiliency and redundancy of NVIDIA’s global supply chain. “We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Our supply chain partners are the world’s best manufacturers. I’m grateful they are expanding capacity around the globe to scale production and help us deliver the AI supercomputing systems powering this new industrial revolution.” Expanding Substrate Capacity to Support Volume Growth NVIDIA plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. The agreements below will contribute to this capacity expansion, with more underway. Under an agreement signed and announced earlier this year by IBIDEN, NVIDIA is providing a multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to support IBIDEN’s Ono Plant in Japan. The expansion targets capacity reaching 3x current levels at the plant, with additional capacity expected to begin ramping in the first quarter of 2028. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is joining NVIDIA’s substrate supply chain, bringing immediate capacity from its existing operations in South Korea. The collaboration also supports facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan, South Korea. By 2028, production allocated to NVIDIA is projected to account for a significant portion of Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ total annual package substrate production capacity. NVIDIA is supporting Unimicron’s KF substrate manufacturing expansion in Taiwan with a capacity reservation agreement. The expansion is expected to begin adding capacity in the second quarter of 2027 and reach full capacity by mid-2028. Scaling Advanced Packaging for Next-Generation Platforms NVIDIA and Amkor plan to expand advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, targeting a greater than 300% increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028. The planned capacity expansion, alongside Amkor’s development of new manufacturing facilities in South Korea, will support higher production volumes for NVIDIA’s current and next-generation platforms. Expanding Semiconductor Testing and Strengthening US Manufacturing NVIDIA expects its total semiconductor testing capacity to double from calendar 2026 to 2027, supported by buildouts in the U.S., Taiwan and Singapore. NVIDIA’s $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to KYEC will support new U.S. testing facilities and equipment, with high-volume production targeted for April 2027. In Singapore, expanded testing operations are expected to begin high-volume production in February 2027. Creating the Infrastructure for Co-Packaged Optics NVIDIA and SPIL plan to expand manufacturing capacity in Taiwan for optical engines used in co-packaged optics, supporting the growing connectivity requirements of large-scale computing infrastructure. The expansion targets an increase of 15x by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. items.raw_text: NVIDIA and Supply Chain Partners Expand Capacity to Accelerate AI Infrastructure Buildout New Capacity Agreements and Manufacturing Facilities to Support Volume Growth and Strengthen Supply Chain Resiliency October 21, 2026 News Summary: Substrate agreements with IBIDEN, Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Unimicron Technology Corporation will, in aggregate, drive a 2.5x increase in capacity over the next three years. Amkor plans to increase its advanced packaging capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028. KYEC will build new facilities in the U.S., supported by a $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance from NVIDIA. SPIL is targeting to increase its optical-engine capacity for co-packaged optics by 15x by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. GTC Berlin— NVIDIA today announced plans with a group of supply chain partners to expand global manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and full-stack AI factory platform. Working with Amkor Technology, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Unimicron Technology Corporation, NVIDIA is enabling new and existing suppliers to expand critical manufacturing capabilities across substrates, advanced packaging, testing and optical engines, strengthening the resiliency and redundancy of NVIDIA’s global supply chain. “We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Our supply chain partners are the world’s best manufacturers. I’m grateful they are expanding capacity around the globe to scale production and help us deliver the AI supercomputing systems powering this new industrial revolution.” Expanding Substrate Capacity to Support Volume Growth NVIDIA plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. The agreements below will contribute to this capacity expansion, with more underway. Under an agreement signed and announced earlier this year by IBIDEN, NVIDIA is providing a multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to support IBIDEN’s Ono Plant in Japan. The expansion targets capacity reaching 3x current levels at the plant, with additional capacity expected to begin ramping in the first quarter of 2028. Samsung Electro-Mechanics is joining NVIDIA’s substrate supply chain, bringing immediate capacity from its existing operations in South Korea. The collaboration also supports facility upgrades and new factories in Sejong and Busan, South Korea. By 2028, production allocated to NVIDIA is projected to account for a significant portion of Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ total annual package substrate production capacity. NVIDIA is supporting Unimicron’s KF substrate manufacturing expansion in Taiwan with a capacity reservation agreement. The expansion is expected to begin adding capacity in the second quarter of 2027 and reach full capacity by mid-2028. Scaling Advanced Packaging for Next-Generation Platforms NVIDIA and Amkor plan to expand advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, targeting a greater than 300% increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028. The planned capacity expansion, alongside Amkor’s development of new manufacturing facilities in South Korea, will support higher production volumes for NVIDIA’s current and next-generation platforms. Expanding Semiconductor Testing and Strengthening US Manufacturing NVIDIA expects its total semiconductor testing capacity to double from calendar 2026 to 2027, supported by buildouts in the U.S., Taiwan and Singapore. NVIDIA’s $1.1 billion capacity reservation advance to KYEC will support new U.S. testing facilities and equipment, with high-volume production targeted for April 2027. In Singapore, expanded testing operations are expected to begin high-volume production in February 2027. Creating the Infrastructure for Co-Packaged Optics NVIDIA and SPIL plan to expand manufacturing capacity in Taiwan for optical engines used in co-packaged optics, supporting the growing connectivity requirements of large-scale computing infrastructure. The expansion targets an increase of 15x by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. items.content: NVIDIA Launches OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe AI Agents Platform Brings Together NVIDIA Vera Rubin, Vera CPUs and BlueField-4 to Power Enterprise Infrastructure to Build, Run, Observe and Enforce Safe Agents at Industrial Scale October 21, 2026 News Summary: The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture delivers enterprise governance, isolation and security for building, containing, observing and enforcing safe agents across enterprise infrastructure and edge systems. Built on the foundation of NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime software, the architecture brings together NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for model inference, NVIDIA Vera CPUs for agent harnesses and tool use, and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for in-silicon enforcement. The OpenShell Reference Architecture extends to the edge with NVIDIA RTX Spark, NVIDIA DGX Spark and NVIDIA DGX Station systems. The OpenShell Reference Architecture runs on leading enterprise operating systems, including Canonical, Red Hat, and Microsoft Windows and Microsoft Execution Containers. Anthropic, AWS, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Dassault Systèmes, Dell Technologies, Google Cloud, HPE, IBM, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Perplexity, SAP, ServiceNow, Siemens, SpaceX Super Intelligence and others are among those working with the OpenShell Reference Architecture to enhance the security of agent deployments. GTC Berlin— NVIDIA today announced the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture , which enables building, containing, observing and enforcing safe agents on enterprise infrastructure and edge systems. The OpenShell Reference Architecture builds on the foundation of NVIDIA OpenShell ™ secure runtime software, extending it into full-stack, industrial-scale infrastructure for agent development and operations. It includes NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for running enterprise workloads, including closed and open models built with NVIDIA Nemotron ™; NVIDIA Vera CPUs for operating agent harnesses; open source NVIDIA OpenShell software; and NVIDIA BlueField ® DPUs for running the NVIDIA Sentry unified security software framework that provides continuous out-of-band monitoring of agent behavior and in-silicon policy enforcement. The OpenShell Reference Architecture is extensible to agents running at the edge across industries such as retail, healthcare, manufacturing, robotics, software development and telecommunications with NVIDIA RTX Spark ™, NVIDIA DGX Spark ™ and NVIDIA DGX Station ™ systems. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “As enterprises prepare to deploy billions of AI agents, safety and control must be built into the computing architecture. NVIDIA created OpenShell to give agents the freedom to do useful work within clearly defined boundaries — contained, monitored and under control. With the OpenShell Reference Architecture, agents can think on Rubin, act on Vera and be governed on BlueField.” Full-Stack Infrastructure Built for Agents The OpenShell Reference Architecture features NVIDIA accelerated computing paired with software for secure agent operations. NVIDIA Vera Rubin , with NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 infrastructure at its core, is fungible across pretraining, post-training and inference. For agentic workloads, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver 30x higher throughput per megawatt. NVIDIA Vera CPUs deliver 2x the performance of x86 processors with greater energy efficiency and run NVIDIA OpenShell , which provides a secure runtime boundary for autonomous agents. NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs continuously monitor agent behavior with NVIDIA Sentry , built on NVIDIA DOCA ™ software. BlueField and NVIDIA Sentry together provide in-silicon security enforcement — if an agent attempts to move outside its software boundary, NVIDIA Sentry quarantines and stops it in milliseconds. NVIDIA Sentry, powered by DOCA and running on BlueField-4, boosts agent capacity by up to 20%. NVIDIA Partners Building Secure Agent Deployments With OpenShell NVIDIA is working with industry leaders building infrastructure, models and software to enable industries to safely deploy agents in production. The OpenShell Reference Architecture runs on leading enterprise operating systems and container orchestration layers, including Linux and Kubernetes infrastructure powered by Canonical, SUSE and Red Hat , as well as Microsoft Windows using Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC). It can run on cloud operating systems from Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Enterprises can run agents from model builders including Anthropic, Cohere, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Perplexity, Reflection and SpaceX Super Intelligence on OpenShell infrastructure. NVIDIA is also working with model builder partners on OpenShell deployments for advanced model research. Cybersecurity leaders 1Password, Check Point , CrowdStrike , Cisco , F5 , Fortinet, Microsoft, Okta, Palo Alto Networks , TrendAI and Zscaler are integrating support for the OpenShell Reference Architecture into their agent security solutions. Leading banks — including Europe’s BBVA and Santander — are working with NVIDIA to explore the OpenShell Reference Architecture as a framework for strengthening agent safety, security and governance. Enterprise software leaders Cadence , Dassault Systèmes , IBM, SAP , Siemens and Synopsys are working with OpenShell to build agent software platforms. Palantir and NVIDIA are working with customers to deploy secure agents in production. SAP is integrating the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture with Joule Studio runtime, part of SAP Business AI Platform, connecting business governance with secure agent execution. ServiceNow today announced the general availability of ServiceNow Arc, a personal long-running AI agent with actions governed at runtime by the ServiceNow Super Intelligence Control Tower and enforced by NVIDIA OpenShell. In addition, ServiceNow’s recently announced AI Passport authority layer carries those policies to NVIDIA OpenShell and NVIDIA Sentry, so enterprises can revoke an AI agent’s access across software and hardware within seconds. NVIDIA system manufacturers Dell Technologies , Cisco , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are among those building infrastructure with the OpenShell Reference Architecture. NVIDIA is also working with cloud service providers including CoreWeave, Crusoe, Firebird, Firmus, GMI Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Vultr to deploy OpenShell-ready infrastructure. Inference and post-training service providers including Baseten, Deepinfra, Fireworks and Together AI are building OpenShell Reference Architecture integrations into their model development pipelines. Availability The NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture is now available . About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. items.content: European Ecosystem Builds World’s Most Efficient AI Factories With NVIDIA DSX NVIDIA DSX Enables European Companies to Reduce Water Consumption for Cooling by up to 100% and Generate the Same AI Output With up to 30% Less Power October 21, 2026 News Summary: NVIDIA DSX reference designs use closed-loop liquid cooling and dry coolers to enable near-zero facility cooling water consumption, with potential savings of 54 million liters a day for a 2-gigawatt deployment — equivalent to the daily water use of 180,000 households. AI clouds in Europe are building and operating NVIDIA DSX-based AI factories, expanding access to accelerated computing for the continent’s enterprises, developers and governments. NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS software helps operators use up to 30% less power to generate the same number of tokens, with CoreWeave, Firmus, Google Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Sharon AI planning to use the technology, while DSX Flex software turns AI factories into flexible power loads to support grid reliability and enable faster grid connection. NVIDIA SimReady Central, a hub for simulation-ready digital models of physical equipment, launches on Hugging Face with validated power and cooling assets, helping operators build and simulate DSX AI factory digital twins faster. New NVIDIA DSX OS open source software automates infrastructure lifecycle and improves health automation as well as resiliency capabilities to help operators run AI factories at scale. An expanding ecosystem — including technology and industrial AI leaders AVEVA, Dassault Systèmes and Siemens, and energy and cooling providers ABB, Eaton, GE Vernova, Hitachi Energy, Schneider Electric, Siemens Energy, Trane Technologies and Vertiv — is connecting AI factory design, power, cooling and operations to support Europe’s accelerated computing buildout. GTC Berlin— NVIDIA today announced that Europe’s leading ecosystem partners are adopting the NVIDIA DSX™ AI Factory Platform to build AI factories that minimize water consumption for cooling and use less power for the same AI output. The platform also helps partners bring new capacity online faster and adapt workload power consumption to support grid reliability. NVIDIA DSX is a full-stack AI factory reference architecture, co-innovated with the world’s leading infrastructure companies. Compute, networking, storage, software, power and cooling are codesigned as one system — optimized from design to operation. AI clouds and leading design, construction, energy and cooling providers are using DSX to build and operate infrastructure serving Europe’s enterprises, developers and governments. “Europe’s technology leadership depends on how efficiently we turn power and infrastructure into intelligence,” said Warren Barkley, vice president of DSX product management at NVIDIA. “NVIDIA DSX brings together the technologies and ecosystem expertise operators need to build responsibly, operate efficiently at scale and bring intelligence to the market faster.” The NVIDIA DSX platform includes DSX MaxLPS™ for dynamic power allocation, DSX Flex for coordinating workload power consumption with grid conditions, DSX Reference Design for validated infrastructure architectures, DSX Sim™ for simulation, DSX OS™ for infrastructure management and DSX Exchange™ for connecting computing and facility systems. These technologies help operators design, deploy and run AI factories that save valuable resources. NVIDIA DSX Rethinks Cooling Conventional cooling towers remove heat by evaporating water, requiring a continual supply of replacement water. NVIDIA DSX reference designs connect liquid-cooled computing with dry-cooler-based heat rejection that avoids evaporation: Cooling liquid absorbs heat from computing equipment and circulates in a closed loop, while outdoor dry coolers, similar to large radiators, release that heat into the air without evaporating water. NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure supports 100% liquid cooling with coolant temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius. With dry-cooler-based designs, this architecture can reduce facility cooling water consumption to near zero. At 2-gigawatt scale, NVIDIA DSX can save 54 million liters of water a day compared with conventional cooling-tower-based systems — equivalent to the daily water use of 180,000 households. Local climate determines whether supplemental mechanical cooling is needed during the hottest periods. Delivering the Same AI Output With Less Power Power availability defines how much capacity operators can bring online. DSX MaxLPS and DSX Flex address this constraint. DSX MaxLPS dynamically allocates power within an AI factory’s provisioned budget, helping operators generate the same number of tokens with up to 30% less power. Operators can also use this efficiency to support more GPU capacity and higher throughput within existing power budgets. CoreWeave, Firmus, Google Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale and Sharon AI are exploring the software. In a proof of concept across NVIDIA HGX™ B200 systems with DSX MaxLPS, Lambda demonstrated 24% more cluster token throughput and 19% more GPU capacity within a fixed power budget. Coordinating AI Factory Power Demand With the Grid DSX Flex helps AI factories become flexible assets for the power grid, enabling operators to adapt workload power consumption to utility needs, demand-response events and energy prices. It can also coordinate electricity from the grid, onsite renewables and energy storage, helping AI factories operate as flexible power loads that support grid reliability and enable faster grid connection. In an early trial, Emerald AI, EPRI, Nebius, the U.K. National Grid and NVIDIA demonstrated reductions of up to 40% in the cluster’s power draw on an NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPU cluster in response to simulated grid events, while critical workloads continued running. Nscale Advances AI Factory Efficiency With NVIDIA DSX Using DSX MaxLPS, DSX Flex and DSX Sim, Nscale is demonstrating how the NVIDIA DSX platform connects power optimization, grid-responsive operations and design. Based on an evaluation run in Nscale AI factory in Iceland, using DSX MaxLPS across four NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, Nscale demonstrated 49% higher inference throughput and 37% more managed GPU capacity within the same 264-kilowatt provisioned power budget. The results demonstrate how dynamic power allocation can unlock additional capacity from existing infrastructure. Nscale is also exploring DSX Flex to align workload power consumption with grid conditions. “Europe’s AI ambitions demand that we make every megawatt count,” said Josh Payne, founder and CEO of Nscale. “With NVIDIA DSX, we’re building AI factories that deliver more compute from available power, respond to grid conditions and move faster from design to deployment.” For its facilities in Portugal and Iceland, Nscale is using DSX Sim to create digital twins that help evaluate power, cooling and infrastructure configurations before deployment. By validating designs virtually, Nscale can identify potential issues earlier, reduce deployment risk and accelerate the path from planning to productive capacity. Accelerating AI Factory Design With DSX Sim and SimReady Central Library NVIDIA is launching SimReady Central Library with validated power and cooling equipment assets from partners like Vertiv, accelerating the creation of DSX AI factory digital twins. Used with DSX Sim, ecosystem partners including PTC are helping create these simulation-ready assets with computer-aided design to enable SimReady workflows that let builders model infrastructure configurations and evaluate power and cooling decisions before equipment is installed. Operators can validate designs earlier, reduce deployment risk and move faster from planning to construction. Driving Production Readiness With NVIDIA DSX OS To help operators turn installed infrastructure into productive capacity, NVIDIA is expanding its modular, open source DSX OS portfolio with three components in developer preview: NVIDIA Config Manager automates AI factory network configuration. NVIDIA Rack Management Service provides rack-level power, inventory, firmware and switch management. NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine runs distributed workloads to validate GPU clusters before production workloads arrive and isolate failures to specific nodes. Together with NVIDIA Infrastructure Controller, NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime and NVSentinel, these components help operators automate infrastructure lifecycle management, maintain consistent runtime environments and strengthen health validation, fault attribution and recovery. Cloud partners including Aleria, Cassava, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Firmus, Firebird, G42, GMI Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Nebius, Nscale, Radiant, Sharon AI and Volta are exploring the latest components of NVIDIA DSX OS to automate infrastructure lifecycle management, and improve resiliency and reliability. Connecting Design, Power and Cooling Across Europe’s AI Factory Ecosystem NVIDIA’s industrial software, power and cooling partners are advancing Europe’s AI factory buildout with DSX reference designs, lifecycle digital twins and qualified equipment that connect facility infrastructure with accelerated computing. Schneider Electric has developed power and cooling reference designs for NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure and is working with AVEVA on digital twins spanning infrastructure design, construction and operations. Procore is helping manage AI factory builds with its construction management platform, integrated with DSX Sim. Siemens is using DSX Sim to simulate power, cooling and acoustics, while Dassault Systèmes and Vertiv are developing digital twin models of Vertiv’s OneCore infrastructure, enabling simulation and optimization through model-based systems engineering. ABB is developing SimReady assets with NVIDIA DSX Sim, enabling engineers to evaluate source-to-rack architectures before construction while advancing 800 VDC development through its newly announced Infinitus Direct Current portfolio. Partners are also delivering coordinated power and cooling infrastructure aligned with DSX reference designs. Trane Technologies and Eaton recently collaborated with NVIDIA to help boost data center efficiency and cut installation costs with an integrated design built for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory Reference Design, bringing together Eaton’s Beam platform and power infrastructure with Trane Continuum cooling and coordinated controls in a grid-to-chip architecture. Trane Technologies has published seven thermal management system reference designs, including three 250-megawatt DSX-based cooling reference designs to support thermal infrastructure planning at scale. Through the NVIDIA DSX Ready program, builders can select equipment qualified under applicable DSX categories. Trane Technologies’ LiquidStack GigaModular and Vertiv’s 2.3-megawatt CoolChip — both coolant distribution units — have qualified under their applicable categories, while Hitachi Energy’s battery energy storage system has earned NVIDIA DSX Ready BESS qualification. For energy supply and grid integration, GE Vernova, Hitachi Energy and Siemens Energy are collaborating with NVIDIA on power infrastructure and digital twin initiatives that connect energy-system engineering and grid planning based on the facility’s requirements. Hitachi Energy is developing an integration between its energy management system and DSX Flex to optimize grid, generation and storage resources with workload demand. items.content: NVIDIA Introduces DSX POD AI Factories to Accelerate Europe’s Infrastructure Deployment Factory-Built With a Global Ecosystem Including Bull, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Schneider Electric and Vertiv, the New Reference Design Speeds Infrastructure Deployment From Months to Weeks, Accelerating Time to First Production Tokens October 21, 2026 News Summary: NVIDIA introduces DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners in modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery. Factory-built units reduce deployment time at a prepared site from six months to as little as 14 days, helping customers begin generating production tokens and earning revenue sooner. A global ecosystem of computing and infrastructure partners are working with NVIDIA to deliver modular AI factories worldwide in early 2027. GTC Berlin— NVIDIA today introduced DSX POD , a reference design for complete NVIDIA Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners inside modular containers, integrated and validated before delivery. The units arrive ready to connect out of the box to a prepared site’s power, cooling, networking and other supporting infrastructure, reducing deployment time from six months to as little as 14 days. DSX POD moves the integration and installation of computing, networking, cabling, rack-level power and liquid cooling to the manufacturing facility, reducing the extensive planning, construction, specialized labor and logistics of a traditional onsite build. Factory-tested containers reduce exposure to component delays and costly, error-prone onsite work, creating a shorter path to model training and production inference so customers can begin generating tokens and earning revenue sooner. “An AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens — not when construction is complete,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “With NVIDIA DSX POD, we’re bringing factory-built precision and speed to AI infrastructure construction — reducing deployment time from months to weeks so customers can scale capacity and bring revenue-generating production online faster.” Factory-Built Infrastructure NVIDIA DSX POD brings Vera Rubin systems together with the infrastructure needed to operate them in repeatable, factory-built, containerized designs that partners can manufacture and deliver at scale. It carries forward the design philosophy of the broader NVIDIA DSX™ infrastructure platform , with a distinct architecture that integrates and validates systems in purpose-built containers before transport and deployment. Partners complete rack-to-rack cabling, wiring, piping and functional validation before shipment. This work takes place separately from site preparation, further shortening the time needed to bring new capacity online. That earlier start to production is the link between deployment speed and economics. Time to first token marks when a new AI factory begins running models to serve production workloads, giving operators the opportunity to put their infrastructure to work for customers sooner. Global Partner Ecosystem and Availability NVIDIA is working with Anduril, Armada , Bull, Crusoe , DayOne, Dell Technologies , Delta, Eaton, Foxconn (Ingrasys), GIGABYTE, HPE , Lenovo, Pegatron, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Schneider Electric, Vertiv and Wistron to deliver DSX POD AI factories worldwide in early 2027. items.content: Featured projects TL;DR TorchTPU is an open source collaboration between Google and Meta that introduces a native and principled PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables seamless out-of-the-box model execution and TPU migration while delivering industry-competitive inference and training performance through eager execution optimizations, torch.compile integration, and native hardware acceleration. Introducing TorchTPU Google TPUs have been used very successfully, both within and outside of Google, to train and deploy large ML models at massive scale. They are specifically designed for ML and, as such, they provide significant benefits in terms of performance, energy, and cost. While TPUs have been historically associated with the TensorFlow and the JAX ecosystems, we’re excited to introduce TorchTPU , a new effort started at Google in mid 2025, in collaboration with the PyTorch Team at Meta, to run PyTorch natively on TPUs. To program Google’s TPU at a level below the Python framework, developers utilize the XLA compiler stack. In 2020, Google introduced the first compiled version of PyTorch for TPU, PyTorch/XLA, based on Lazy Tensors. While foundational, this initial integration struggled to keep pace with the rapid, community-driven evolution of PyTorch. Crucially, PyTorch/XLA required intrusive source-code modifications to explicitly define compilable regions, suffered from severe compile-time latency, lacked support for PyTorch’s native imperative (“eager”) execution mode, and lagged in supporting emerging distributed computing primitives within the PyTorch ecosystem. In contrast with previous efforts such as PyTorch/XLA and TorchAX, which shoehorn PyTorch into JAX’s modus operandi, TorchTPU was built as a principled TPU backend for PyTorch: eager execution is a top priority, and existing PyTorch workloads run out of the box with trivial code changes (e.g., .to("cuda") → .to("tpu") ). More specifically, as we started TorchTPU we deliberately formulated a set of principles to follow: PyTorch Citizenship : No JAX dependencies in the runtime; Solid eager mode; Torch.compile() based on Torch Dynamo (not Lazy Tensor) and with similar performance to JAX compile; Wide support for PyTorch distributed idioms (DDP, FSDP, DTensor, …) by providing TPU collectives at the lowest level in the PyTorch stack (e.g. Process Group API); Seamless integration into the PyTorch ecosystem; Community engagement. Focus on the User: Porting a workload to TPU should be as simple as changing model.to("cuda") to model.to("tpu") . (One cannot achieve peak TPU performance with that simple change, since a model’s shapes, sharding and ops may be skewed toward a GPU architecture; however, the model should run out of the box.) Provide user-friendly and actionable messages for runtime/compiler errors; Integrate with the tools and frameworks that the PyTorch community already uses (e.g., torch.profiler, DTensor, Ray). Improve the State of the Art : Build a solution that can compete with PyTorch on GPUs for large scale workloads; Introduce a JIT compilation approach for eager execution, with runtime optimizations that can bridge the performance gap between op-by-op execution and compiled execution; Improve the TPU programming stack by introducing bounded dynamism, by avoiding XLA recompilation due to shape changes, and by exploring dynamic TPU kernels that can be precompiled ahead of time. TorchTPU is in active development, it is used in production for both inference and training workloads for some of the largest Google Cloud customers, and can be found as an Open Source project in this GitHub repo . Architecture Deep Dive A TPU Primer Google TPUs are specialized ASICs designed specifically to perform the massive tensor operations that are the foundation of deep learning. A large High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) – 288 GB at 8.6 TB/s in TPU 8i , which can be used to store ML data and share that with the CPU. TPUs are programmed with the XLA compiler stack through two different entry points: StableHLO (higher-level IR for ML ops) and Mosaic (lower-level IR for custom kernels). The actual TPU ISA is proprietary, subject to change, and not publicly available. Effectively, one can think of StableHLO and (even more so) of Mosaic as equivalent to PTX. See picture below for a high-level sketch. A C++ program can access a local TPU by instantiating a PjRT Client , whose API provides methods to compile MLIR (StableHLO or Mosaic) into a TPU executable, to launch that executable, and to copy data to-from the TPU. Note that TPU execution is asynchronous and the CPU can wait for a TPU result to be ready by waiting on the associated PjRTBuffer. Consequently, to reach peak performance it is key that a model’s shapes be sufficiently wide to exploit the full potential of the MXU. This differs from GPUs where launching multiple smaller kernels in parallel can help maximize HW utilization. The XLA compiler can instruct a TensorCore to offload sparse and collective operations to SparseCore, for more efficient and/or parallel execution. This happens either automatically or through user-supplied MLIR annotation in a compiled StableHLO module. A TPU device can be accessed by only one user-space process. Following our goal of seamless integration in the PyTorch ecosystem, for distributed TorchTPU workloads we adopt a one-process-per-device model in contrast with JAX’s one-process-per-host model. However, because a TPU can be accessed by only one user-space process, RL colocation can’t be supported out of the box and we are investigating ways to relax or workaround this TPU limitation. StableHLO follows the SSA paradigm and, hence, doesn’t allow for in-place mutations, i.e., a write operation always produces a new value (at least conceptually). This is particularly significant for TorchTPU, which does provide familiar Pytorch “view” semantics, including mutations, through view decomposition and inversion, as explained later in this doc. The XLA compiler and PjRT runtime assume that tensor shapes are known at compile time. Recognizing this as a limitation for PyTorch workloads, we have been adding support for bounded dynamism, i.e., when the maximum bounds of a shape’s dimensions are known at compile time, but the actual dimensions are known only at runtime. Collective ops are lowered to XLA as StableHLO ops, versus using a separate library such as NCCL. Usability and Autoload Mechanism We designed TorchTPU with usability in mind. When the user imports PyTorch on a TPU machine where TorchTPU wheel is installed, running the PyTorch code on TPU involves only trivial changes and can be done in a couple of lines of code thanks to PyTorch’s autoload mechanism: See the table below for a side-by-side comparison. Before (GPU) After (TPU) Alternative (TPU or GPU) import torch import torch.distributed as dist def main(): device = torch.device("cuda") dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl") rank = dist.get_rank() word_size = dist.get_world_size() ... model = model.to(device) ... import torch import torch.distributed as dist def main(): device = torch.device("tpu") dist.init_process_group(backend="tpu_dist") rank = dist.get_rank() word_size = dist.get_world_size() ... model = model.to(device) ... import torch import torch.distributed as dist def main(): device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator() dist.init_process_group() rank = dist.get_rank() word_size = dist.get_world_size() ... model = model.to(device) ... Numerical Precision TorchTPU adapts standard PyTorch precision APIs for TPU hardware. Like all high-performance machine learning architectures, TPUs are optimized to deliver peak performance and energy efficiency using specific native data types preferred by their particular generation. For TPUs the native matrix multiplication format is bfloat16 (BF16), which balances high dynamic range with efficient throughput. Because the TPU Matrix Multiply Units (MXUs) are engineered to execute arithmetic using BF16 inputs with 32-bit floating-point intermediate accumulation, this configuration is the cornerstone of TPU high-performance computing. For non-contracting operations (such as element wise additions, activations, layernorm, and softmax), TorchTPU executes FP32 tensor operations using the TPU Vector Execution Unit (VPU), which natively performs full IEEE-754 FP32 arithmetic. TorchTPU maps PyTorch precision modes to underlying XLA/StableHLO configurations to expose this hardware capability: medium : Uses lower precision for multiplication (converting inputs to native BF16 for the MXU), while accumulation is performed in FP32 to maintain stability. TorchTPU defaults to this mode to fully leverage TPU hardware acceleration, as single-pass BF16 multiplication with FP32 accumulation provides sufficient accuracy for nearly all deep learning workloads. high : Uses a 3-pass algorithm where inputs are split into high and low components to compute three cross-terms, recovering most FP32 precision at roughly 3× the compute cost. highest : Uses a 6-pass algorithm that computes all cross-terms to approximate full IEEE FP32 accuracy, incurring roughly 6× compute overhead on the MXU. For the vast majority of deep learning workloads, we recommend using the medium (default) precision. Explicitly selecting high or highest in TorchTPU triggers a performance warning ( TORCH_WARN_ONCE ). Only switch to high or highest if you explicitly identify precision-related convergence issues, as these modes trigger a significant performance overhead. In addition to the global setting, TorchTPU provides a thread-local context manager ( torch.tpu.precision ) for fine-grained scoping (e.g., for numerically sensitive layers).
