items.content: Simulation / Modeling / Design Design Proteins with RFD4-Proteina Using Reward-Guided Inference-Time Search Oct 21, 2026 By Kyle Tretina , Kyle Gion , Neha Tadimeti , Gloria Macia and Kieran Didi Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary RFD4-Proteina co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures using reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on promising candidates. The model combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff required by prior approaches. Residue-level latent representation and engineered diffusion reduce sampling from about 400 steps to 60, delivering 3.8x faster generation and 84% less peak memory than RFD3 at 200 residues. Both the open model and NIM microservice accept annotated CIFs or condition specifications for tasks such as PD-L1 binder design with hotspot constraints. Inference-time search integrates CUDA-accelerated oracles including OpenFold3 and TMol to score and refine designs against geometry, interaction, and confidence metrics. rfd4-proteina-campaign and rfd4-proteina-package skills coordinate generation, search, evaluation, and results archiving for iterative design campaigns. Next Steps Explore the RFD4-Proteina NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface. Explore the open model on GitHub for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code. Point your agent at BioNeMo Agent Toolkit skills to coordinate generation, search, and evaluation in automated campaigns. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Protein design is a search problem. Choose amino acids for an eight-residue protein sequence and more than 25 billion combinations are possible. Choose amino acids for a 100-residue protein sequence and the number of possibilities exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Somewhere in that space is a protein that opens a path to a new therapy. There are too many combinations to search exhaustively, so finding it depends on knowing where to look. RFD4-Proteina , an NVIDIA BioNeMo open model co-developed with the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington’s School of Medicine, navigates that space using patterns learned from nature. It co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures, and uses reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on the most promising candidates. This tutorial shows computational biologists, ML engineers and drug discovery researchers how to design protein binder candidates against PD-L1, an oncology target, using reward-guided inference-time search and introduces experimental validation results across design tasks. You can access RFD4-Proteina in two ways: Choose the open model for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code or Choose the NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface Building on Proteina-Complexa ’s partially latent approach, RFD4-Proteina combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, learned sequence and atomistic variables. Its autoencoder decoder produces the sequence and all-atom structure together, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff to a model such as ProteinMPNN . Prerequisites Open model Supported Linux GPU host and Python 3.12; follow the repository setup guide and use a supported NVIDIA GPU. Model cache: Setup downloads the Hugging Face bundle automatically; set HF_HOME only if you want a different cache directory. NIM Self-host: x86_64 or arm64 Linux meeting the NIM prerequisites , Docker, NVIDIA Driver, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and an NGC API key . NIM API endpoint (not recommended for production runs): HTTP access through NVIDIA build.nvidia.com via Shell and Python scripts, no local GPU or model installation required. About RFD4-Proteina Figure 1. RFD4-Proteina uses molecular context, design constraints, and design regions to generate protein sequences and all-atom structures, with optional reward-guided search to guide generation The search loop shown in Figure 1, above, is where RFD4-Proteina focuses its compute. During inference-time reasoning search, the model denoises generation trajectories to obtain structures, scores these designs, retains and branches promising partial states, and continues until the generation criteria are reached. Rewards can measure geometry, interactions, or independent prediction confidence. This kind of extra search optimizes designs against a specified objective to yield higher-scoring designs. Later in this tutorial, you will see how a user can enable this functionality through the open model and the NIM. RFD4-Proteina is faster and uses less memory than RFD3 for several reasons: It works on a residue-level latent representation instead of atom-level, which avoids memory blow-up. Engineering of the diffusion process cuts sampling from about 400 steps in Proteina-Complexa to 60, and computation is concentrated on the parts of the process that matter most thanks to reasoning capabilities in the model. Inference-time search is also faster, since the oracles (OF3 and physics methods like tmol ) are CUDA-accelerated. The model and kernels were co-designed with the cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BIR) teams for speed and scalability. Figure 2. At 200 residues, RFD4-Proteina delivers 3.8x faster generation and uses 84% leeds peak reserved memory than RFD3 in the reported generation benchmark From a molecular design idea to candidate designs Figure 3. The reference workflow links molecular design, computational evaluation, and experimental testing in an iterative cycle The workflow in Figure 3, above, demonstrates how to use RFD4-Proteina to go from a scientific objective to candidates for experimental testing. An agent can coordinate these tools and track results, while scientists define the objectives and use experimental evidence to guide the next round. Preparing the molecular inputs and environment Begin by defining the criteria and requirements for generation. For example, RFD4-Proteina expects users to define what may change, what must remain fixed, and computational and experimental success criteria. Use AtomWorks to generate /manipulate the input data. AtomWorks is the molecular data layer used to prepare structures and design annotations for RFD4-Proteina. Its Python and PyMOL workflows prepare fixed atoms, designable residues, hotspots, and molecular context. Preserve the supplied ligand or motif chemistry when designing surrounding protein. Both the open model and NIM accept annotated CIFs or a condition specification plus its source structure. The specification below fixes the target and defines the new binder. The repository’s cropped PD-L1 structure from PDB 5O45 serves as the target. Fix the target’s sequence and backbone coordinates, allow its side chains to repack, and direct binder generation toward hotspot atoms on Tyr56, Met115, and Tyr123. The new binder has 100–150 residues, with free sequence and coordinates. Clone the repository, then run the examples from its root. This writes pdl1.json ; both paths use the same target CIF and conditions. git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/RFD4-Proteina.git cd RFD4-Proteina cat > pdl1.json <<'JSON' { "pdl1_binder": { "input": "docs/examples/inputs/5o45_cropped.cif", "contig": "100-150, /0, A17-131", "conditions": { "C_CRD": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A') and is_protein_backbone"}]}, "C_SEQ": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A')"}]}, "C_HOT": {"true": [ {"select": "sel('A/*/56/[CG,OH]')"}, {"select": "sel('A/*/115/[CG,SD]')"}, {"select": "sel('A/*/123/[CD2,OH]')"} ]} } } } JSON Open model setup On a supported Linux/CUDA system, install the repository environment with a current uv release (validated with 0.12.24). If uv is already installed, update it first so it recognizes CUDA 13.2. Setup caches the Hugging Face model bundle, including the paired autoencoder. While the model repository is private, authenticate with hf auth login using an account with access. bash setup.sh --native source .venv/bin/activate NIM environment setup To host the NIM, run this block in Bash on a supported GPU host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed. read -rsp 'NGC API key: ' NGC_API_KEY; echo export NGC_API_KEY printf '%s' "$NGC_API_KEY" | docker login nvcr.io \ -u '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin image=nvcr.io/nim/ipd/rfd4-proteina:latest docker pull "$image" export RFD4_NIM_IMAGE="$(docker image inspect \ --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$image")" printf '%s\n' "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" > nim-image.txt export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/nim" mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE" docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \ --runtime=nvidia --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 \ -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE":/opt/nim/.cache \ --shm-size=16g "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" Generate sequences and structures Open-model generation Save the following as design.py in the repository root. The same script supports generation and search. Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") loads the current Hugging Face model and paired autoencoder checkpoints. import hydra from rfd4_proteina import Proteina from rfproteina.generate import run_generation @hydra.main(config_path="configs", config_name="inference", version_base="1.3") def main(cfg): model = Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") run_generation(cfg, model=model) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Generate one candidate from the repository root: python design.py inputs=pdl1.json out_dir=runs/pdl1-open seed=42 compile_lengths=null Outputs are saved under runs/pdl1-open/inference_samples/. Add num_replicates=10 for ten candidates and choose a new out_dir for each run. Hugging Face caches downloads; add revision=”<commit>” to from_pretrained to reproduce a particular model version. NIM generation Save this as nim_client.py . It sends the PD-L1 condition spec and target CIF to the NIM, then saves generated structures and response metrics. import json from pathlib import Path import requests spec = json.loads(Path("pdl1.json").read_text())["pdl1_binder"] target = Path(spec["input"]) spec["input"] = target.name payload = { "task": "motif_scaffolding", "input": {"format": "condition_spec", "example_id": "pdl1_binder", "spec": spec, "files": [{"filename": target.name, "content": target.read_text()}]}, "sampling": {"num_replicates": 1, "seed": 42}, "metrics": {"tags": ["design", "hotspot_conditioning"]}, } def submit(payload, out): out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) response = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/biology/ipd/rfd4-proteina/generative", json=payload, timeout=1800) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() (out / "response.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2)) for i, design in enumerate(result["designs"]): dest = out / f"design-{i}.cif" dest.write_text(design["structure"]["content"]) print(design["design_id"], dest) if __name__ == "__main__": submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim")) Install requests and run the client from the repository root. Keep pdl1.json beside the target CIF. python -m pip install requests python nim_client.py Performance optimizations across open model and NIM For faster design iteration, the BioIR backend accelerates RFD4-Proteina by 1.37–1.73× over the default compiled backend across six tested Hopper GPU configurations (see Figure 4, below). On H100 PCIe, total suite time drops from 161 to 111 seconds, about 31% less runtime. The benchmark uses batch size 1 and sums warm end-to-end timings across 15 sequence lengths (128–1,024 tokens). Figure 4. BioIR accelerates RFD4-Proteina by up to 1.73× over the default compiled backend on tested Hopper GPUs Inference-time search with external oracles Open-model search with OpenFold3 Install the optional OpenFold3 runtime and weights with ./scripts/download_example_data.sh ./data_path . Set OF3_IMAGE , OF3_MODEL_DIR , and OF3_JAX_CACHE_DIR to the paths it prints, then run mkdir -p "$OF3_JAX_CACHE_DIR" . Apptainer must be available on the GPU host. This example uses the AlphaFold3 codebase , which is released under the open-source Apache 2.0 license , and the OpenFold3 model weights , which are also released under the Apache 2.0 license . Reuse design.py with the search preset: python design.py inference_experiment=inference_beam_example \ metrics/refolding_oracles=of3 inputs=pdl1.json subset_to_examples=null \ num_replicates=1 out_dir=runs/pdl1-open-search seed=42 compile_lengths=null The preset uses two branches, a beam width of three, and scoring at steps 20, 40, 50 and 60. It rewards the designed chain’s OpenFold3 pLDDT ( oracle.plddt_coi ), with a floor of 50, and saves qualifying rollouts at reward 80. This measures confidence in the binder, not evidence of binding; inspect interface and refolding metrics separately. Outputs are under runs/pdl1-open-search/. NIM search with OpenFold3 Save this as nim_search_request.py . It reuses the PD-L1 input and submits a reward-guided OpenFold3 search. from pathlib import Path from nim_client import payload, submit key = "oracle_of3_nvcf.overall_plddt" payload["sampling"]["num_steps"] = 60 payload["search"] = { "step_checkpoints": [0, 20, 40, 50, 60], "n_branch": 2, "beam_width": 3, "reward_metrics_tags": ["unconditional_refolding"], "weights": {key: 1.0}, "clip_values": {key: {"min": 50.0}}, "intermediate_save_min_reward": 80.0, } payload["metrics"] = {"tags": ["design", "unconditional_refolding"]} submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim-search")) Enable the NIM oracle Mount the OpenFold3 reward.py callback as described in the oracle guide . It reports oracle_of3_nvcf.overall_plddt for the whole complex; evaluate the binder interface separately. Save the OpenFold3 NVCF callback from the oracle guide as reward.py and export OF3_NIM_API_KEY with an NVCF invoke credential. Relaunch the service with this callback: docker stop rfd4-proteina docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \ --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 --shm-size=16g \ -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" \ -v "$PWD/reward.py:/opt/nim/reward.py:ro" \ -e NIM_ALLOW_ORACLE_PLUGIN=true -e OF3_NIM_API_KEY \ "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" Run the search script. It saves designs and response metrics under runs/pdl1-nim-search/. python nim_search_request.py This request uses two branches, checkpoints [0, 20, 40, 50, 60], and a beam width of three. It sets a reward floor of 50 and saves intermediate designs with scores of at least 80. These are example thresholds for OpenFold3 overall pLDDT, a prediction-confidence metric for the whole complex. Search-time reward tags and final reporting tags are separate. Search output counts vary. Inspect the generated CIFs and retained metrics before selecting candidates. Include refolding and scoring in compute comparisons. Filter and rank candidates Check constraints, motif preservation, clashes, interfaces, refolding consistency, and structural diversity metrics. OpenFold3 , and RoseTTAFold3 provide prediction options; TMol provides Rosetta-inspired all-atom scoring and optimization. Common metrics include ipTM (interface Predicted Template Modeling), ipSAE (interaction prediction Score from Aligned Errors), and RMSD (Root Mean Square Deviation) scores from protein structure prediction models like OpenFold 3, along with interaction energies from physics-based models like TMol. Test experimentally and refine Table 1. items.raw_text: Simulation / Modeling / Design Design Proteins with RFD4-Proteina Using Reward-Guided Inference-Time Search Oct 21, 2026 By Kyle Tretina , Kyle Gion , Neha Tadimeti , Gloria Macia and Kieran Didi Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary RFD4-Proteina co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures using reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on promising candidates. The model combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff required by prior approaches. Residue-level latent representation and engineered diffusion reduce sampling from about 400 steps to 60, delivering 3.8x faster generation and 84% less peak memory than RFD3 at 200 residues. Both the open model and NIM microservice accept annotated CIFs or condition specifications for tasks such as PD-L1 binder design with hotspot constraints. Inference-time search integrates CUDA-accelerated oracles including OpenFold3 and TMol to score and refine designs against geometry, interaction, and confidence metrics. rfd4-proteina-campaign and rfd4-proteina-package skills coordinate generation, search, evaluation, and results archiving for iterative design campaigns. Next Steps Explore the RFD4-Proteina NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface. Explore the open model on GitHub for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code. Point your agent at BioNeMo Agent Toolkit skills to coordinate generation, search, and evaluation in automated campaigns. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Protein design is a search problem. Choose amino acids for an eight-residue protein sequence and more than 25 billion combinations are possible. Choose amino acids for a 100-residue protein sequence and the number of possibilities exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Somewhere in that space is a protein that opens a path to a new therapy. There are too many combinations to search exhaustively, so finding it depends on knowing where to look. RFD4-Proteina , an NVIDIA BioNeMo open model co-developed with the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington’s School of Medicine, navigates that space using patterns learned from nature. It co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures, and uses reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on the most promising candidates. This tutorial shows computational biologists, ML engineers and drug discovery researchers how to design protein binder candidates against PD-L1, an oncology target, using reward-guided inference-time search and introduces experimental validation results across design tasks. You can access RFD4-Proteina in two ways: Choose the open model for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code or Choose the NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface Building on Proteina-Complexa ’s partially latent approach, RFD4-Proteina combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, learned sequence and atomistic variables. Its autoencoder decoder produces the sequence and all-atom structure together, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff to a model such as ProteinMPNN . Prerequisites Open model Supported Linux GPU host and Python 3.12; follow the repository setup guide and use a supported NVIDIA GPU. Model cache: Setup downloads the Hugging Face bundle automatically; set HF_HOME only if you want a different cache directory. NIM Self-host: x86_64 or arm64 Linux meeting the NIM prerequisites , Docker, NVIDIA Driver, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and an NGC API key . NIM API endpoint (not recommended for production runs): HTTP access through NVIDIA build.nvidia.com via Shell and Python scripts, no local GPU or model installation required. About RFD4-Proteina Figure 1. RFD4-Proteina uses molecular context, design constraints, and design regions to generate protein sequences and all-atom structures, with optional reward-guided search to guide generation The search loop shown in Figure 1, above, is where RFD4-Proteina focuses its compute. During inference-time reasoning search, the model denoises generation trajectories to obtain structures, scores these designs, retains and branches promising partial states, and continues until the generation criteria are reached. Rewards can measure geometry, interactions, or independent prediction confidence. This kind of extra search optimizes designs against a specified objective to yield higher-scoring designs. Later in this tutorial, you will see how a user can enable this functionality through the open model and the NIM. RFD4-Proteina is faster and uses less memory than RFD3 for several reasons: It works on a residue-level latent representation instead of atom-level, which avoids memory blow-up. Engineering of the diffusion process cuts sampling from about 400 steps in Proteina-Complexa to 60, and computation is concentrated on the parts of the process that matter most thanks to reasoning capabilities in the model. Inference-time search is also faster, since the oracles (OF3 and physics methods like tmol ) are CUDA-accelerated. The model and kernels were co-designed with the cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BIR) teams for speed and scalability. Figure 2. At 200 residues, RFD4-Proteina delivers 3.8x faster generation and uses 84% leeds peak reserved memory than RFD3 in the reported generation benchmark From a molecular design idea to candidate designs Figure 3. The reference workflow links molecular design, computational evaluation, and experimental testing in an iterative cycle The workflow in Figure 3, above, demonstrates how to use RFD4-Proteina to go from a scientific objective to candidates for experimental testing. An agent can coordinate these tools and track results, while scientists define the objectives and use experimental evidence to guide the next round. Preparing the molecular inputs and environment Begin by defining the criteria and requirements for generation. For example, RFD4-Proteina expects users to define what may change, what must remain fixed, and computational and experimental success criteria. Use AtomWorks to generate /manipulate the input data. AtomWorks is the molecular data layer used to prepare structures and design annotations for RFD4-Proteina. Its Python and PyMOL workflows prepare fixed atoms, designable residues, hotspots, and molecular context. Preserve the supplied ligand or motif chemistry when designing surrounding protein. Both the open model and NIM accept annotated CIFs or a condition specification plus its source structure. The specification below fixes the target and defines the new binder. The repository’s cropped PD-L1 structure from PDB 5O45 serves as the target. Fix the target’s sequence and backbone coordinates, allow its side chains to repack, and direct binder generation toward hotspot atoms on Tyr56, Met115, and Tyr123. The new binder has 100–150 residues, with free sequence and coordinates. Clone the repository, then run the examples from its root. This writes pdl1.json ; both paths use the same target CIF and conditions. git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/RFD4-Proteina.git cd RFD4-Proteina cat > pdl1.json <<'JSON' { "pdl1_binder": { "input": "docs/examples/inputs/5o45_cropped.cif", "contig": "100-150, /0, A17-131", "conditions": { "C_CRD": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A') and is_protein_backbone"}]}, "C_SEQ": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A')"}]}, "C_HOT": {"true": [ {"select": "sel('A/*/56/[CG,OH]')"}, {"select": "sel('A/*/115/[CG,SD]')"}, {"select": "sel('A/*/123/[CD2,OH]')"} ]} } } } JSON Open model setup On a supported Linux/CUDA system, install the repository environment with a current uv release (validated with 0.12.24). If uv is already installed, update it first so it recognizes CUDA 13.2. Setup caches the Hugging Face model bundle, including the paired autoencoder. While the model repository is private, authenticate with hf auth login using an account with access. bash setup.sh --native source .venv/bin/activate NIM environment setup To host the NIM, run this block in Bash on a supported GPU host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed. read -rsp 'NGC API key: ' NGC_API_KEY; echo export NGC_API_KEY printf '%s' "$NGC_API_KEY" | docker login nvcr.io \ -u '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin image=nvcr.io/nim/ipd/rfd4-proteina:latest docker pull "$image" export RFD4_NIM_IMAGE="$(docker image inspect \ --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$image")" printf '%s\n' "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" > nim-image.txt export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/nim" mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE" docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \ --runtime=nvidia --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 \ -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE":/opt/nim/.cache \ --shm-size=16g "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" Generate sequences and structures Open-model generation Save the following as design.py in the repository root. The same script supports generation and search. Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") loads the current Hugging Face model and paired autoencoder checkpoints. import hydra from rfd4_proteina import Proteina from rfproteina.generate import run_generation @hydra.main(config_path="configs", config_name="inference", version_base="1.3") def main(cfg): model = Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") run_generation(cfg, model=model) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Generate one candidate from the repository root: python design.py inputs=pdl1.json out_dir=runs/pdl1-open seed=42 compile_lengths=null Outputs are saved under runs/pdl1-open/inference_samples/. Add num_replicates=10 for ten candidates and choose a new out_dir for each run. Hugging Face caches downloads; add revision=”<commit>” to from_pretrained to reproduce a particular model version. NIM generation Save this as nim_client.py . It sends the PD-L1 condition spec and target CIF to the NIM, then saves generated structures and response metrics. import json from pathlib import Path import requests spec = json.loads(Path("pdl1.json").read_text())["pdl1_binder"] target = Path(spec["input"]) spec["input"] = target.name payload = { "task": "motif_scaffolding", "input": {"format": "condition_spec", "example_id": "pdl1_binder", "spec": spec, "files": [{"filename": target.name, "content": target.read_text()}]}, "sampling": {"num_replicates": 1, "seed": 42}, "metrics": {"tags": ["design", "hotspot_conditioning"]}, } def submit(payload, out): out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) response = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/biology/ipd/rfd4-proteina/generative", json=payload, timeout=1800) response.raise_for_status() result = response.json() (out / "response.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2)) for i, design in enumerate(result["designs"]): dest = out / f"design-{i}.cif" dest.write_text(design["structure"]["content"]) print(design["design_id"], dest) if __name__ == "__main__": submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim")) Install requests and run the client from the repository root. Keep pdl1.json beside the target CIF. python -m pip install requests python nim_client.py Performance optimizations across open model and NIM For faster design iteration, the BioIR backend accelerates RFD4-Proteina by 1.37–1.73× over the default compiled backend across six tested Hopper GPU configurations (see Figure 4, below). On H100 PCIe, total suite time drops from 161 to 111 seconds, about 31% less runtime. The benchmark uses batch size 1 and sums warm end-to-end timings across 15 sequence lengths (128–1,024 tokens). Figure 4. BioIR accelerates RFD4-Proteina by up to 1.73× over the default compiled backend on tested Hopper GPUs Inference-time search with external oracles Open-model search with OpenFold3 Install the optional OpenFold3 runtime and weights with ./scripts/download_example_data.sh ./data_path . Set OF3_IMAGE , OF3_MODEL_DIR , and OF3_JAX_CACHE_DIR to the paths it prints, then run mkdir -p "$OF3_JAX_CACHE_DIR" . Apptainer must be available on the GPU host. This example uses the AlphaFold3 codebase , which is released under the open-source Apache 2.0 license , and the OpenFold3 model weights , which are also released under the Apache 2.0 license . Reuse design.py with the search preset: python design.py inference_experiment=inference_beam_example \ metrics/refolding_oracles=of3 inputs=pdl1.json subset_to_examples=null \ num_replicates=1 out_dir=runs/pdl1-open-search seed=42 compile_lengths=null The preset uses two branches, a beam width of three, and scoring at steps 20, 40, 50 and 60. It rewards the designed chain’s OpenFold3 pLDDT ( oracle.plddt_coi ), with a floor of 50, and saves qualifying rollouts at reward 80. This measures confidence in the binder, not evidence of binding; inspect interface and refolding metrics separately. Outputs are under runs/pdl1-open-search/. NIM search with OpenFold3 Save this as nim_search_request.py . It reuses the PD-L1 input and submits a reward-guided OpenFold3 search. from pathlib import Path from nim_client import payload, submit key = "oracle_of3_nvcf.overall_plddt" payload["sampling"]["num_steps"] = 60 payload["search"] = { "step_checkpoints": [0, 20, 40, 50, 60], "n_branch": 2, "beam_width": 3, "reward_metrics_tags": ["unconditional_refolding"], "weights": {key: 1.0}, "clip_values": {key: {"min": 50.0}}, "intermediate_save_min_reward": 80.0, } payload["metrics"] = {"tags": ["design", "unconditional_refolding"]} submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim-search")) Enable the NIM oracle Mount the OpenFold3 reward.py callback as described in the oracle guide . It reports oracle_of3_nvcf.overall_plddt for the whole complex; evaluate the binder interface separately. Save the OpenFold3 NVCF callback from the oracle guide as reward.py and export OF3_NIM_API_KEY with an NVCF invoke credential. Relaunch the service with this callback: docker stop rfd4-proteina docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \ --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 --shm-size=16g \ -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" \ -v "$PWD/reward.py:/opt/nim/reward.py:ro" \ -e NIM_ALLOW_ORACLE_PLUGIN=true -e OF3_NIM_API_KEY \ "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" Run the search script. It saves designs and response metrics under runs/pdl1-nim-search/. python nim_search_request.py This request uses two branches, checkpoints [0, 20, 40, 50, 60], and a beam width of three. It sets a reward floor of 50 and saves intermediate designs with scores of at least 80. These are example thresholds for OpenFold3 overall pLDDT, a prediction-confidence metric for the whole complex. Search-time reward tags and final reporting tags are separate. Search output counts vary. Inspect the generated CIFs and retained metrics before selecting candidates. Include refolding and scoring in compute comparisons. Filter and rank candidates Check constraints, motif preservation, clashes, interfaces, refolding consistency, and structural diversity metrics. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Teacher specialization Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Benchmark results We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters. items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 67 +61 Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow merve merve Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Guarin Flück guarin Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Serveurperso Serveurperso Follow Jun Kim Jundot Follow Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. Inference Support Transformers The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. You can initialize the model and processor as follows. import os from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B " ) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , distributed_config=distributed_config, ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue." }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, reasoning_effort= "medium" , # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) Text-only Inference Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt. messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "high" , # options:low/medium/high/xhigh ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) generated_tokens = output[ 0 ][inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens= False )) Images and Text The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt. image_url = ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/" "resolve/main/pills.jpg" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : image_url, }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?" , }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize= True , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_effort= "medium" , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) response = processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False ) processor.parse_response(response) Video Inference Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor: processor.video_processor.fps = 4.0 As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template . Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate. import torch messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "text" , "text" : ( "Describe what happens in this video. " "Use timestamps and include relevant speech or sounds." ), }, { "type" : "video" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vlm_test_images/resolve/main/ramen.mp4" }, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_from_video= True , return_metadata= True , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 256 , do_sample= False , ) generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] response = processor.batch_decode( generated_ids, skip_special_tokens= True , )[ 0 ] print (response) Audio Inference The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings. Tool Calling Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. What clothes should I wear?" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_strength= "high" ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs) response = processor.parse_response( completion, prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools, ) print (response) Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). In the input message below: <|begin_of_text|> <|start|>system<|message|> You are a helpful AI assistant. Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04. Current date: ... ... <|eot|> <|start|>user<|message|>... <|eot|> <|start|>assistant <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . You can install this with following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K The repository containing quants is here . Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. ## Text-only inference curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' ## Image-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' ## Audio-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."}, {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K . SGLang The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs. From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \ uv run sglang_meta serve \ --model-path "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 \ --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \ --tp-size 4 \ --ep-size 4 \ --port 30000 The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP

The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. Inference Support Transformers The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. You can initialize the model and processor as follows. import os from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B " ) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , distributed_config=distributed_config, ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue." }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, reasoning_effort= "medium" , # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) Text-only Inference Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. ## Text-only inference curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' ## Image-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' ## Audio-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."}, {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K . SGLang The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs. From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \ uv run sglang_meta serve \ --model-path "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 \ --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \ --tp-size 4 \ --ep-size 4 \ --port 30000 The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP
