items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 50 +44 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM . SGLang Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s: python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 4 \ --attention-backend trtllm_mha \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell): python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 8 \ --attention-backend fa3 \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 Inference Providers Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon. import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "https://router.huggingface.co/v1" , api_key=os.environ[ "HF_TOKEN" ], ) completion = client.chat.completions.create( model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto" , messages=[{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is the capital of France?" }], ) print (completion.choices[ 0 ].message) Inference Endpoints We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4 , or install with the hf cli like so: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam What we tested We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809 Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088 * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. Post-training Beam You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT with TRL The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes. After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself. Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR . GRPO with Miles Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. items.raw_text: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 50 +44 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. items.summary: Back to Articles TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 28 +22 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. items.content: Back to Articles TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 28 +22 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron. Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx . New backend, native interface in HF libraries To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron . This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so. TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile . For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron. Transformers Inference Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices. The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations. import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401 from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B" MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024 PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512 dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) world_size = dist.get_world_size() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.bfloat16, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size), device_mesh=DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range (world_size))), ). eval () tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) if tokenizer.pad_token is None : tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token tokenizer.padding_side = "left" inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "The future of AI is" }], add_generation_prompt= True , padding= True , tokenizer_kwargs={ "pad_to_multiple_of" : PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE}, return_tensors= "pt" , ) generation_config = GenerationConfig( max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , use_cache= True , pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, cache_implementation= "static" , max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN, prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE, compile_config=CompileConfig(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= False , dynamic= False ), ) with torch.no_grad(): output_ids = model.generate( inputs[ "input_ids" ], attention_mask=inputs[ "attention_mask" ], generation_config=generation_config, ) if dist.get_rank() == 0 : prompt_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] print (tokenizer.decode(output_ids[ 0 , prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens= True )) Training Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings. Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer . If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar. import os import torch from datasets import load_dataset from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser def main ( script_args, training_args, model_args ): # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660) torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False training_args.model_init_kwargs = { "revision" : model_args.model_revision, "trust_remote_code" : training_args.trust_remote_code, "attn_implementation" : model_args.attn_implementation, "dtype" : model_args.dtype, "device_map" : None , } if int (os.environ.get( "WORLD_SIZE" , "1" )) > 1 : # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded training_args.model_init_kwargs[ "distributed_config" ] = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ.get( "TP_SIZE" , "1" )), fsdp_size= int (os.environ.get( "FSDP_SIZE" , "1" )), ) # Prepare dataset train_dataset = load_dataset( script_args.dataset_name, name=script_args.dataset_config, split=script_args.dataset_train_split, ) # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset. train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns([ "messages" ]) # Training trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model_args.model_name_or_path, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir) trainer.end() if __name__ == "__main__" : parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig)) script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config() main(script_args, training_args, model_args) Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs , SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained , and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config. Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium: Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure. Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 . The command below launches training with torchrun , which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node . The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups. TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \ --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \ --dataset_train_split train_sft \ --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max_length 2048 \ --packing true \ --packing_strategy wrapped \ --learning_rate 2e-5 \ --warmup_steps 0.03 \ --num_train_epochs 1 \ --logging_steps 2 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --save_only_model true \ --torch_compile true We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance. Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware. Diffusers Inference Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP: import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig # Distributed devices initialization dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) # TP dev = torch.neuron.current_device() mesh = DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range ( 8 ))) # TP=8 # Pipeline initialization model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1" transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( model, subfolder= "transformer" , torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP ) pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( model, transformer=transformer, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe.vae.to(dev) pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) # Image generation emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt= "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting" , device= "cpu" ) # text encoder stays on CPU image = pipe( prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev), prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None , height= 1024 , width= 1024 , num_inference_steps= 40 , generator=torch.Generator( "cpu" ).manual_seed( 0 ), # same noise on every rank ).images[ 0 ] if dist.get_rank() == 0 : image.save( "out.png" ) You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py . More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . Kernels Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub. You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium! Acknowledgments Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible. items.content: Back to Articles ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model Enterprise Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 24 +18 Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan ashwath-vaithina Follow ibm-research Vatche Isahagian Vatche Follow ibm-research Vinod Muthusamy vinodmut Follow ibm-research Jayaram Radhakrishnan jayaramkr Follow ibm-research Evelyn Duesterwald evduester Follow ibm-research Gaodan Fang gaodan-fang Follow ibm-research Punleuk Oum illeatmyhat Follow ibm-research G Thomas gsthomasx Follow ibm-research Michał Ulewicz Michal Follow ibm-research Merve Unuvar mrvnvr Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights. Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt. ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed. Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions. τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline . We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using gpt-4.1 as the agent model and gpt-5.5 as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list: You are a customer service agent that helps users according to the policy below. Always follow the policy strictly. Use the provided tools when needed. <policy> # Retail agent policy As a retail agent, you can help users: - cancel or modify pending orders - return or exchange delivered orders - modify their default user address … </policy> ## Guidelines learned from past task attempts (follow these carefully): - Authenticate the user before taking any order-related action. Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1). Table 1. Guideline configurations and retained guideline counts by domain. Variant Guidelines included in context Retail Airline baseline no guidelines 0 0 sup3 support n ≥ 3 (high-support core) 31 14 lossless all guidelines 292 101 The metrics we track. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average. Held-out agent performance using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Parentheses show percentage-point changes from baseline. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw. ALTK-Evolve tops the leaderboard comparison Submissions are scored on the full base split (train ∪ test), as τ²-bench requires, and reported at Pass^4 . This is where the practical upshot shows up — prompt-level memory carries agents using each base model into , or past , current frontier company: Retail: #1 . Using stock gpt-4.1 and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points . Pass^4 comparison between ALTK-Evolve runs and the τ²-bench leaderboard snapshot from October 12, 2026. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs , automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage. items.content: Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. items.content: Back to Articles NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required Enterprise + Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 7 +1 Joshua Przybylko jprzybylko Follow nvidia Jure Leskovec profjure Follow nvidia Matthias Fey rusty1s Follow nvidia Federico Lopez flopeznv Follow nvidia Valter Hudovernik valterh-nv Follow nvidia Akihiro Nitta akihironitta-nv Follow nvidia Ramona Bendias RBendiasN Follow nvidia Ardrian Wong aw777 Follow nvidia TL;DR NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596 Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications. The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons: Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational. Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization. Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions. Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational ( paper , documentation ), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required. How Kumo Relational Works Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation ( e.g. , "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort. Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning , reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target ( e.g. , "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units"). ![Overview of the NVIDIA Kumo Relational system: (a) database integration, (b) a prompting interface that turns natural language into a predictive query, and (c) automatic context generation feeding the NVIDIA Kumo Relational model, which scales horizontally across tenants.] Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference. To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works: ![Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input with task, users, orders and items tables; (b) column and row attention within tables with injected context targets; (c) graph attention and cross-sample attention across tables.] Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables. Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL) , a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage. Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates. Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs. How Kumo Relational Was Built Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures. The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. Members of the Kumo team helped develop PluRel and co-authored the original paper. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the PluRel paper shows that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases. Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. When maximum accuracy matters, Kumo Relational can also be fine-tuned on a specific dataset and task. Performance In this paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On the RelArena-α leaderboard, which compares relational models and systems on RelBench V1, it also sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front out of the box: ![Scatter plot of the RelArena-α leaderboard: relative accuracy as Elo across tasks (y-axis) versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (x-axis, log scale). Kumo Relational sits on the Pareto front at about 17 seconds and Elo 1,842. The highest-scoring entry, rt-plurel, reaches Elo 1,878 at about 7,300 seconds, roughly 430 times slower. Every other foundation model, feature-engineering system, and supervised model scores lower and runs slower than Kumo Relational.] Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard: Elo across tasks versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than the highest-scoring entry at similar accuracy. The paper also reports that on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and recent tabular foundation models by about 25%, and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when many noisy columns are added. Limitations Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions, which used at most 10,000 context examples in our benchmarks. Fine-tuning of the foundation model is designed for exactly this case. Predictive signals must also be reachable within a limited number of hops, so start with a focused query over a few relevant tables and expand the graph as needed. Demo Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through a custom graph engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. It is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular . The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The code below passes context examples, prediction entities, and their related tables to the model: # pip install structured-data-models import sdm model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device= "cuda" ) pred = model( # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets): x_context=..., y_context=..., # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps): x_query=..., # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities: related_context_tables=..., related_query_tables=..., ) See the library's relational examples for complete RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines, including how to sample each entity's related tables. To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request: # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]' import sdm_client client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url= "http://localhost:8001" ) # NIM URL query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery( # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL): "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id" , # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred): { "users" : ..., "orders" : ...}, ) pred = client.predict( # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict: query.materialize(indices=[ 1 , 2 , 3 ]), model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(), ) See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks. Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper , explore the quickstart notebook , or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here . Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596 Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models/ Client code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client Client PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models-client/ Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational Quickstart notebook: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client/blob/main/examples/local/relational.ipynb Related Research: Predictive Query Language (PQL) , PluRel , Kumo Tabular Acknowledgements We thank the entire Kumo team for their invaluable support. Special thanks go to Josh Przybylko, Adi Wadaskar, Hema Raghavan, Manush Murali, Raja Rao DV, Keti Jovanovska, Zack Drach, Vanja Josifovski, Myungwhan Kim, Blaž Stojanovič, Siyang Xie, Alan Krumholz, Effy Fang, Abdullah Al-chihabi, Disha Dubey, Devan Johnson, Joseph Oliveira, Angela Liu, Miha Pelko, Vedaant Jain, Sally Liu, Aleksandar S. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.30118 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks Authors: Francesco Mori , Melanie Weber View a PDF of the paper titled The role of locality and weight sharing in convolutional neural networks, by Francesco Mori and Melanie Weber View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The success of convolutional neural networks is often attributed to locality and weight sharing. However, how these two properties separately shape learning, and how their effects depend on the spatial correlations of natural images, remain poorly understood. We address these questions in a teacher-student model with a convolutional teacher acting on $P$ input positions with correlation $c$ between positions. We compare convolutional and locally connected students trained by online stochastic gradient descent, and derive ordinary differential equations that describe their dynamics exactly in the limit of large feature dimension $D$. For uncorrelated positions ($c = 0$), the two students follow the same learning trajectory, with the convolutional student learning exactly $P$ times faster. We also find that locality affects the sample complexity: a student that matches the kernel size of the teacher recovers it from $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D)$ samples, whereas $\mathcal{O}_{D}(D\log(D))$ samples are needed with a larger kernel. For $c > 0$, spatial correlations can reduce the advantage of weight sharing. The asymptotic error of the convolutional student grows with $c$, whereas that of the locally connected student is independent of $c$ and overall lower when evaluated at the same learning rate. When the learning rate is instead tuned to the training horizon, however, the locally connected student wins at early times and the convolutional student at late times, with a transition that we predict analytically.
