items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.30107 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching Authors: Yunpeng Mei , Xiaowen Zhu , Chenyu Wang , Chenbo Xin , Hongjie Cao , Jiamin Wang , Jie Chen , Gang Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching, by Yunpeng Mei and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Flow matching trains a continuum of velocity regression problems but usually reports a loss averaged over interpolation time, obscuring which regions are limited by intrinsic ambiguity and which remain data-limited. We introduce the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP), $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$, the time-local Bayes-risk floor of velocity prediction, and decompose time-resolved loss as $L_N(t)=\mathcal{A}_v(t)+R(t;N)$, where only the excess term $R(t;N)$ is reducible by more data or a different estimator. For $N$ training samples and a $K$-component mixture in the structured example, we prove two statistical benchmarks. In an intrinsic local-regression benchmark, $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$ enters the time-dependent noise factor of the standard nonparametric rate. In separated isotropic Gaussian mixtures, the Bayes velocity becomes locally affine, and a label-oracle residual-regression benchmark has parametric excess-risk scale $K\mathcal{A}_v(t)/N$, matched within the same separated residual Gaussian-location subproblem. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate this diagnostic through a dense transition sweep, calibrated oracle-to-blind and empirical-proxy audits, and a local controlled time-sampler stress test in which a frozen reducible-error proxy reduces reducible loss while cross-cell sensitivity delimits aggressive sampling. On CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature flow, guided time sampling reduces uniformly evaluated velocity loss by $6.78\%$ and global feature Fréchet distance (FD) by $23.6\%$, while class-conditional kernel inception distance (KID) shows no improvement. VAP turns an averaged flow-matching objective into a time-resolved diagnostic for locating ambiguity-limited and data-limited regions. For any trained velocity estimator, the time-resolved loss decomposes as L N ​ ( t ) = 𝒜 v ​ ( t ) + R ⁡ ( t , N ) L_{N}(t)=\mathcal{A}_{v}(t)+R(t;N) , where 𝒜 v ​ ( t ) \mathcal{A}_{v}(t) is the irreducible Bayes-risk floor and R ⁡ ( t , N ) R(t;N) is the reducible excess risk. Only R ⁡ ( t , N ) R(t;N) can be lowered by collecting more data or changing the estimator. VAP complements empirical scaling laws and time-aggregated generative-model baselines [ 14 , 6 , 24 , 16 ] . It asks which interpolation times are data-limited, which are ambiguity-limited, and where controlled models separate these regimes. Figure 1 previews this time-local view. Figure 1: Velocity ambiguity profiles localize where flow matching needs data. The flow matching path defines a continuum of velocity prediction problems. VAP separates the irreducible ambiguity floor from the reducible excess error that more data or a different estimator can affect. Main results. The paper develops VAP at three levels. First, we prove the exact Bayes-risk decomposition above and instantiate a time-local intrinsic regression benchmark: on compact time intervals, the local excess-risk rate has the usual nonparametric exponent, with time dependence controlled by 𝒜 v ​ ( t ) \mathcal{A}_{v}(t) up to bounded factors. Third, controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate the diagnostic when the ambiguity floor is observable. They show separated-regime parametric scaling under a reliability-filtered readout, oracle-to-blind agreement with the analytic between-component label cost, and small but measurable blind neural residuals. A local time-sampler stress test further shows that a frozen proxy from disjoint source runs can produce same-sign paired reducible-loss reductions in the canonical balanced cell, while cross-cell sensitivity delimits aggressive pure sampling. Fourth, a CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature-flow experiment tests transfer to natural feature distributions: guided sampling reduces uniformly evaluated velocity loss by 6.78 % 6.78\% and global feature FD by 23.6 % 23.6\% . Macro conditional KID shows no gain, and lower recall and effective covariance rank reveal a diversity cost. Contributions. This paper makes the following five contributions. 1. A time-local Bayes-risk diagnostic for flow matching. This turns one averaged flow matching loss into a time-resolved separation between irreducible ambiguity and reducible error. 2. Scoped statistical benchmarks for reducible error. For an intrinsic local regression benchmark, 𝒜 v ​ ( t ) \mathcal{A}_{v}(t) enters the standard nonparametric rate as the time-dependent noise level up to bounded factors. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate VAP as a time-resolved diagnostic, showing analytic-empirical agreement, separated-regime parametric scaling, and documented sensitivity to the reliability readout. A local controlled time-sampler stress test further shows that a frozen reducible-error proxy from disjoint source runs can produce same-sign paired reducible-loss reductions, with cross-cell sensitivity delimiting aggressive pure sampling. 4. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.30104 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard Authors: Sonja Topf , Ana Sanchez-Fernandez , Günter Klambauer View a PDF of the paper titled BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images - A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard, by Sonja Topf and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench, a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes. items.content: \tl_set:Ne \code code BatchBench: Benchmarking AI Robustness to Batch Effects and Domain Shift in Biomedical Images – A JUMP Cell Painting Leaderboard Sonja Topf Affiliation: ELLIS Unit Linz and LIT AI Lab, Institute for Machine Learning Affiliation: Clinical Research Institute for Medical AIJohannes Kepler University, Linz, Austria Ana Sanchez-Fernandez Affiliation: ELLIS Unit Linz and LIT AI Lab, Institute for Machine Learning Günter Klambauer Affiliation: ELLIS Unit Linz and LIT AI Lab, Institute for Machine Learning Affiliation: Clinical Research Institute for Medical AIJohannes Kepler University, Linz, Austria Abstract Despite recent advances, current AI systems remain highly susceptible to domain shifts, particularly in biomedical imaging, where images are usually acquired under substantially different experimental conditions. Although recent domain adaptation methods have made substantial progress, significant performance gaps under domain shift persist. To measure progress in this regard, we introduce BatchBench , a leaderboard that evaluates and compares the robustness of AI systems on biomedical images from unseen experimental batches and data sources. BatchBench is built on JUMP-CP, one of the largest publicly available biomedical imaging datasets. Generated using the Cell Painting assay, JUMP-CP exhibits pronounced batch effects and domain shifts, making it a challenging testbed for evaluating robustness to distributional changes. Keywords: biomedical imaging, domain-adaptation, test-time-adaptation, cell-painting, jump-cp, microscopy, distribution-shift 1 Introduction Figure 1: Source-level split of the BatchBench leaderboard. Nine sources of JUMP-CP-2k are public (eight for training, source 2 for validation). Sources 4, 6, 9, and 13 are held out as the private test set, so that every leaderboard entry is evaluated on unseen data-generating sources. Vulnerability of AI systems under domain shift and batch effects. Deep learning methods often assume that training and test data are sampled from the same underlying distribution. However, in practice, biological images are acquired across experimental batches, plates, and sites, which introduces non-biological variation known as batch effects . These effects shift the distribution of the input images, such that a model that performs well on its training distribution can fail on images from a new experimental batch or laboratory. This limits the use of AI in applications such as drug discovery, where new data are generated continuously and under changing conditions. JUMP-CP and CellPainting. High-content screening data obtained with the Cell Painting assay 1 provide a clear example of this problem. The JUMP Cell Painting dataset (JUMP-CP) 2 , one of the largest public biomedical imaging datasets, was obtained from 13 data-generating centers ( sources ) using different microscopes and laboratory workflows. As a result, JUMP-CP exhibits substantial batch effects across multiple levels of its data hierarchy. Because every image is annotated with its source, experimental batch, and plate, JUMP-CP provides a exceptional setting in which domain shifts are both pronounced and explicitly annotated at multiple levels. Domain adaptation (DA) methods address domain shift either by learning domain-invariant representations during training or by adapting the model to unlabeled target data at inference time, i.e. test-time adaptation (TTA) 9 , 8 , 3 , 5 , 11 , 7 . These methods have substantially improved robustness on natural images. Nevertheless, their effectiveness on biomedical images from unseen experimental conditionsremains poorly characterized, and results reported on different subsets, splits, and metrics are rarely comparable. The BatchBench Leaderboard. We introduce the BatchBench leaderboard , an open benchmark for comparing AI models on the identification of chemical perturbations in Cell Painting images acquired from sources not seen during training. The leaderboard is designed to be used by several research communities: • Domain adaptation and test-time adaptation. BatchBench evaluates multi-source adaptation to unseen target domains under combined covariate and label shift. Methods that adapt to unlabeled test images, as well as methods that do not perform test-time adaptation, can be submitted through a common \code adapt()/ \code predict() interface. • Biomedical imaging and foundation models. BatchBench evaluates whether pretrained image encoders and specialized architectures generalize to unseen imaging sites, an important requirement for deployment that is not captured by in-distribution evaluation. • Cell Painting and JUMP-CP. BatchBench provides a standardized source-level evaluation of image-based compound profiling on JUMP-CP using fixed splits and a private test set. The leaderboard presents three components: (i) JUMP-CP-2k , a curated subset of JUMP-CP covering 2,000 compounds, with nine public sources and four sources held out as a private test set (Section 2 ); (ii) a containerized submission protocol that keeps the test data private and supports both conventional and test-time adaptation methods (Section 3 ); and (iii) six baseline entries covering standard supervised training, domain-invariant training, test-time adaptation, and meta-learning (Sections 5 and 6 ). The baseline entries show that test-time adaptation reduces the domain gap but does not close it. For compounds with few training images, every current entry remains close to chance level. The leaderboard is open for submissions on Hugging Face . 2 The BatchBench leaderboard Problem setting. Let 𝒟 ( 1 ) , … , 𝒟 ( S ) \mathcal{D}^{(1)},\ldots,\mathcal{D}^{(S)} denote labeled data from S S training sources, where each sample consists of an image 𝒙 \boldsymbol{x} , its compound label y ∈ { 1 , … , K } y\in\{1,\ldots,K\} , and its domain metadata 𝒅 = ( source , batch , plate ) \boldsymbol{d}=(\text{source},\text{batch},\text{plate}) . At test time, a submission receives the unlabeled images { 𝒙 n } n = 1 N \{\boldsymbol{x}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} and their metadata { 𝒅 n } n = 1 N \{\boldsymbol{d}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} from sources that do not occur in the training data. It may adapt to these images before predicting their labels. The leaderboard thus evaluates multi-source domain adaptation to unseen target domains . The setting covers domain generalization (no adaptation), test-time adaptation, and in-context adaptation as special cases. As the the domain metadata are hierarchical, submissions can define domains at the level of sources, experimental batches, or plates. Task. Each input is a single five-channel Cell Painting image (DNA, RNA, ER, AGP, and Mito). The task is to identify which of the K = 2,000 K=2{,}000 compounds the imaged cells were treated with. Test images come exclusively from held-out sources, so every test image also originates from an unseen experimental batch and an unseen plate. Compound selection and sampling. JUMP-CP comprises images from 13 sources and more than 100,000 compound and genetic perturbations 2 . We used the dataset cpg0016 2 , available from the Cell Painting Gallery 10 on the Registry of Open Data on AWS (https://registry.opendata.aws/cellpainting-gallery/). To obtain a dataset that is practical to download and train on, we selected the 2,000 most frequent compounds, retained all wells treated with these compounds, and sampled one image (field of view) per well uniformly at random. Domain metadata and controls. Each sample is annotated with its source, experimental batch, and plate identifiers. Submissions may use these identifiers as domain labels during training and to group test images at inference. Images of negative-control wells (DMSO-treated, unperturbed cells) from the training sources are provided as a separate file. They can be used, for example, for control-based normalization 7 . Preprocessing. From each original image we extract a 500 × 500 500\times 500 pixel center crop. We then apply illumination correction by clipping the top 0.01% of pixel intensities in each channel. Splits. Sources 4, 6, 9, and 13 form the private test set of the leaderboard and are never released (Figure 1 ). The remaining nine sources are public. Source 2 serves as the validation set for model selection, and the other eight sources form the training set. Evaluation subsets. Compounds differ greatly in their number of training images and in the strength of their phenotypes. In addition to the overall accuracy, the leaderboard therefore reports accuracy on three subsets of the test set: • POSCON : the eight positive-control compounds, present on every plate, usually at fixed well positions. They have many training images and strong, well-characterized phenotypes. • TARGET : 293 compounds from the JUMP-Target collection, a reference library chosen to cover diverse biological targets and mechanisms of action. • REST : all remaining compounds, each represented by few images (about 12 per compound in the public split). The three subsets correspond to increasingly difficult regimes: abundant data with strong phenotypes ( POSCON ), a curated mechanism-of-action reference set ( TARGET ), and a long tail of rare classes ( REST ). Label shift. In addition to the source shift, the class distribution differs between the public and the test split. POSCON images make up 51% of the public split but 36% of the test set; TARGET images increase from 25% to 55%; REST images decrease from 24% to 9% (Table 1 ). The leaderboard therefore evaluates adaptation under combined covariate and label shift, a setting in which many TTA methods are known to degrade 6 , 12 . Table 1: Statistics of JUMP-CP-2k per split and evaluation subset. The private test set of the leaderboard consists of the held-out sources 4, 6, 9, and 13. Samples/compound is the mean number of images per compound. Source, batch, and plate identifiers are provided for every sample. Split Subset Compounds Samples Samples/compound Sources Batches Plates Public (train + val) POSCON 8 48,574 6,071.75 9 102 1,534 TARGET 293 23,455 80.05 7 63 76 REST 1,926 23,186 12.04 9 85 931 Private test POSCON 8 16,691 2,086.38 4 42 370 TARGET 293 25,352 86.53 4 40 62 REST 1,864 4,107 2.20 2 18 179 Research questions. The leaderboard is designed to answer questions that are open in each of the communities above, for example: • Do domain adaptation and TTA methods developed on natural-image benchmarks transfer to biological domain shift? • At which level of the domain hierarchy (source, batch, or plate) should adaptation be performed? • Do pretrained microscopy foundation models generalize to unseen imaging sources better than models trained from scratch? • Can models identify compounds with weak phenotypes and few training images ( TARGET , REST ) on unseen sources? 3 Submitting to the leaderboard Submission format. A leaderboard submission is a public Git repository together with a commit hash. The repository must contain the training code and a Dockerfile from which the evaluation server builds a container image. Submissions are therefore independent of the deep learning framework and model architecture. The image must provide a \code Submission class that implements two methods, \code adapt() and \code predict(). Ready-to-run example submissions for all baseline entries are available in our baseline repository and can serve as templates. Evaluation. The evaluation server passes the private test images, as an array of shape ( N , H , W , 5 ) (N,H,W,5) , together with a metadata list containing the source, batch, and plate identifier of every image, to both \code adapt() and \code predict(). No labels are provided. \code adapt() may update the model using the unlabeled test images and their metadata, which permits test-time adaptation. Methods that do not adapt should implement it as a no-op. \code predict() must return one prediction per image, in the original order. Metric and ranking. Leaderboard entries are ranked by overall accuracy, i.e., the fraction of correctly classified images in the entire test set. Because POSCON and TARGET together contain over 90% of the test images, this metric is dominated by these two subsets. The leaderboard therefore additionally reports accuracy on POSCON , TARGET , and REST separately, so that progress on rare compounds remains visible. Scores are published on the leaderboard once the manual evaluation finishes. Rules. Submissions may not use any data from the held-out sources (4, 6, 9, and 13) for training, pre-training, or model selection. This also applies to pretrained models whose pre-training data include these sources. Test-time adaptation on the unlabeled test images through \code adapt() is permitted. 4 Development datasets To lower the entry barrier and enable fast prototyping before a leaderboard submission, we release two smaller variants of JUMP-CP-2k: • JUMP-CP-MNIST contains only the eight positive-control compounds. Its images are downsampled to 200 × 200 200\times 200 pixels, and the five imaging channels (DNA, RNA, ER, AGP, and Mito) are combined into three channels, so that standard RGB architectures and pretrained models can be applied without modification. • JUMP-CP-2k-200 contains all 2,000 compounds of JUMP-CP-2k at the reduced resolution of 200 × 200 200\times 200 pixels, with all five channels. Both variants use the same source-level split as JUMP-CP-2k. Leaderboard rankings are computed on the full-resolution private test set. 5 Baseline entries The leaderboard is initialized with six baseline entries that represent the main strategies for handling domain shift. All use a ResNet18 4 backbone whose first convolution takes five input channels. • No adaptation (ResNet18). A classifier trained with standard empirical risk minimization on the training sources and applied to the test sources unchanged. • Domain-invariant training: DANN 3 and deepCORAL 8 . Both methods encourage representations that do not depend on the domain during training, adversarially (DANN) or by aligning second-order feature statistics (deepCORAL). We use the source identifier as the domain label. • Test-time adaptation: AdaBN 5 and TENT 9 . Both use the trained ResNet18 baseline and adapt it only at inference. AdaBN replaces the BatchNorm statistics with statistics computed on the test images. TENT additionally updates the BatchNorm affine parameters by minimizing the entropy of the predictions. For both methods, test images are grouped by plate, so that each plate is adapted separately. • Meta-learning: ARM-BN 11 . and CS-ARM-BN 7 ARM-BN trains the model episodically to classify images using BatchNorm statistics computed from an unlabeled context batch of the same domain. At test time, the statistics are computed in the same way from the unlabeled test images. Hyperparameters were tuned with Bayesian optimization, and for every method the model with the highest accuracy on source 2 was selected. The code of all baseline entries is available in our GitHub repository . 6 Results Table 2 reports the current leaderboard entries. Test-time adaptation reduces the domain gap. Without adaptation, ResNet18 reaches an average overall accuracy of 0.175. Re-estimating the BatchNorm statistics on each test plate (AdaBN) raises this to 0.244. Most of this gain comes from POSCON , where accuracy increases from 0.465 to 0.646. TENT’s additional entropy minimization yields a higher performance in the POSCON group, but no improvement in TARGET or REST . Domain-invariant training does not improve over the non-adapted baseline: DANN reaches 0.170. The domain gap remains for compounds with few images. Performance on POSCON is substantially higher than on TARGET and REST , consistent with the much larger number of training images per compound, lower number of classes and strong phenotypes. These factors are absent for most TARGET and REST compounds, and none of the current entries compensates for them. Identifying compounds with weak phenotypes and few training images on unseen sources is therefore the main open problem posed by the leaderboard. Table 2: Baseline entries of the BatchBench leaderboard, evaluated on the private test set (held-out sources 4, 6, 9, and 13). Values are the mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over three runs with different random seeds. Chance level is 1 / 2,000 = 0.0005 1/2{,}000=0.0005 . Preprocessing. From each original image we extract a 500 × 500 500\times 500 pixel center crop. We then apply illumination correction by clipping the top 0.01% of pixel intensities in each channel. Splits. Sources 4, 6, 9, and 13 form the private test set of the leaderboard and are never released (Figure 1 ). The remaining nine sources are public. Source 2 serves as the validation set for model selection, and the other eight sources form the training set. Evaluation subsets. Compounds differ greatly in their number of training images and in the strength of their phenotypes. In addition to the overall accuracy, the leaderboard therefore reports accuracy on three subsets of the test set: • POSCON : the eight positive-control compounds, present on every plate, usually at fixed well positions. They have many training images and strong, well-characterized phenotypes. • TARGET : 293 compounds from the JUMP-Target collection, a reference library chosen to cover diverse biological targets and mechanisms of action. • REST : all remaining compounds, each represented by few images (about 12 per compound in the public split). The three subsets correspond to increasingly difficult regimes: abundant data with strong phenotypes ( POSCON ), a curated mechanism-of-action reference set ( TARGET ), and a long tail of rare classes ( REST ). Label shift. In addition to the source shift, the class distribution differs between the public and the test split. POSCON images make up 51% of the public split but 36% of the test set; TARGET images increase from 25% to 55%; REST images decrease from 24% to 9% (Table 1 ). The leaderboard therefore evaluates adaptation under combined covariate and label shift, a setting in which many TTA methods are known to degrade 6 , 12 . Table 1: Statistics of JUMP-CP-2k per split and evaluation subset. The private test set of the leaderboard consists of the held-out sources 4, 6, 9, and 13. Samples/compound is the mean number of images per compound. Source, batch, and plate identifiers are provided for every sample. Split Subset Compounds Samples Samples/compound Sources Batches Plates Public (train + val) POSCON 8 48,574 6,071.75 9 102 1,534 TARGET 293 23,455 80.05 7 63 76 REST 1,926 23,186 12.04 9 85 931 Private test POSCON 8 16,691 2,086.38 4 42 370 TARGET 293 25,352 86.53 4 40 62 REST 1,864 4,107 2.20 2 18 179 Research questions. The leaderboard is designed to answer questions that are open in each of the communities above, for example: • Do domain adaptation and TTA methods developed on natural-image benchmarks transfer to biological domain shift? • At which level of the domain hierarchy (source, batch, or plate) should adaptation be performed? • Do pretrained microscopy foundation models generalize to unseen imaging sources better than models trained from scratch? • Can models identify compounds with weak phenotypes and few training images ( TARGET , REST ) on unseen sources? 3 Submitting to the leaderboard Submission format. A leaderboard submission is a public Git repository together with a commit hash. The repository must contain the training code and a Dockerfile from which the evaluation server builds a container image. Submissions are therefore independent of the deep learning framework and model architecture. The image must provide a \code Submission class that implements two methods, \code adapt() and \code predict(). Ready-to-run example submissions for all baseline entries are available in our baseline repository and can serve as templates. Evaluation. The evaluation server passes the private test images, as an array of shape ( N , H , W , 5 ) (N,H,W,5) , together with a metadata list containing the source, batch, and plate identifier of every image, to both \code adapt() and \code predict(). No labels are provided. \code adapt() may update the model using the unlabeled test images and their metadata, which permits test-time adaptation. Methods that do not adapt should implement it as a no-op. \code predict() must return one prediction per image, in the original order. Metric and ranking. Leaderboard entries are ranked by overall accuracy, i.e., the fraction of correctly classified images in the entire test set. Because POSCON and TARGET together contain over 90% of the test images, this metric is dominated by these two subsets. The leaderboard therefore additionally reports accuracy on POSCON , TARGET , and REST separately, so that progress on rare compounds remains visible. Scores are published on the leaderboard once the manual evaluation finishes. Rules. Submissions may not use any data from the held-out sources (4, 6, 9, and 13) for training, pre-training, or model selection. This also applies to pretrained models whose pre-training data include these sources. Test-time adaptation on the unlabeled test images through \code adapt() is permitted. 4 Development datasets To lower the entry barrier and enable fast prototyping before a leaderboard submission, we release two smaller variants of JUMP-CP-2k: • JUMP-CP-MNIST contains only the eight positive-control compounds. Its images are downsampled to 200 × 200 200\times 200 pixels, and the five imaging channels (DNA, RNA, ER, AGP, and Mito) are combined into three channels, so that standard RGB architectures and pretrained models can be applied without modification. • JUMP-CP-2k-200 contains all 2,000 compounds of JUMP-CP-2k at the reduced resolution of 200 × 200 200\times 200 pixels, with all five channels. Both variants use the same source-level split as JUMP-CP-2k. Leaderboard rankings are computed on the full-resolution private test set. 5 Baseline entries The leaderboard is initialized with six baseline entries that represent the main strategies for handling domain shift. All use a ResNet18 4 backbone whose first convolution takes five input channels. • No adaptation (ResNet18). A classifier trained with standard empirical risk minimization on the training sources and applied to the test sources unchanged. • Domain-invariant training: DANN 3 and deepCORAL 8 . Both methods encourage representations that do not depend on the domain during training, adversarially (DANN) or by aligning second-order feature statistics (deepCORAL). We use the source identifier as the domain label. • Test-time adaptation: AdaBN 5 and TENT 9 . Both use the trained ResNet18 baseline and adapt it only at inference. AdaBN replaces the BatchNorm statistics with statistics computed on the test images. TENT additionally updates the BatchNorm affine parameters by minimizing the entropy of the predictions. For both methods, test images are grouped by plate, so that each plate is adapted separately. • Meta-learning: ARM-BN 11 . and CS-ARM-BN 7 ARM-BN trains the model episodically to classify images using BatchNorm statistics computed from an unlabeled context batch of the same domain. At test time, the statistics are computed in the same way from the unlabeled test images. Hyperparameters were tuned with Bayesian optimization, and for every method the model with the highest accuracy on source 2 was selected. The code of all baseline entries is available in our GitHub repository . 6 Results Table 2 reports the current leaderboard entries. Test-time adaptation reduces the domain gap. Without adaptation, ResNet18 reaches an average overall accuracy of 0.175. Re-estimating the BatchNorm statistics on each test plate (AdaBN) raises this to 0.244. Most of this gain comes from POSCON , where accuracy increases from 0.465 to 0.646. TENT’s additional entropy minimization yields a higher performance in the POSCON group, but no improvement in TARGET or REST . Domain-invariant training does not improve over the non-adapted baseline: DANN reaches 0.170. The domain gap remains for compounds with few images. Performance on POSCON is substantially higher than on TARGET and REST , consistent with the much larger number of training images per compound, lower number of classes and strong phenotypes. These factors are absent for most TARGET and REST compounds, and none of the current entries compensates for them. Identifying compounds with weak phenotypes and few training images on unseen sources is therefore the main open problem posed by the leaderboard. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.30072 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis Authors: Xinzhe Wang , Xudong Weng , Zang Li , Shaolei Zhang View a PDF of the paper titled Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis, by Xinzhe Wang and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters. Comments: 23 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables. The right column reports the Chart-only minus Text-only gap. 3 Learning to Use Charts through Experience Section 2 leaves a concrete target. Charts already carry sufficient evidence, yet agents do not invoke them where they help, so representation choice has to become a decision the agent makes from the current analysis state. Reaching that target requires three things. The agent needs a place to hold representation knowledge, a way to acquire that knowledge from its own behaviour, and a way to consult it while analysing. ChartMind addresses these three needs in order. Section 3.1 stores experience as editable documents that keep analytical and representational knowledge side by side. Section 3.2 distils those documents from conditioned rollouts under outcome and step-level supervision, with a validation gate on every update. Section 3.3 lets the data agent consult the frozen documents inside its own analysis loop. Figure 3 shows the pipeline. Base model parameters stay unchanged throughout. 3.1 Storing Experience as Editable Documents Representation choice depends on the analysis state, so the knowledge that governs it has to stay inspectable and revisable after training ends. We therefore keep experience outside the model as a document store that the agent reads during analysis and a builder revises during distillation. This choice also lets us audit what the agent learned and freeze it before any external evaluation. Two-layer storage. To make experience readable, editable, and callable on demand, we organise it as a two-layer package. The storage layer is a filesystem tree in which an entry document indexes independent experience documents. Each document carries metadata fields name , description , and category together with its content, which supports direct reading, targeted editing, and versioning. The tool layer exposes Read , Create , Edit , and Bash for managing the package. The builder agent uses all four, while the data agent accesses experience only through a read-only retrieval interface, implemented as kb_read in downstream experiments. The data agent first fetches document metadata and then reads relevant content on demand, so context load stays low and grows with task complexity. Analysis and representation experience. To separate what to compute from how to represent it, we index two experience families under different categories. Analysis experience ℰ ana \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ana}} holds reusable rules for selecting, organising, and verifying analytical operations. Representation experience ℰ repr \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{repr}} holds rules for when intermediate evidence should be represented as text, charts, or a mixture, and for how to consume the resulting evidence in later steps. The two families share the same storage and tool interface, and they are always updated and validated as one package. We write the v v -th accepted version as ℰ ( v ) = ( ℰ ana ( v ) , ℰ repr ( v ) ) \mathcal{E}^{(v)}=\bigl(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ana}}^{(v)},\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{repr}}^{(v)}\bigr) . 3.2 Distilling Experience from Conditioned Rollouts A single rollout per task reveals only the habit the backbone already has, and Section 2.2 shows that this habit is text-heavy for most backbones. Distillation from such data would reproduce the gap we want to close. We therefore force each task to be solved several times under different representation conditions, so the corpus contains chart-led trajectories even for backbones that would never produce them on their own, and outcome differences become attributable to representation choice. Conditioned rollout bundle. To realise this, we generate multiple trajectories per task while holding the base agent, tools, and interaction budget fixed. Let p i = ( D i , q i , z i , y i ⋆ ) p_{i}=(D_{i},q_{i},z_{i},y_{i}^{\star}) denote the i i -th ProbeBench , where the four elements are the data, question, task context, and reference answer. A trajectory generated under representation condition ρ ∈ { U , T , C 1 , C 2 , C 3 } \rho\in\{\mathrm{U},\mathrm{T},\mathrm{C}_{1},\mathrm{C}_{2},\mathrm{C}_{3}\} is denoted by τ i ρ \tau_{i}^{\rho} , and each task yields a bundle ℬ i = { τ i U , τ i T , τ i C 1 , τ i C 2 , τ i C 3 } , \mathcal{B}_{i}=\bigl\{\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{U}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{T}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{1}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{2}},\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{3}}\bigr\}, (1) where τ i U \tau_{i}^{\mathrm{U}} is an unconstrained rollout, τ i T \tau_{i}^{\mathrm{T}} is a text-preferred rollout, and { τ i C k } k = 1 3 \{\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{C}_{k}}\}_{k=1}^{3} are three chart-preferred rollouts. To keep the chart-preferred rollouts from collapsing onto a single visual habit, we enforce type exclusion across them. The second rollout cannot reuse any chart type used by the first, and the third cannot reuse any type used by the first two. This diversifies visual analyses without presuming that any chart type is intrinsically superior. Figure 3: Overall pipeline of ChartMind . Conditioned rollouts diversify representation preferences over each ProbeBench . A trajectory judge produces outcome scores and step-level attributions. A builder agent distils analysis and representation experience under a validation gate. Outcome and step signals. Bundle-level outcomes alone would tell the builder which trajectory performed best but not which decisions contributed to its performance, so we attach two labels to every trajectory. The outcome scoring function f score ​ ( τ i ρ ∣ q i , y i ⋆ ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] f_{\mathrm{score}}(\tau_{i}^{\rho}\mid q_{i},y_{i}^{\star})\!\in\![0,1] evaluates the final answer against the reference. The step-level attribution function f attr ​ ( τ i ρ ∣ q i , y i ⋆ ) f_{\mathrm{attr}}(\tau_{i}^{\rho}\mid q_{i},y_{i}^{\star}) labels each key step with a tag in { Helpful , Ineffective , Harmful } \{\texttt{Helpful},\texttt{Ineffective},\texttt{Harmful}\} and separates the contribution of analytical operations from that of representation choices. Together the two functions tell the builder which behaviours to retain and which to avoid. Insight induction and package revision. To turn labelled trajectories into transferable rules, we split ProbeBench into construction and validation sets so that all trajectories from one task remain in the same split. At each iteration, we sample b b tasks from the construction set and feed their bundles and labels to the builder. The builder first performs insight induction , comparing trajectories and their attributions to identify transferable analytical and representational patterns. It then performs package revision , reading the current package ℰ ( v − 1 ) \mathcal{E}^{(v-1)} and either merging new patterns into existing documents or creating fresh entries. Validation-gated update. An unconstrained builder can overwrite a working document with a pattern that held only for a single batch, so every proposal must demonstrate transferable value. Let Q ⁡ ( ℰ ) Q(\mathcal{E}) denote validation performance with package ℰ \mathcal{E} , and let ℰ ~ ( v ) \widetilde{\mathcal{E}}^{(v)} be the proposal at iteration v v . The update rule is ℰ ( v ) = { ℰ ~ ( v ) , Q ⁡ ( ℰ ~ ( v ) ) > Q ⁡ ( ℰ ( v − 1 ) ) , ℰ ( v − 1 ) , otherwise . \mathcal{E}^{(v)}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}^{(v)},&Q(\widetilde{\mathcal{E}}^{(v)})>Q(\mathcal{E}^{(v-1)}),\\[2.0pt] \mathcal{E}^{(v-1)},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (2) After multiple iterations, the accepted package ℰ ⋆ \mathcal{E}^{\star} is frozen for downstream use. The gate keeps validation performance monotonically nondecreasing and filters proposals that fit a single batch. 3.3 Consulting Experience inside the Analysis Loop A frozen package is useful only if the agent consults it when a representation decision arises. We therefore attach the package to the running analysis loop as a read-only resource, so no extra training, retrieval model, or change to the core ReAct execution loop is needed. Access to the frozen package. The data agent treats ℰ ⋆ \mathcal{E}^{\star} as external memory. It first receives document metadata, then reads the entries that match the question and the current analysis state. Reading costs a few tool calls and leaves the backbone untouched, so the same package serves every backbone we evaluate. Representation choice at each step. Analysis experience ℰ ana ⋆ \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ana}}^{\star} guides operation selection and verification, and representation experience ℰ repr ⋆ \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{repr}}^{\star} guides whether an intermediate result should be represented as text, charts, or both. Charts therefore enter the loop when the analysis state calls for visual pattern recognition, instead of appearing only as a final artefact. 4 Experiments This section evaluates ChartMind on three held-out benchmarks that cover analytical report generation, long-horizon exploration, and exact-answer analysis. We describe the benchmarks and evaluation protocol, report main results by capability, and analyse the mechanism through ablations. 4.1 Benchmarks To cover the main task forms of agentic data analysis, we adopt three benchmarks with complementary demands and use each benchmark’s official protocol. Analytical report generation. DAComp-DA ( Lei et al., 2025 ) contains open-ended tasks over potentially multi-table SQLite databases and requires reports with analysis, conclusions, and visualisations. It is evaluated by Completeness, Accuracy, Insightfulness, Readability, Analytical Depth, Visualisation, and Overall. Long-horizon exploration. DDR-Bench ( Liu et al., 2026 ) evaluates long-horizon exploration without predefined queries in a 10-K setting over SEC disclosures. It is evaluated by Message-Wise accuracy, Trajectory-Wise accuracy, and Overall. Exact-answer analysis. DSBench ( Jing et al., 2025 ) derives exact-answer analytical tasks from ModelOff competitions with spreadsheet, text, and image inputs. It is evaluated by Task-level Accuracy, Competition-level Accuracy, and Overall. Table 2: Analytical report generation on DAComp-DA. Higher is better on all metrics. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.30045 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: Which Differences Matter? Controlled Tests of Rule Transfer, Joint Reliability, and Information Use in Decision Models Authors: Tianyou Lai , Wentao Yue , Zhiwei Zuo , Qilei Li View a PDF of the paper titled Which Differences Matter? Controlled Tests of Rule Transfer, Joint Reliability, and Information Use in Decision Models, by Tianyou Lai and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Decision models map stated rules and observed states to discrete answers. Aggregate accuracy leaves unresolved which rule and information changes guide those answers. We connect controlled input changes to transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use through executable arithmetic rules. Semantic rule separation and crossed rule and state tests make transfer and joint success separately measurable. We compare equivalent wordings, calibrate joint correctness through marginal-preserving reassociation, and alter tables to define alternative answer targets. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement; fully conflicting quartets yield small pooled gains and different gain signs across source splits. Equivalent rewrites have opposing task-level effects, linking transfer gains to rule presentation. Joint-score departures depend on which rule and state associations the reference preserves. A decision service changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and usually follows the answer targets implied by altered table values or mappings. items.content: Which Differences Matter? Controlled Tests of Rule Transfer, Joint Reliability, and Information Use in Decision Models Tianyou Lai † † thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Wentao Yue 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Shenzhen University Zhiwei Zuo Affiliation: Central China Normal University Qilei Li † † thanks: Corresponding author: qilei.li@ccnu.edu.cn . Affiliation: Central China Normal University Abstract Decision models map stated rules and observed states to discrete answers. Aggregate accuracy leaves unresolved which rule and information changes guide those answers. We connect controlled input changes to transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use through executable arithmetic rules. Semantic rule separation and crossed rule and state tests make transfer and joint success separately measurable. We compare equivalent wordings, calibrate joint correctness through marginal-preserving reassociation, and alter tables to define alternative answer targets. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement; fully conflicting quartets yield small pooled gains and different gain signs across source splits. Equivalent rewrites have opposing task-level effects, linking transfer gains to rule presentation. Joint-score departures depend on which rule and state associations the reference preserves. A decision service changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and usually follows the answer targets implied by altered table values or mappings. Code and data will be made available. Figure 1: Overview of the three behavioral diagnostics: rule transfer and wording, joint reliability, and external information use. Scores and interventions illustrate the design. 1 Introduction “A difference which makes a difference” — Gregory Bateson, Form, Substance and Difference (1970) Decision models turn stated rules and observed states into labels, ratings, or selected records. Accuracy measures agreement with the prescribed answer, but equal scores can conceal different responses to the inputs. In an archived routing example, two models answer half the questions correctly. One ignores both rule and state changes; the other responds to states alone. Valid option selection can also coexist with answer-symbol binding errors ( Balepur et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2024 ) . Understanding success therefore requires testing which input changes guide each rule-based decision. Research Question How can we determine which rule and information changes guide a decision model's answers? A gain on unfamiliar rules can still depend on familiar wording. Low all-four correctness can follow from individual errors, so its magnitude alone does not establish unusual joint behavior. Better performance with an external table also leaves open whether its values and mappings direct the answers. Behavioral tests and contrast sets motivate controlled input changes ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ; Gardner et al., 2020 ) ; rule-following benchmarks examine inference, counterfactual rules, and regulations ( Parmar et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . We connect these controls to the specific ambiguities in interpreting decision accuracy. Executable arithmetic rules make intended answers and controlled changes checkable. We separate rules by finite-domain behavior to evaluate transfer to semantic components excluded from training. Equivalent rewrites hold those behaviors fixed while changing presentation. Crossing rules and states tests responses to each factor. Marginal-preserving reassociation calibrates all-four correctness against the observed individual predictions. More restrictive references retain rule or state associations to identify what drives departures from that calibration. Finally, changing table values or mappings defines alternative answer targets. Transitions toward those targets reveal directed information use beyond an arbitrary answer change. Figure 1 links input changes to behavioral diagnostics. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves accuracy on reserved rules, with larger gains at higher nearest-source answer agreement. Fully conflicting quartets have low joint success and opposite gain signs across source splits. Equivalent wording increases the adaptation advantage on binary decisions and reduces it on the other tasks. Joint-score departures further depend on the rule and state associations retained by the calibration reference. The decision service Jev changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats. It benefits from complete value tables and follows the alternative targets implied by altered values and mappings. These diagnostics distinguish conflict-conditioned transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use in model decisions. • We establish an oracle-checked evaluation that uses semantic rule separation and paired input changes to distinguish transfer, wording sensitivity, and responses to rules and states. • We show that transfer gains depend on source-answer agreement and the source split under complete conflict. Joint-score departures depend on the associations retained by different marginal-preserving calibration references. • We identify directed use of external values through paired answer transitions under value and mapping interventions, complementing the evidence from aggregate accuracy gains. 2 Related Work Behavioral evaluation and explicit rules. Behavioral evaluation tests whether predictions respond correctly to controlled input changes. CheckList and contrast sets target capabilities through local perturbations ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ; Gardner et al., 2020 ) . Metric rankings also depend on the evaluation context ( Deviyani and Diaz, 2025 ) . RuleTaker and ProofWriter evaluate inference from stated facts and rules ( Clark et al., 2020 ; Tafjord et al., 2021 ) . LogicBench spans logical systems; RuleArena separates rule selection from application in regulations ( Parmar et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . RuleBench and IRFT extend inferential rule-following evaluation and training ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . These designs motivate testing which inputs guide decisions. Our executable grammar combines finite-domain semantic separation with crossed rule and state changes, linking success to responses along each input axis. Appendix Table 28 compares these paired evaluation designs. Generalization, wording, and answer interfaces. Generalization benchmarks vary combinations, presentations, and answer interfaces. CFQ and COGS test composition; Ordered CommonGen tests requested concept order ( Keysers et al., 2020 ; Kim and Linzen, 2020 ; Sakai et al., 2025 ) . Prompt-format and answer-symbol binding studies document interface effects ( Voronov et al., 2024 ; Xue et al., 2024 ) . LoRA supports adaptation tests ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Cacheable-model studies test rule following with independently encoded inputs ( Rajput et al., 2026 ) . Choice2Seq measures correctness retained from complete-answer selection to sequential construction on matched problems ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . These studies motivate paired evaluations of generalization and presentation sensitivity. Our semantic rule separation and equivalent rewrites measure how adaptation to unfamiliar rule behavior changes across presentations of identical questions with fixed model weights and intended answers. Information use and internal mechanisms. Information-use studies examine how context and representations influence decisions. Performance depends on where relevant context appears ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Probing separates recoverable information from information used to answer ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) . Causal abstraction and interchange-intervention training connect representations to high-level variables ( Geiger et al., 2021 ; Geiger et al., 2022 ) . Logit inspection and attention modification examine factual recall under contextual counterfactuals ( Ortu et al., 2024 ) . Accuracy gains from supplied values leave their influence on individual answers unresolved. We alter table values and mappings to define alternative targets. Paired transitions toward those targets test directed information use. Source-selected donor replacements separately test whether recovered rule-value information influences the final selected answer. Takeaway Choose input interventions that distinguish the behavioral properties behind a score. Separate evidence of transfer, responsiveness, and information use when designing each evaluation. 3 Controlled Rule–State Evaluation 3.1 States, Rules, and Decisions A decision instance is ( s , r , t , O ) (s,r,t,O) : a state s s , an explicitly specified rule r r , a task family t t , and an ordered option set O O of size K K . A programmatic oracle returns the semantic answer y = g t ​ ( r , s ) y=g_{t}(r,s) and its index in O O . A model predicts an option index. The semantic answers align option permutations. Controlled Tests of Rule Transfer, Joint Reliability, and Information Use in Decision Models Tianyou Lai † † thanks: These authors contributed equally to this work. Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Wentao Yue 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Shenzhen University Zhiwei Zuo Affiliation: Central China Normal University Qilei Li † † thanks: Corresponding author: qilei.li@ccnu.edu.cn . Affiliation: Central China Normal University Abstract Decision models map stated rules and observed states to discrete answers. Aggregate accuracy leaves unresolved which rule and information changes guide those answers. We connect controlled input changes to transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use through executable arithmetic rules. Semantic rule separation and crossed rule and state tests make transfer and joint success separately measurable. We compare equivalent wordings, calibrate joint correctness through marginal-preserving reassociation, and alter tables to define alternative answer targets. Adaptation gains increase with nearest-source answer agreement; fully conflicting quartets yield small pooled gains and different gain signs across source splits. Equivalent rewrites have opposing task-level effects, linking transfer gains to rule presentation. Joint-score departures depend on which rule and state associations the reference preserves. A decision service changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and usually follows the answer targets implied by altered table values or mappings. Code and data will be made available. Figure 1: Overview of the three behavioral diagnostics: rule transfer and wording, joint reliability, and external information use. Scores and interventions illustrate the design. 1 Introduction “A difference which makes a difference” — Gregory Bateson, Form, Substance and Difference (1970) Decision models turn stated rules and observed states into labels, ratings, or selected records. Accuracy measures agreement with the prescribed answer, but equal scores can conceal different responses to the inputs. In an archived routing example, two models answer half the questions correctly. One ignores both rule and state changes; the other responds to states alone. Valid option selection can also coexist with answer-symbol binding errors ( Balepur et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2024 ) . Understanding success therefore requires testing which input changes guide each rule-based decision. Research Question How can we determine which rule and information changes guide a decision model's answers? A gain on unfamiliar rules can still depend on familiar wording. Low all-four correctness can follow from individual errors, so its magnitude alone does not establish unusual joint behavior. Better performance with an external table also leaves open whether its values and mappings direct the answers. Behavioral tests and contrast sets motivate controlled input changes ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ; Gardner et al., 2020 ) ; rule-following benchmarks examine inference, counterfactual rules, and regulations ( Parmar et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . We connect these controls to the specific ambiguities in interpreting decision accuracy. Executable arithmetic rules make intended answers and controlled changes checkable. We separate rules by finite-domain behavior to evaluate transfer to semantic components excluded from training. Equivalent rewrites hold those behaviors fixed while changing presentation. Crossing rules and states tests responses to each factor. Marginal-preserving reassociation calibrates all-four correctness against the observed individual predictions. More restrictive references retain rule or state associations to identify what drives departures from that calibration. Finally, changing table values or mappings defines alternative answer targets. Transitions toward those targets reveal directed information use beyond an arbitrary answer change. Figure 1 links input changes to behavioral diagnostics. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) improves accuracy on reserved rules, with larger gains at higher nearest-source answer agreement. Fully conflicting quartets have low joint success and opposite gain signs across source splits. Equivalent wording increases the adaptation advantage on binary decisions and reduces it on the other tasks. Joint-score departures further depend on the rule and state associations retained by the calibration reference. The decision service Jev changes answers more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats. It benefits from complete value tables and follows the alternative targets implied by altered values and mappings. These diagnostics distinguish conflict-conditioned transfer, joint reliability, and directed information use in model decisions. • We establish an oracle-checked evaluation that uses semantic rule separation and paired input changes to distinguish transfer, wording sensitivity, and responses to rules and states. • We show that transfer gains depend on source-answer agreement and the source split under complete conflict. Joint-score departures depend on the associations retained by different marginal-preserving calibration references. • We identify directed use of external values through paired answer transitions under value and mapping interventions, complementing the evidence from aggregate accuracy gains. 2 Related Work Behavioral evaluation and explicit rules. Behavioral evaluation tests whether predictions respond correctly to controlled input changes. CheckList and contrast sets target capabilities through local perturbations ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ; Gardner et al., 2020 ) . Metric rankings also depend on the evaluation context ( Deviyani and Diaz, 2025 ) . RuleTaker and ProofWriter evaluate inference from stated facts and rules ( Clark et al., 2020 ; Tafjord et al., 2021 ) . LogicBench spans logical systems; RuleArena separates rule selection from application in regulations ( Parmar et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . RuleBench and IRFT extend inferential rule-following evaluation and training ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . These designs motivate testing which inputs guide decisions. Our executable grammar combines finite-domain semantic separation with crossed rule and state changes, linking success to responses along each input axis. Appendix Table 28 compares these paired evaluation designs. Generalization, wording, and answer interfaces. Generalization benchmarks vary combinations, presentations, and answer interfaces. CFQ and COGS test composition; Ordered CommonGen tests requested concept order ( Keysers et al., 2020 ; Kim and Linzen, 2020 ; Sakai et al., 2025 ) . Prompt-format and answer-symbol binding studies document interface effects ( Voronov et al., 2024 ; Xue et al., 2024 ) . LoRA supports adaptation tests ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Cacheable-model studies test rule following with independently encoded inputs ( Rajput et al., 2026 ) . Choice2Seq measures correctness retained from complete-answer selection to sequential construction on matched problems ( Lai et al., 2026 ) . These studies motivate paired evaluations of generalization and presentation sensitivity. Our semantic rule separation and equivalent rewrites measure how adaptation to unfamiliar rule behavior changes across presentations of identical questions with fixed model weights and intended answers. Information use and internal mechanisms. Information-use studies examine how context and representations influence decisions. Performance depends on where relevant context appears ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Probing separates recoverable information from information used to answer ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) . Causal abstraction and interchange-intervention training connect representations to high-level variables ( Geiger et al., 2021 ; Geiger et al., 2022 ) . Logit inspection and attention modification examine factual recall under contextual counterfactuals ( Ortu et al., 2024 ) . Accuracy gains from supplied values leave their influence on individual answers unresolved. We alter table values and mappings to define alternative targets. Paired transitions toward those targets test directed information use. Source-selected donor replacements separately test whether recovered rule-value information influences the final selected answer. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.30042 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning Authors: Sudipta Paul , Pengrui Quan , Aounon Kumar , Nicholas Tzou , Vivek Kulkarni , Srinivas Chappidi View a PDF of the paper titled HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning, by Sudipta Paul and 5 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants' final performance with 2x-4x fewer evaluation budget. items.content: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning Sudipta Paul † † thanks: Equal contribution. Pengrui Quan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Aounon Kumar Nicholas Tzou Vivek Kulkarni Srinivas Chappidi Affiliation: Samsung Research America Affiliation: {sudipta.paul, pengrui.quan, aounon.kumar, n.tzou,} Affiliation: {v.kulkarni1, vasu.c}@samsung.com Abstract Harness optimization, which improves an agent’s prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin–Gödel Machine and the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit–outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent’s highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45 % 14.45\% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final performance with 2 × 2\times – 4 × 4\times fewer evaluation budget. 1 Introduction Agent harness optimization Khattab et al. (2024) ; Yuksekgonul et al. (2024) improves large language model (LLM) agents without updating model parameters by optimizing the prompts, tools, and workflows that govern agent behavior. Recent self-improving systems Novikov et al. (2025) automate this process through evolutionary search. The Darwin–Gödel Machine (DGM) Zhang et al. (2026b) maintains an archive of agents and generates new candidates by modifying selected parents, while the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) Wang et al. (2026) selects candidates based on clade-metaproductivity , their potential to produce strong descendants. This paradigm is well suited to coding agents because the ability being improved, understanding and modifying code, also enables self-modification. Planning tasks, however, require sequences of actions that satisfy interacting constraints Zhang et al. (2026d) ; Xie et al. (2024) , creating a mismatch that poses two challenges for existing recursive self-improvement methods. First, effective improvement requires a structured context of the search history . Planning benchmarks expose a relatively small and recurring set of constraint failures, so different agents in the search tree often encounter similar problems. If an editor observes only its current parent’s evaluation logs, it cannot determine whether a similar fix has already been attempted elsewhere, whether it improved or degraded performance, or which previous modifications led to the current behavior. As a result, different branches may repeatedly rediscover the same ineffective changes. In HGM’s shopping search, 41.8% of edits repeat an edit pattern already present in the tree (Figure 1 , left), with each repeated attempt consuming another full planning evaluation. What is needed is not simply access to more previous agents, but explicit edit–outcome context : a concise record of what was changed, what behavior changed as a result, and which changes succeeded, regressed, or proved ineffective. Figure 1: Edit behavior in HGM. Among child nodes, 41.8% repeat previous edits, 19.4% target an error category absent from the parent’s observed failures, and 64.2% retain the parent’s dominant error category. See Appendix A.1 for details. Second, improvement must be targeted at the specific constraints the agent violates . Planning success depends on the correctness of many interdependent decisions: a single infeasible transfer, invalid coupon, or unmet product requirement can invalidate an otherwise valid itinerary or cart. Consequently, a broad modification that improves behavior in general may still leave the failing case unresolved unless it corrects the particular constraint violation responsible for failure. Without explicit guidance, open-ended editing may instead modify an unrelated harness component or make a diffuse change that does not address the observed error. In HGM’s shopping search, 19.4% of edits target a constraint category that the parent never failed (Figure 1 , middle), and in 64.2% of edits the child retains its parent’s dominant failure category (Figure 1 , right). These results suggest that efficient self-improvement for planning requires both learning from prior edit outcomes and directing new edits toward the specific constraint failures observed in the current agent. We introduce the Huxley–Gödel Machine Dual (HGM-Dual), a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient agent harness evolution. First, it represents agentic evolution as structured contextual information. This agent-evolution context records what was changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which attempted modifications were ineffective. The editor therefore receives explicit edit–outcome attribution instead of treating previous agent snapshots as an unstructured archive. This context discourages repeated failures and allows subsequent edits to build systematically on evidence collected throughout the search. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation . For each selected parent, the framework generates complementary children: a general child , which preserves the broad and open-ended exploration of existing evolutionary methods, and specialized children , which target the harness component most likely responsible for the parent’s observed errors. The general path retains the ability to discover unexpected improvements, while the specialized path provides diagnostic-guided local refinement. Together, the dual paths balance exploration with targeted exploitation and direct the evaluation budget toward more informative regions of the harness search space. Experiments on travel and shopping planning tasks show that HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45 % 14.45\% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final performance with 2 × 2\times – 4 × 4\times fewer evaluation budget. These results demonstrate that structured evolutionary context and diagnostic guidance can make harness self-improvement both more effective and substantially more resource-efficient. 2 Related Works Harness Optimization through Self-Improvement. Recent methods improve frozen LLMs by automatically modifying their agentic harnesses, including prompts, tools, skills, and workflows Khattab et al. (2024) ; Opsahl-Ong et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2026) ; Karten et al. (2026) ; Lou et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026a) . ADAS Hu et al. (2025) , DGM Zhang et al. (2026b) , HGM Wang et al. (2026) , GEPA Agrawal et al. (2026) , and HyperAgents Zhang et al. (2026c) search over agent implementations through iterative or evolutionary self-modification. Meta-Harness Lee et al. (2026) gives an agentic proposer access to the code, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates, while SkillOpt Yang et al. (2026) optimizes a natural-language skill through bounded edits and validation. Collectively, these methods demonstrate that harness optimization can substantially improve agent performance without updating model parameters. Nevertheless, two challenges remain. First, prior edit experience is either local or excessive: DGM Zhang et al. (2026b) and HGM Wang et al. (2026) primarily generate modifications from the selected parent’s code and evaluation logs, without providing enough context on the effectiveness of all edits attempted. On the other hand, archive-based methods Hu et al. (2025) ; Lee et al. (2026) ; Lin et al. (2026) ; Jiang et al. (2026) may flood the evolution context with numerous previous candidates and raw execution traces. This can obscure useful edit-outcome relationships and lead to repeated ineffective modifications across the search tree. Second, although prior methods guide candidate selection or validation Yang et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026b) ; Zhang et al. (2026c) , edit generation itself remains largely open-ended and may not target the harness component responsible for observed failures. Such weakly targeted exploration can require substantial evaluation resources. HGM-Dual addresses these limitations by maintaining a concise, structured agent-evolution context and by generating both a general child for broad exploration and an error-conditioned specialized child for targeted refinement. 3 HGM-Dual 3.1 Problem Setup Agent Harness Optimization. We consider a frozen language model whose behavior is controlled by an agent harness ℋ = ( 𝒫 , 𝒯 , 𝒲 ) , \mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{W}), (1) where 𝒫 \mathcal{P} specifies the prompt and instructions provided to the model, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} denotes the set of available tools, and 𝒲 \mathcal{W} defines the agentic workflow that governs how the model and tools interact to solve a task. The parameters of the underlying language model remain fixed throughout optimization; only the components of ℋ \mathcal{H} are modified. Given a task x x sampled from a task distribution 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , executing the frozen language model under harness ℋ \mathcal{H} produces an output ℋ ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{H}(x) . We evaluate this output using a task-specific scoring function J ⁡ ( x , ℋ ⁡ ( x ) ) J(x,\mathcal{H}(x)) , which measures the quality of the harness execution on task x x . Agent harness optimization seeks a harness that maximizes expected performance over the task distribution: ℋ ∗ = arg ⁡ max ℋ ​ 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ J ⁡ ( x , ℋ ⁡ ( x ) ) ] . \mathcal{H}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{H}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[J\!\left(x,\mathcal{H}(x)\right)\right]. (2) 3.2 Overview Figure 2: HGM search: select a parent, generate an open-ended edit, evaluate the child, and add it to the archive. HGM. HGM optimizes an agent harness through evolutionary self-modification. Starting from an initial harness ℋ 0 \mathcal{H}_{0} , HGM maintains an archive 𝒜 \mathcal{A} of previously evaluated harnesses organized as an evolutionary tree (Figure 2 ). Each node corresponds to a harness, and each edge corresponds to a modification that produces a child from its parent. At each iteration, HGM selects a parent harness ℋ i ∈ 𝒜 \mathcal{H}_{i}\in\mathcal{A} using its clade-metaproductivity criterion, which is designed to favor candidates with the potential to produce strong descendants. An editor then examines the selected harness and its evaluation feedback, proposes an open-ended modification, evaluates the resulting child, and adds it to the archive. The editor primarily conditions on the selected harness and its current evaluation context ε i \varepsilon_{i} : ℋ ′ = Edit ⁡ ( ℋ i , ε i ) . \mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Edit}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i}\right). (3) Thus, the archive records an evolutionary history, but that history is not explicitly represented as structured edit-outcome evidence for the editor. Moreover, because the edit is open-ended, it is not explicitly constrained to address the failures observed in the selected parent. Figure 3: Overview of HGM-Dual and one expansion round. Given a selected parent ℋ i \mathcal{H}_{i} , HGM-Dual constructs an evolution context 𝒵 i \mathcal{Z}_{i} by summarizing edits and outcomes along its ancestral path Anc ⁡ ( ℋ i ) \mathrm{Anc}(\mathcal{H}_{i}) . The evolution context is provided to both editing paths: a general editor proposes an open-ended improvement, while specialized editors target the highest-ranked errors in the parent’s error profile ε i \varepsilon_{i} . The resulting children are evaluated under the same protocol, and only the strongest child is added to the archive. HGM-Dual. HGM-Dual retains HGM’s evolutionary search procedure but changes how each selected parent is expanded (we refer readers to Section A.4 for full integration). As illustrated in Figure 3 , it introduces two mechanisms. First, rather than conditioning an edit only on the selected harness ℋ i \mathcal{H}_{i} and its evaluation context ε i \varepsilon_{i} , HGM-Dual additionally provides an evolution context 𝒵 i \mathcal{Z}_{i} that summarizes the edits and outcomes along its ancestral lineage: ℋ ′ = Edit ⁡ ( ℋ i , ε i , 𝒵 i ) . \mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\operatorname{Edit}\left(\mathcal{H}_{i},\varepsilon_{i},\mathcal{Z}_{i}\right). (4) Second, HGM-Dual augments HGM’s open-ended child generation with error-conditioned editing. Each expansion generates both general and error-conditioned children. Thus, HGM-Dual retains HGM’s evolutionary backbone while making edit generation both history-aware and error-aware . We summarize the HGM-Dual expansion process in Algorithm 1 and describe them in Sections 3.3 and 3.4 , respectively. 3.3 Agent Evolution as Interpretable Context An editor observing only the current harness and its evaluation feedback cannot reliably attribute performance changes to prior edits or identify previously failed modifications. Providing the full archive and raw traces would address this limitation but is costly and difficult to interpret. HGM-Dual therefore compresses the relevant evolutionary history into a structured context.
