items.raw_text: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning Sudipta Paul † † thanks: Equal contribution. Pengrui Quan 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Aounon Kumar Nicholas Tzou Vivek Kulkarni Srinivas Chappidi Affiliation: Samsung Research America Affiliation: {sudipta.paul, pengrui.quan, aounon.kumar, n.tzou,} Affiliation: {v.kulkarni1, vasu.c}@samsung.com Abstract Harness optimization, which improves an agent’s prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin–Gödel Machine and the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit–outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent’s highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45 % 14.45\% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final performance with 2 × 2\times – 4 × 4\times fewer evaluation budget. 1 Introduction Agent harness optimization Khattab et al. (2024) ; Yuksekgonul et al. (2024) improves large language model (LLM) agents without updating model parameters by optimizing the prompts, tools, and workflows that govern agent behavior. Recent self-improving systems Novikov et al. (2025) automate this process through evolutionary search. The Darwin–Gödel Machine (DGM) Zhang et al. (2026b) maintains an archive of agents and generates new candidates by modifying selected parents, while the Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) Wang et al. (2026) selects candidates based on clade-metaproductivity , their potential to produce strong descendants. This paradigm is well suited to coding agents because the ability being improved, understanding and modifying code, also enables self-modification. Planning tasks, however, require sequences of actions that satisfy interacting constraints Zhang et al. (2026d) ; Xie et al. (2024) , creating a mismatch that poses two challenges for existing recursive self-improvement methods. First, effective improvement requires a structured context of the search history . Planning benchmarks expose a relatively small and recurring set of constraint failures, so different agents in the search tree often encounter similar problems. If an editor observes only its current parent’s evaluation logs, it cannot determine whether a similar fix has already been attempted elsewhere, whether it improved or degraded performance, or which previous modifications led to the current behavior. As a result, different branches may repeatedly rediscover the same ineffective changes. In HGM’s shopping search, 41.8% of edits repeat an edit pattern already present in the tree (Figure 1 , left), with each repeated attempt consuming another full planning evaluation. What is needed is not simply access to more previous agents, but explicit edit–outcome context : a concise record of what was changed, what behavior changed as a result, and which changes succeeded, regressed, or proved ineffective. Figure 1: Edit behavior in HGM. Among child nodes, 41.8% repeat previous edits, 19.4% target an error category absent from the parent’s observed failures, and 64.2% retain the parent’s dominant error category. See Appendix A.1 for details. Second, improvement must be targeted at the specific constraints the agent violates . Planning success depends on the correctness of many interdependent decisions: a single infeasible transfer, invalid coupon, or unmet product requirement can invalidate an otherwise valid itinerary or cart. Consequently, a broad modification that improves behavior in general may still leave the failing case unresolved unless it corrects the particular constraint violation responsible for failure. Without explicit guidance, open-ended editing may instead modify an unrelated harness component or make a diffuse change that does not address the observed error. In HGM’s shopping search, 19.4% of edits target a constraint category that the parent never failed (Figure 1 , middle), and in 64.2% of edits the child retains its parent’s dominant failure category (Figure 1 , right). These results suggest that efficient self-improvement for planning requires both learning from prior edit outcomes and directing new edits toward the specific constraint failures observed in the current agent. We introduce the Huxley–Gödel Machine Dual (HGM-Dual), a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient agent harness evolution. First, it represents agentic evolution as structured contextual information. This agent-evolution context records what was changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which attempted modifications were ineffective. The editor therefore receives explicit edit–outcome attribution instead of treating previous agent snapshots as an unstructured archive. This context discourages repeated failures and allows subsequent edits to build systematically on evidence collected throughout the search. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation . For each selected parent, the framework generates complementary children: a general child , which preserves the broad and open-ended exploration of existing evolutionary methods, and specialized children , which target the harness component most likely responsible for the parent’s observed errors. The general path retains the ability to discover unexpected improvements, while the specialized path provides diagnostic-guided local refinement. Together, the dual paths balance exploration with targeted exploitation and direct the evaluation budget toward more informative regions of the harness search space. Experiments on travel and shopping planning tasks show that HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45 % 14.45\% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants’ final performance with 2 × 2\times – 4 × 4\times fewer evaluation budget. These results demonstrate that structured evolutionary context and diagnostic guidance can make harness self-improvement both more effective and substantially more resource-efficient. 2 Related Works Harness Optimization through Self-Improvement. Recent methods improve frozen LLMs by automatically modifying their agentic harnesses, including prompts, tools, skills, and workflows Khattab et al. (2024) ; Opsahl-Ong et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2026) ; Karten et al. (2026) ; Lou et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026a) . ADAS Hu et al. (2025) , DGM Zhang et al. (2026b) , HGM Wang et al. (2026) , GEPA Agrawal et al. (2026) , and HyperAgents Zhang et al. (2026c) search over agent implementations through iterative or evolutionary self-modification. Meta-Harness Lee et al. (2026) gives an agentic proposer access to the code, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates, while SkillOpt Yang et al. (2026) optimizes a natural-language skill through bounded edits and validation. Collectively, these methods demonstrate that harness optimization can substantially improve agent performance without updating model parameters. Nevertheless, two challenges remain. First, prior edit experience is either local or excessive: DGM Zhang et al. (2026b) and HGM Wang et al. (2026) primarily generate modifications from the selected parent’s code and evaluation logs, without providing enough context on the effectiveness of all edits attempted. On the other hand, archive-based methods Hu et al. (2025) ; Lee et al. (2026) ; Lin et al. (2026) ; Jiang et al. (2026) may flood the evolution context with numerous previous candidates and raw execution traces. This can obscure useful edit-outcome relationships and lead to repeated ineffective modifications across the search tree. Second, although prior methods guide candidate selection or validation Yang et al. (2026) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026b) ; Zhang et al. (2026c) , edit generation itself remains largely open-ended and may not target the harness component responsible for observed failures. Such weakly targeted exploration can require substantial evaluation resources. HGM-Dual addresses these limitations by maintaining a concise, structured agent-evolution context and by generating both a general child for broad exploration and an error-conditioned specialized child for targeted refinement. 3 HGM-Dual 3.1 Problem Setup Agent Harness Optimization. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.30041 (cs) [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026] Title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents Authors: Zijian Jiang , Xilu Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents, by Zijian Jiang and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10\% of trajectory positions capture 96.12\% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36\% with full trajectory to 36.79\%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10\% localized positions achieves 57.38\%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills. items.content: \workshoptitle Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents Zijian Jiang Affiliation: School of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Surrey Affiliation: Guildford, Surrey GU2 7XH, UK Email: z.jiang@surrey.ac.uk Xilu Wang Affiliation: School of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Surrey Affiliation: Guildford, Surrey GU2 7XH, UK Email: wangxilu@surrey.ac.uk Abstract Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10% of trajectory positions capture 96.12% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36% with full trajectory to 36.79%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10% localized positions achieves 57.38%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills. 1 Introduction As agents are increasingly deployed across diverse domains, tasks often differ substantially in their knowledge requirements, operational procedures, and behavioral patterns. These task-specific differences are difficult to address efficiently through repeated retraining or modification of the underlying agent Liu et al. (2024) . A flexible solution is to provide agents with task-specific guidance that helps them develop more effective task behaviors Li et al. (2026) . A direct approach to task adaptation is known as an agent skill, where natural language prompts are used to specify task goals, operational rules, and expected behaviors, allowing the model to perform new tasks without updating its parameters Anthropic (2025) . However, this approach often relies on lengthy and carefully designed prompts, and its effectiveness can be sensitive to wording and example selection. As tasks become more complex, the prompts typically grow longer, increasing both context usage and inference cost Mu et al. (2023) . To obtain more compact and learnable skill representations, prior work has explored directly optimizing prompts in continuous representation spaces. Compared with natural language instructions, soft prompts typically require less storage and can support task adaptation by updating a small set of trainable prompt embeddings Tao et al. (2026) ; Lester et al. (2021) . However, these continuous vectors lack clear counterparts in natural language Deng et al. (2022) . As a result, while learning a target skill, a soft prompt can also introduce unexpected behavioral changes Ma et al. (2022) . For agents, because generation is sequential, even small shifts in early predictions can propagate and amplify over subsequent steps, leading to incorrect tool selection, malformed outputs, or task execution failures Bengio et al. (2015) ; Li et al. (2023) . Thus, acquiring new capabilities may come at the cost of degrading abilities that the base model already possesses Zhu et al. (2022) . We find that the behavioral effect of a skill is highly concentrated in a small number of critical decision points, while much of the remaining trajectory is already correctly handled by the base agent. This suggests that robust soft skill adaptation should focus on which behaviors truly need to be learned. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which identifies the trajectory positions where a text skill meaningfully changes the predictions of base agent and selectively uses these positions to train a compact soft skill. At the same time, we constrain selected preservation positions toward the base distribution to reduce unnecessary behavioral drift. Our contributions are shown below. First, through token-level distributional analysis, we find that skill induced behavioral changes are highly sparse. Second, we show that training a soft prompt using only selected positions by Behavioral Localization in the trajectory as supervision outperforms training on the full trajectory. 2 Related Work Prompt learning provides a foundation for representing task-specific capabilities in continuous spaces. Prompt Tuning, Prefix-Tuning, and P-Tuning show that a frozen base model can be adapted by optimizing only a small set of continuous prompt embeddings Lester et al. (2021) ; Li and Liang (2021) ; Liu et al. (2022) . Later work explores how these representations can be reused. For example, SPoT transfers learned soft prompts from source tasks to similar target tasks Vu et al. (2022) . XPrompt finds that some prompt tokens can hurt downstream performance and removes these negative parts Ma et al. (2022) . These studies mainly focus on how soft prompts are parameterized and reused. Another line of work compresses long natural language contexts into compact latent representations. Gisting compresses long prompts into a small number of reusable gist tokens Mu et al. (2023) . ICAE encodes long contexts into a few memory slots that can directly condition a language model Ge et al. (2024) . These methods mainly aim to preserve the semantics of the original text after compression. Agent skills differ from general text compression because their main purpose is to guide an agent’s behavior. Therefore, a compressed representation should preserve the behavioral effect introduced by the skill. Recent work has begun to reuse successful agent trajectories to compress textual skills offline. SoftSkill compresses a natural-language skill into a short continuous prefix while keeping the base model frozen Tao et al. (2026) . It trains the prefix by predicting the next tokens in successful trajectories. LatentSkill instead converts textual skills into task-specific LoRA adapters, moving reusable skill knowledge from the context space into the model’s weight space Yu et al. (2026) . These studies show that textual agent skills can be encoded as compact latent representations. However, they mainly focus on how a skill should be represented or stored. In contrast, we study which behavioral changes introduced by a skill should be used to learn such a representation. 3 Behavioral Locator 3.1 Problem formulation Let p θ p_{\theta} be a frozen agent and let S S denote a text skill shared by a family of tasks. Our training set consists of task description x i x^{i} and it’s trajectory τ i = ( y 1 i , … , y T i ) \tau^{i}=(y^{i}_{1},\ldots,y^{i}_{T}) . τ i \tau^{i} is a verified successful trajectory called the teacher trajectory. τ t i \tau^{i}_{t} denotes the sequence before position t t . If we seek a soft prompt P ∗ ∈ ℝ L × d P^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} that can replace S S at inference time. The parameters of the base model θ \theta remain frozen, only P P is optimized. We aim to identify a sparse set of trajectory positions 𝒞 ⊆ 1 , … , T , | 𝒞 | ≪ T , \displaystyle\mathcal{C}\subseteq{1,\ldots,T},\qquad|\mathcal{C}|\ll T, (1) We use 𝒞 \mathcal{C} to supervise a short soft prompt. The goal is to focus on skill useful behavior while avoiding harmful updates induced by other trajectory positions. 3.2 Method We compute the next token probability distributions along the teacher trajectory under three different conditions. p t s \displaystyle p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}} = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ S , x , τ i t ) \displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid S,x,\tau^{i}_{t}) (2) p t n \displaystyle p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}} = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , τ i t ) \displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\tau^{i}_{t}) p t \displaystyle p_{t} = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ P , x , τ i t ) \displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid P,x,\tau^{i}_{t}) Here, p s p^{\mathrm{s}} , p n p^{\mathrm{n}} , and p p denote the next token distributions under the text skill, non-skill, and soft prompt, respectively. First, we define the positive gain G G induced by the skill on the base model as follows. G t i = log ⁡ p t s ​ ( y t i ) − log ⁡ p t n ​ ( y t i ) \displaystyle G_{t}^{i}=\log p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}(y_{t}^{i})-\log p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}(y_{t}^{i}) (3) at position t t of the teacher trajectory, it measures how much the probability of the successful token y t y_{t} increases after adding the text Skill, compared with the no-skill condition. Next, we define the distributional shift J ​ S JS induced by the skill on the base model as follows. J S t i = 1 2 D KL ( p t s ∥ m t i ) + 1 2 D KL ( p t n ∥ m t i ) \displaystyle JS_{t}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}\;\|\;m_{t}^{i}\right)+\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}\;\|\;m_{t}^{i}\right) (4) where m t i \displaystyle m_{t}^{i} = 1 2 ​ ( p t s + p t n ) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}+p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}\right) (5) at position t t of the teacher trajectory, it measures how much the full next-token distribution changes after adding the text Skill, compared with the no-skill condition. By combining the two metrics, we define the localization score U t i = G t i ​ J ​ S t i U_{t}^{i}=G_{t}^{i}JS_{t}^{i} at each position. We then select the top k % k\% of positions as the training targets. At the selected core positions, we minimize the full vocabulary KL divergence between the predictive distributions under the text skill and soft skill conditions. At the unselected preservation positions, we use the token distribution of the no-skill model as a behavioral anchor, encouraging the soft-prompt model to preserve the original predictive behavior of the base model as much as possible. 4 Experiment Figure 1: Aggregate concentration on 61 successful training trajectories. Positive gold token gain is highly concentrated under teacher forcing. 4.1 Setup We conduct our experiments on SpreadsheetBench Ma et al. (2024) . We use GPT-5.5 to generate the successful teacher trajectories. All experiments use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the frozen student model, with all parameters fixed during training. Each soft prompt has a length of 8 and is initialized using the embeddings of the first same tokens of the full text skill. During evaluation, we use greedy decoding with a maximum of 4,096 token cost and set the execution timeout for each task to 600 seconds. A task is considered successful only if the generated output passes all SpreadsheetBench checks. 4.2 Main Result We use the Behavioral Locator to select key positions and optimize both a shared soft prompt across tasks and task-specific soft prompts for individual tasks. As shown in Figure 1 , the positive gain is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Selecting only 10% of the tokens captures 96.12% of the total positive Skill effect. This motivates us to use a sparse set of relevant tokens as supervision for soft skill learning. Table 1: Main SpreadsheetBench results. Bold denotes the best learned soft prompt under each setting. Setting Method Success Rate Shared soft prompt No Skill 97/280 (34.64%) Text Skill 118/280 (42.14%) SoftSkill 85/280 (30.36%) OPCD 107/280 (38.21%) Ours (5%) 101/280 (36.07%) Ours (10%) 103/280 (36.79%) Task-specific soft prompt No Skill 26/61 (42.62%) Text Skill 32/61 (52.46%) SoftSkill 28/61 (45.90%) OPCD 30/61 (49.18%) Ours (5%) 28/61 (45.90%) Ours (10%) 35/61 (57.38%) No Skill measures the capability of the base agent, while Text Skill represents the up bound by providing the full text skill. SoftSkill is the offline full-trajectory compression baseline. OPCD is an important on-policy distillation baseline that trains online rather than relying on fixed teacher trajectories. Our method instead relies on lower cost offline teacher trajectories. Under the shared prompt setting, our method improves over full-trajectory SoftSkill, although it remains below the on-policy OPCD baseline. More importantly, under task-specific condition, selecting the top 10% localized positions achieves 57.38%, outperforming both Text Skill and OPCD. These results support a small subset of token can provide sufficient supervision for learning effective soft prompts. items.raw_text: \workshoptitle Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents Zijian Jiang Affiliation: School of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Surrey Affiliation: Guildford, Surrey GU2 7XH, UK Email: z.jiang@surrey.ac.uk Xilu Wang Affiliation: School of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Surrey Affiliation: Guildford, Surrey GU2 7XH, UK Email: wangxilu@surrey.ac.uk Abstract Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which compares the frozen agent with and without the text skill to identify positions where the skill both increases the likelihood of successful tokens and meaningfully changes the next token distribution. We use these localized positions to supervise a short soft prompt. Experiments on SpreadsheetBench with a frozen Qwen3.6-35B-A3B agent show that the top 10% of trajectory positions capture 96.12% of the total positive skill gain. In the shared prompt setting, selective supervision improves success from 30.36% with full trajectory to 36.79%. Under task-specific conditions, using the top 10% localized positions achieves 57.38%, outperforming both the full text skill and the on-policy OPCD baseline. These results show that a small set of behaviorally relevant trajectory positions can provide effective supervision of soft skills. 1 Introduction As agents are increasingly deployed across diverse domains, tasks often differ substantially in their knowledge requirements, operational procedures, and behavioral patterns. These task-specific differences are difficult to address efficiently through repeated retraining or modification of the underlying agent Liu et al. (2024) . A flexible solution is to provide agents with task-specific guidance that helps them develop more effective task behaviors Li et al. (2026) . A direct approach to task adaptation is known as an agent skill, where natural language prompts are used to specify task goals, operational rules, and expected behaviors, allowing the model to perform new tasks without updating its parameters Anthropic (2025) . However, this approach often relies on lengthy and carefully designed prompts, and its effectiveness can be sensitive to wording and example selection. As tasks become more complex, the prompts typically grow longer, increasing both context usage and inference cost Mu et al. (2023) . To obtain more compact and learnable skill representations, prior work has explored directly optimizing prompts in continuous representation spaces. Compared with natural language instructions, soft prompts typically require less storage and can support task adaptation by updating a small set of trainable prompt embeddings Tao et al. (2026) ; Lester et al. (2021) . However, these continuous vectors lack clear counterparts in natural language Deng et al. (2022) . As a result, while learning a target skill, a soft prompt can also introduce unexpected behavioral changes Ma et al. (2022) . For agents, because generation is sequential, even small shifts in early predictions can propagate and amplify over subsequent steps, leading to incorrect tool selection, malformed outputs, or task execution failures Bengio et al. (2015) ; Li et al. (2023) . Thus, acquiring new capabilities may come at the cost of degrading abilities that the base model already possesses Zhu et al. (2022) . We find that the behavioral effect of a skill is highly concentrated in a small number of critical decision points, while much of the remaining trajectory is already correctly handled by the base agent. This suggests that robust soft skill adaptation should focus on which behaviors truly need to be learned. Based on this observation, we propose Behavioral Localization, which identifies the trajectory positions where a text skill meaningfully changes the predictions of base agent and selectively uses these positions to train a compact soft skill. At the same time, we constrain selected preservation positions toward the base distribution to reduce unnecessary behavioral drift. Our contributions are shown below. First, through token-level distributional analysis, we find that skill induced behavioral changes are highly sparse. Second, we show that training a soft prompt using only selected positions by Behavioral Localization in the trajectory as supervision outperforms training on the full trajectory. 2 Related Work Prompt learning provides a foundation for representing task-specific capabilities in continuous spaces. Prompt Tuning, Prefix-Tuning, and P-Tuning show that a frozen base model can be adapted by optimizing only a small set of continuous prompt embeddings Lester et al. (2021) ; Li and Liang (2021) ; Liu et al. (2022) . Later work explores how these representations can be reused. For example, SPoT transfers learned soft prompts from source tasks to similar target tasks Vu et al. (2022) . XPrompt finds that some prompt tokens can hurt downstream performance and removes these negative parts Ma et al. (2022) . These studies mainly focus on how soft prompts are parameterized and reused. Another line of work compresses long natural language contexts into compact latent representations. Gisting compresses long prompts into a small number of reusable gist tokens Mu et al. (2023) . ICAE encodes long contexts into a few memory slots that can directly condition a language model Ge et al. (2024) . These methods mainly aim to preserve the semantics of the original text after compression. Agent skills differ from general text compression because their main purpose is to guide an agent’s behavior. Therefore, a compressed representation should preserve the behavioral effect introduced by the skill. Recent work has begun to reuse successful agent trajectories to compress textual skills offline. SoftSkill compresses a natural-language skill into a short continuous prefix while keeping the base model frozen Tao et al. (2026) . It trains the prefix by predicting the next tokens in successful trajectories. LatentSkill instead converts textual skills into task-specific LoRA adapters, moving reusable skill knowledge from the context space into the model’s weight space Yu et al. (2026) . These studies show that textual agent skills can be encoded as compact latent representations. However, they mainly focus on how a skill should be represented or stored. In contrast, we study which behavioral changes introduced by a skill should be used to learn such a representation. 3 Behavioral Locator 3.1 Problem formulation Let p θ p_{\theta} be a frozen agent and let S S denote a text skill shared by a family of tasks. Our training set consists of task description x i x^{i} and it’s trajectory τ i = ( y 1 i , … , y T i ) \tau^{i}=(y^{i}_{1},\ldots,y^{i}_{T}) . τ i \tau^{i} is a verified successful trajectory called the teacher trajectory. τ t i \tau^{i}_{t} denotes the sequence before position t t . If we seek a soft prompt P ∗ ∈ ℝ L × d P^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} that can replace S S at inference time. The parameters of the base model θ \theta remain frozen, only P P is optimized. We aim to identify a sparse set of trajectory positions 𝒞 ⊆ 1 , … , T , | 𝒞 | ≪ T , \displaystyle\mathcal{C}\subseteq{1,\ldots,T},\qquad|\mathcal{C}|\ll T, (1) We use 𝒞 \mathcal{C} to supervise a short soft prompt. The goal is to focus on skill useful behavior while avoiding harmful updates induced by other trajectory positions. 3.2 Method We compute the next token probability distributions along the teacher trajectory under three different conditions. p t s \displaystyle p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}} = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ S , x , τ i t ) \displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid S,x,\tau^{i}_{t}) (2) p t n \displaystyle p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}} = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , τ i t ) \displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\tau^{i}_{t}) p t \displaystyle p_{t} = p θ ( ⋅ ∣ P , x , τ i t ) \displaystyle=p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid P,x,\tau^{i}_{t}) Here, p s p^{\mathrm{s}} , p n p^{\mathrm{n}} , and p p denote the next token distributions under the text skill, non-skill, and soft prompt, respectively. First, we define the positive gain G G induced by the skill on the base model as follows. G t i = log ⁡ p t s ​ ( y t i ) − log ⁡ p t n ​ ( y t i ) \displaystyle G_{t}^{i}=\log p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}(y_{t}^{i})-\log p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}(y_{t}^{i}) (3) at position t t of the teacher trajectory, it measures how much the probability of the successful token y t y_{t} increases after adding the text Skill, compared with the no-skill condition. Next, we define the distributional shift J ​ S JS induced by the skill on the base model as follows. J S t i = 1 2 D KL ( p t s ∥ m t i ) + 1 2 D KL ( p t n ∥ m t i ) \displaystyle JS_{t}^{i}=\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}\;\|\;m_{t}^{i}\right)+\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}\;\|\;m_{t}^{i}\right) (4) where m t i \displaystyle m_{t}^{i} = 1 2 ​ ( p t s + p t n ) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{t}^{\mathrm{s}}+p_{t}^{\mathrm{n}}\right) (5) at position t t of the teacher trajectory, it measures how much the full next-token distribution changes after adding the text Skill, compared with the no-skill condition. By combining the two metrics, we define the localization score U t i = G t i ​ J ​ S t i U_{t}^{i}=G_{t}^{i}JS_{t}^{i} at each position. We then select the top k % k\% of positions as the training targets. At the selected core positions, we minimize the full vocabulary KL divergence between the predictive distributions under the text skill and soft skill conditions. At the unselected preservation positions, we use the token distribution of the no-skill model as a behavioral anchor, encouraging the soft-prompt model to preserve the original predictive behavior of the base model as much as possible. 4 Experiment Figure 1: Aggregate concentration on 61 successful training trajectories. Positive gold token gain is highly concentrated under teacher forcing. 4.1 Setup We conduct our experiments on SpreadsheetBench Ma et al. (2024) . We use GPT-5.5 to generate the successful teacher trajectories. All experiments use Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the frozen student model, with all parameters fixed during training. Each soft prompt has a length of 8 and is initialized using the embeddings of the first same tokens of the full text skill. During evaluation, we use greedy decoding with a maximum of 4,096 token cost and set the execution timeout for each task to 600 seconds. A task is considered successful only if the generated output passes all SpreadsheetBench checks. 4.2 Main Result We use the Behavioral Locator to select key positions and optimize both a shared soft prompt across tasks and task-specific soft prompts for individual tasks. As shown in Figure 1 , the positive gain is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. Selecting only 10% of the tokens captures 96.12% of the total positive Skill effect. This motivates us to use a sparse set of relevant tokens as supervision for soft skill learning. Table 1: Main SpreadsheetBench results. Bold denotes the best learned soft prompt under each setting. Setting Method Success Rate Shared soft prompt No Skill 97/280 (34.64%) Text Skill 118/280 (42.14%) SoftSkill 85/280 (30.36%) OPCD 107/280 (38.21%) Ours (5%) 101/280 (36.07%) Ours (10%) 103/280 (36.79%) Task-specific soft prompt No Skill 26/61 (42.62%) Text Skill 32/61 (52.46%) SoftSkill 28/61 (45.90%) OPCD 30/61 (49.18%) Ours (5%) 28/61 (45.90%) Ours (10%) 35/61 (57.38%) No Skill measures the capability of the base agent, while Text Skill represents the up bound by providing the full text skill. SoftSkill is the offline full-trajectory compression baseline. OPCD is an important on-policy distillation baseline that trains online rather than relying on fixed teacher trajectories. Our method instead relies on lower cost offline teacher trajectories. Under the shared prompt setting, our method improves over full-trajectory SoftSkill, although it remains below the on-policy OPCD baseline. More importantly, under task-specific condition, selecting the top 10% localized positions achieves 57.38%, outperforming both Text Skill and OPCD. These results support a small subset of token can provide sufficient supervision for learning effective soft prompts. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback. items.content: Data Center / Cloud Achieve Productive AI Capacity Faster and More Predictably with NVIDIA DSX POD Oct 21, 2026 By Premal Savla Like Discuss (1) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA DSX POD is a standardized, factory-built reference design that pre-integrates rack-scale AI infrastructure into containers for validation before shipment. The architecture aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and defines coordinated requirements across compute, networking, storage, power, liquid cooling, cabling, and mechanical design. Factory integration moves complex assembly and testing into a controlled environment while site teams prepare foundations, power, and external connectivity in parallel. Standardized container interfaces enable repeatable capacity expansion and a consistent foundation for software optimization across deployments. NVIDIA provides the validated design foundation while ecosystem partners handle manufacturing, regional engineering, customization, deployment, and support. Next Steps Learn more about the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design to evaluate how it can accelerate AI factory deployment. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more AI factories turn energy into intelligence. But before an AI workload can produce its first token, operators must bring an interconnected system of compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. In a conventional data center build, teams must first select the site, design power and cooling for the deployment, lay out the data center, and plan and install racks and cables. Then they can validate the network and cluster incrementally and bring service online. This work requires coordinated specialized labor, with critical dependencies among installation, infrastructure readiness, and system testing. Delays can push back bring-up and the date the infrastructure begins producing tokens. NVIDIA DSX POD shifts more of this work into a controlled factory environment. One of multiple AI factory implementation models supported by NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is the standardized, factory-built implementation. It enables partners to build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery. The result is a repeatable approach designed to reduce onsite integration complexity and help operators reach productive AI capacity faster and more predictably. This post explains the foundation of NVIDIA DSX POD, how the reference design aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform , and how NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners work through product engineering, deployment, and support. A design foundation for moving AI factory integration upstream Modular and prefabricated data centers already exist. The engineering challenge for an AI factory extends beyond placing conventional IT equipment in an enclosure. Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, high-speed scale-up and scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software. These elements behave as one system. Their mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must remain within specification during factory integration, transportation, installation, and operation. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the design foundation for partners to install rack-scale systems in containers at the factory, functionally test the integrated unit, transport it, and bring it online safely through repeatable processes at the destination. NVIDIA’s investment spans the engineering disciplines required to make that possible, including rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation. This work extends the progression toward greater factory integration to reduce installation complexity and accelerate deployment. NVIDIA has moved from chips and boards to complete rack-scale systems, and large-scale reference architectures like NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD . NVIDIA DSX POD carries this approach into a factory-built AI factory implementation, moving most component integration from the customer site into a controlled manufacturing environment. The reference design does not make containerization mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional data center construction and onsite-integrated designs remain important options. NVIDIA DSX POD adds a standardized path for large-scale deployments where schedule predictability, repeatability, and reduced onsite work are priorities. Architecture aligned with NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform NVIDIA DSX is the broad design framework for co-designed AI infrastructure. It brings compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, facility controls, and software together at the data center level. Customers and partners can implement that framework in different physical forms. NVIDIA DSX POD is a specific realization of that broader design: a standardized AI factory architecture composed of factory-built container types and defined interfaces between them. The architecture is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and its rack-scale systems. The reference design describes a complete AI factory rather than a compute enclosure in isolation. It accounts for compute, service and management functions, scale-out networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, and other supporting infrastructure. Technical requirements for factory-integrated deployment The central purpose of the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is to make the full deployment process repeatable. That requires coordinated requirements across the following areas: compute integration, networking and storage, cabling and controls, power delivery, liquid cooling, and mechanical design and transportation. Compute integration The NVIDIA DSX POD compute container is designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack scale infrastructure. The design defines how compute and supporting racks fit within the enclosure and how partners address structural support, weight distribution, equipment restraint, service clearances, airflow and liquid-cooling access, rack-level power, and network connectivity. Factory integration also changes the validation boundary. Instead of treating each rack as an independent shipment that will be assembled into a cluster onsite, partners validate the installed compute environment as a deployment unit. The validation plan can cover rack inventory, firmware and configuration baselines, power-on checks, fabric connectivity, sensor operation, cooling integrity, and system-level functional tests before the container leaves the factory. Networking and storage AI workloads depend on predictable movement of model data, training data, checkpoint data, and inference context across the AI factory. The reference design therefore treats networking and storage as part of the system architecture rather than as site-specific additions made after compute arrives. The design defines the connectivity required within a compute container, between containers, and from the modular system to the customer’s external network. It accounts for scale-out fabrics, service and management networks, fiber entry points, trunk cabling, cable routing, labeling, bend radius, service access, and validation of factory-installed link before shipment. Storage requirements follow the same principle. The architecture defines the required capacity, performance, connectivity, management, and service characteristics while allowing the final equipment implementation to reflect the deployment scale and partner solution. This enables storage and networking to arrive as coordinated parts of the AI factory instead of independent systems that must be reconciled late in site integration. Cabling and controls NVIDIA DSX POD reduces the onsite work of cabling in a rack-scale deployment, moving rack-to-rack network cabling, power wiring, control wiring, and sensor integration into the factory wherever practical. The reference design clearly defines cable paths, separation requirements, termination points, labeling conventions, test procedures, and serviceability requirements to help partners easily install and test these connections under controlled conditions to reduce the number of field terminations required after delivery. Power delivery DSX POD makes power delivery seamless with a standard input 800 VDC power design that begins with the electrical input to the core containers and continues through protection, distribution, grounding, rack connections, controls, and telemetry. The reference design defines the power characteristics and interfaces required by the installed AI infrastructure. Partners then engineer the upstream generation, conversion, and regional electrical solution for the customer site. This separation is important because utility conditions, codes, equipment availability, and grid architectures differ across regions. A common interface at the container boundary enables repeatable core designs while preserving flexibility in how ecosystem partners deliver power to each deployment. NVIDIA software can complement the physical design by helping operators manage workloads within available power limits. Policy-driven power control, workload orchestration, and high-fidelity telemetry can help an AI factory convert a fixed power envelope into more productive computing. Liquid cooling Vera Rubin rack-scale systems require coordinated liquid-cooling infrastructure. Within the container, the design covers the plumbing that connects racks to the container cooling interface, including routing, manifolds, isolation, instrumentation, leak detection, pressure integrity, and service access. Partners can assemble, flush, pressure-test, and validate the internal cooling loop at the factory. At the site, they connect the container to prepared water and heat-rejection infrastructure, commission the complete loop, and verify performance under operating conditions. NVIDIA DSX POD changes where integration occurs. It does not eliminate the supporting facility infrastructure. Mechanical design and transportation Shipping high-value rack-scale systems already installed in an enclosure requires a design that treats logistics as an engineering requirement. The container structure, equipment restraints, weight distribution, center of gravity, lifting and handling points, access paths, and transport conditions must work together. The reference design also connects transportation requirements to factory quality gates. Partners inspect the integrated unit before shipment, document its configuration and test status, secure it for transport, and repeat defined checks after arrival. This process helps establish that the system delivered to the site matches the system validated at the factory. Parallelizing factory integration and site preparation The factory-built model changes the deployment sequence. Site teams can prepare land, foundations, power, and external connectivity while partners manufacture and integrate the containers in parallel. At the factory, partners install the rack-scale systems, complete internal cabling and plumbing, integrate controls, load approved configuration baselines, and run functional tests. At the deployment site, construction teams prepare the physical and utility interfaces that the containers require. After delivery, the work focuses on placement, inter-container connections, and hookup to external power, cooling, and networking. Teams then confirm transport integrity, validate the site connections, and complete system commissioning. This model does not remove onsite work. It reduces the amount of complex, repeatable integration performed in the field and moves it into an environment designed for consistent tooling, quality controls, and parallel production. Scaling with standardized deployment units A standardized container architecture gives operators a repeatable unit for planning and expansion. After preparing the supporting site infrastructure, an operator can add compute and supporting capacity using the same defined interfaces and validation process. Standardization also creates a consistent foundation for software optimization. When the underlying compute, network, power, cooling, and telemetry architecture is known software and operational practices for that environment can be tuned easily. Partners can still adapt each implementation to local codes, site conditions, customer requirements, and regional supply chains. This balance is central to NVIDIA DSX POD. The reference design supplies reusable NVIDIA engineering and validation. The ecosystem supplies manufacturing capacity, site expertise, regional engineering, customization, deployment, service, and support. A partner-led delivery model NVIDIA provides the validated AI infrastructure design foundation and works with the ecosystem to prove that rack-scale systems can be integrated, tested, transported, and deployed as repeatable factory-built units. OEMs and ODMs integrate the computing systems. Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and infrastructure specialists adapt power and cooling to the site. Modular solution providers manufacture the enclosures and integrate the subsystems. Site partners prepare the location, complete installation, and support commissioning. Together, these partners turn the reference design into a customer-specific AI factory. The model expands the modular data center market rather than replacing existing offerings. Partners can continue to deliver different levels of integration, from modular infrastructure that customers populate onsite to fully factory-integrated deployments. NVIDIA DSX POD gives the ecosystem a validated path for the latter while preserving room for differentiation in implementation and service. items.raw_text: Data Center / Cloud Achieve Productive AI Capacity Faster and More Predictably with NVIDIA DSX POD Oct 21, 2026 By Premal Savla Like Discuss (1) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA DSX POD is a standardized, factory-built reference design that pre-integrates rack-scale AI infrastructure into containers for validation before shipment. The architecture aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and defines coordinated requirements across compute, networking, storage, power, liquid cooling, cabling, and mechanical design. Factory integration moves complex assembly and testing into a controlled environment while site teams prepare foundations, power, and external connectivity in parallel. Standardized container interfaces enable repeatable capacity expansion and a consistent foundation for software optimization across deployments. NVIDIA provides the validated design foundation while ecosystem partners handle manufacturing, regional engineering, customization, deployment, and support. Next Steps Learn more about the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design to evaluate how it can accelerate AI factory deployment. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more AI factories turn energy into intelligence. But before an AI workload can produce its first token, operators must bring an interconnected system of compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit. In a conventional data center build, teams must first select the site, design power and cooling for the deployment, lay out the data center, and plan and install racks and cables. Then they can validate the network and cluster incrementally and bring service online. This work requires coordinated specialized labor, with critical dependencies among installation, infrastructure readiness, and system testing. Delays can push back bring-up and the date the infrastructure begins producing tokens. NVIDIA DSX POD shifts more of this work into a controlled factory environment. One of multiple AI factory implementation models supported by NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is the standardized, factory-built implementation. It enables partners to build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery. The result is a repeatable approach designed to reduce onsite integration complexity and help operators reach productive AI capacity faster and more predictably. This post explains the foundation of NVIDIA DSX POD, how the reference design aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform , and how NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners work through product engineering, deployment, and support. A design foundation for moving AI factory integration upstream Modular and prefabricated data centers already exist. The engineering challenge for an AI factory extends beyond placing conventional IT equipment in an enclosure. Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, high-speed scale-up and scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software. These elements behave as one system. Their mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must remain within specification during factory integration, transportation, installation, and operation. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the design foundation for partners to install rack-scale systems in containers at the factory, functionally test the integrated unit, transport it, and bring it online safely through repeatable processes at the destination. NVIDIA’s investment spans the engineering disciplines required to make that possible, including rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation. This work extends the progression toward greater factory integration to reduce installation complexity and accelerate deployment. NVIDIA has moved from chips and boards to complete rack-scale systems, and large-scale reference architectures like NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD . NVIDIA DSX POD carries this approach into a factory-built AI factory implementation, moving most component integration from the customer site into a controlled manufacturing environment. The reference design does not make containerization mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional data center construction and onsite-integrated designs remain important options. NVIDIA DSX POD adds a standardized path for large-scale deployments where schedule predictability, repeatability, and reduced onsite work are priorities. Architecture aligned with NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform NVIDIA DSX is the broad design framework for co-designed AI infrastructure. It brings compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, facility controls, and software together at the data center level. Customers and partners can implement that framework in different physical forms. NVIDIA DSX POD is a specific realization of that broader design: a standardized AI factory architecture composed of factory-built container types and defined interfaces between them. The architecture is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and its rack-scale systems. The reference design describes a complete AI factory rather than a compute enclosure in isolation. It accounts for compute, service and management functions, scale-out networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, and other supporting infrastructure. Technical requirements for factory-integrated deployment The central purpose of the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is to make the full deployment process repeatable. That requires coordinated requirements across the following areas: compute integration, networking and storage, cabling and controls, power delivery, liquid cooling, and mechanical design and transportation. Compute integration The NVIDIA DSX POD compute container is designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack scale infrastructure. The design defines how compute and supporting racks fit within the enclosure and how partners address structural support, weight distribution, equipment restraint, service clearances, airflow and liquid-cooling access, rack-level power, and network connectivity. Factory integration also changes the validation boundary. Instead of treating each rack as an independent shipment that will be assembled into a cluster onsite, partners validate the installed compute environment as a deployment unit. The validation plan can cover rack inventory, firmware and configuration baselines, power-on checks, fabric connectivity, sensor operation, cooling integrity, and system-level functional tests before the container leaves the factory. Networking and storage AI workloads depend on predictable movement of model data, training data, checkpoint data, and inference context across the AI factory. The reference design therefore treats networking and storage as part of the system architecture rather than as site-specific additions made after compute arrives. The design defines the connectivity required within a compute container, between containers, and from the modular system to the customer’s external network. It accounts for scale-out fabrics, service and management networks, fiber entry points, trunk cabling, cable routing, labeling, bend radius, service access, and validation of factory-installed link before shipment. Storage requirements follow the same principle. The architecture defines the required capacity, performance, connectivity, management, and service characteristics while allowing the final equipment implementation to reflect the deployment scale and partner solution. This enables storage and networking to arrive as coordinated parts of the AI factory instead of independent systems that must be reconciled late in site integration. Cabling and controls NVIDIA DSX POD reduces the onsite work of cabling in a rack-scale deployment, moving rack-to-rack network cabling, power wiring, control wiring, and sensor integration into the factory wherever practical. The reference design clearly defines cable paths, separation requirements, termination points, labeling conventions, test procedures, and serviceability requirements to help partners easily install and test these connections under controlled conditions to reduce the number of field terminations required after delivery. Power delivery DSX POD makes power delivery seamless with a standard input 800 VDC power design that begins with the electrical input to the core containers and continues through protection, distribution, grounding, rack connections, controls, and telemetry. The reference design defines the power characteristics and interfaces required by the installed AI infrastructure. Partners then engineer the upstream generation, conversion, and regional electrical solution for the customer site. This separation is important because utility conditions, codes, equipment availability, and grid architectures differ across regions. A common interface at the container boundary enables repeatable core designs while preserving flexibility in how ecosystem partners deliver power to each deployment. NVIDIA software can complement the physical design by helping operators manage workloads within available power limits. Policy-driven power control, workload orchestration, and high-fidelity telemetry can help an AI factory convert a fixed power envelope into more productive computing. Liquid cooling Vera Rubin rack-scale systems require coordinated liquid-cooling infrastructure. Within the container, the design covers the plumbing that connects racks to the container cooling interface, including routing, manifolds, isolation, instrumentation, leak detection, pressure integrity, and service access. Partners can assemble, flush, pressure-test, and validate the internal cooling loop at the factory. At the site, they connect the container to prepared water and heat-rejection infrastructure, commission the complete loop, and verify performance under operating conditions. NVIDIA DSX POD changes where integration occurs. It does not eliminate the supporting facility infrastructure. Mechanical design and transportation Shipping high-value rack-scale systems already installed in an enclosure requires a design that treats logistics as an engineering requirement. The container structure, equipment restraints, weight distribution, center of gravity, lifting and handling points, access paths, and transport conditions must work together. The reference design also connects transportation requirements to factory quality gates. Partners inspect the integrated unit before shipment, document its configuration and test status, secure it for transport, and repeat defined checks after arrival. This process helps establish that the system delivered to the site matches the system validated at the factory. Parallelizing factory integration and site preparation The factory-built model changes the deployment sequence. Site teams can prepare land, foundations, power, and external connectivity while partners manufacture and integrate the containers in parallel. At the factory, partners install the rack-scale systems, complete internal cabling and plumbing, integrate controls, load approved configuration baselines, and run functional tests. At the deployment site, construction teams prepare the physical and utility interfaces that the containers require. After delivery, the work focuses on placement, inter-container connections, and hookup to external power, cooling, and networking. Teams then confirm transport integrity, validate the site connections, and complete system commissioning. This model does not remove onsite work. It reduces the amount of complex, repeatable integration performed in the field and moves it into an environment designed for consistent tooling, quality controls, and parallel production. Scaling with standardized deployment units A standardized container architecture gives operators a repeatable unit for planning and expansion. After preparing the supporting site infrastructure, an operator can add compute and supporting capacity using the same defined interfaces and validation process. Standardization also creates a consistent foundation for software optimization. When the underlying compute, network, power, cooling, and telemetry architecture is known software and operational practices for that environment can be tuned easily. Partners can still adapt each implementation to local codes, site conditions, customer requirements, and regional supply chains. This balance is central to NVIDIA DSX POD. The reference design supplies reusable NVIDIA engineering and validation. The ecosystem supplies manufacturing capacity, site expertise, regional engineering, customization, deployment, service, and support. A partner-led delivery model NVIDIA provides the validated AI infrastructure design foundation and works with the ecosystem to prove that rack-scale systems can be integrated, tested, transported, and deployed as repeatable factory-built units. OEMs and ODMs integrate the computing systems. Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and infrastructure specialists adapt power and cooling to the site. Modular solution providers manufacture the enclosures and integrate the subsystems. Site partners prepare the location, complete installation, and support commissioning. Together, these partners turn the reference design into a customer-specific AI factory. The model expands the modular data center market rather than replacing existing offerings. Partners can continue to deliver different levels of integration, from modular infrastructure that customers populate onsite to fully factory-integrated deployments. NVIDIA DSX POD gives the ecosystem a validated path for the latter while preserving room for differentiation in implementation and service. The reference design brings NVIDIA Vera Rubin compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, controls, and validation into one coordinated architecture. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the engineering foundation. Partners build, customize, deliver, and support the resulting solutions.
